The Medical Offizer reported that there had been onts case of scarlet fever at Stockton Heath and one at Appleton. He had received a letter from the head- master of the Church of England school, Norley, re- porting three outbreaks of measles in families attend- ing the school. The writer understood that the disease was prevalent at Weaverham Sandiway and adjoining Stockton Heath's " Plaguti of Dust." parishes where schools had been closed. The Medical Officer was instructed to make inquiries • but not to give an order for the closing of the school unless there was urgent necessity: A NEW BRIDGE. div.head: PARIS MAIL.
div.p: THE PARIS MAIL.
BY ARTHUR W. MARCHMONT, Author of "By Right of Sword," "For Love or Crown," "A Smart Capture," "A King for an Hour," "A Perilous Coincidence," &c.

I think it was the voice that attracted me—deep, resonant, and sonorous even, for a woman, but toned with such an accent of delicate sympathy that it seemed to ease at once the pain of loneliness that was gnawing at my heart. I had just. left home and was on my first :o-riiey alone into the great world of strangers to earn my living. I was going c-art &I be English governess in a family near Paris, and I sat staring biankly away over the steamer's side, straining my eyes to catch a last glimpse of the lights of England and wrestling to keep back the tears, when a hand Wag laid on my shoulder and a voice, with a slight French accent, said: "You are young to be travelling alone, my child, and seem in trouble." I turned at the sound and found a, Sister of Mercy beside me looking out of the murky night into my face. The voice was so full of sympathy that my heart was touched; and, after a few minutes, I began to tell her my very simple story. She sat down by my side, and the mere telling of my little woes of loneliness seemed to comfort me. She did not say much herself, but just put in a word of soothing comfort now and again, and ze led me gradually to talk about the home I had left, the people I was going t'o, and any subject that came uppermost, meaning, as I saw, to draw away my thoughts from my sorrow. She said she was known as Sister Marie, and when she told me she was going through Paris to her home at Orleans, the Convent of the Sacred Heart, I asked her to let me travel with her. The boat was very crowded, and on my other side sat a man for whom I had conceived an instinctive dislike. His face was sallow, dark, hairy, and cadaverous, with bushy eyebrows and blask beard. I had caught him. looking at me several tiThes with

an expression that angered me. A little reflection made me regret, therefore, my lack of caution in speaking so freely in his hearing to the nun about my plans. Presently he began to try and join in the con- versation, and his accent shewed me that he was a foreigner also. He spoke in a high-pitched, thin, half-cracked voice. I snubbed him, and either pretended not to hear or answered sharply and shortly; but he persisted, until I asked the Sister to move to another seat. "The boat is very full, miss. If you leave your seat you will not find another," said the man, over- hearing my request. "Let us try, Sister," I said, pretending not to hear him. "I would go if I could, but I fear that what this gentleman says is true, we should not find another place, and, alas! I cannot stand for long. But go, my child, if you would." I was unwilling to lose her companonship, how- ever, and thus remained where I was and would not see the little smile of triumph which he gave. "You see my advice is best," he said. "I do not like .this man, Sister," I whispered. "Let me change seats with you. lam afraid of him." • "Willingly, child," she assented; and when we had changed places and I felt safer for having her as a buffer between me and the man, she added: "But let me give you a word of warning. You have your way to make in the world. Be careful not to judge by appearances, and neither trust nor mistrust at sight. It may lead you into sserious mistakes." "I cannot help my instincts," I answered, and added, laughing: "I trusted you instinctively.' "That is different, child. I am—well, what my dress denotes, and glad always to offer the sympathy which my religion and my calling bid me offer to the friendless." "It is a noble calling, Sister," said the man. "No calling is of itself noble, sir, except it is made noble by those who follow it. And the best of us can but do our duty." "Your young friend is suspicious," he said. "A bad thing in a young girl." "My little friend is inexperienced, sir, and that is saying everything that need be said about her. The rebuke was simply spoken, and, with such quiet dignity that it had its effect upon fhe man for the time. Evidently the Sister had not the same opinion of he man as I had, and • she appeared rather to encourage him to speak to us, so that before, we had reached Calais they had had more than one little discussion. At Calais I hoped to shake him off and tried to lose him in the hurry of getting off the boat; but he refusei• to be lost, and as Sister Marie could not move qui- Vy: he hung about close to my heels in a way that disrated rue. I wished she would have sent him iihout hi business, but she said he might be of use. as he seemed an experienced traveller. On that I myself gave him a broad hint. "You .will want to see about your luggage, &skim I will not detain you," I said. "I have no luggage more than my bag here," he replied, with a smile that to me was unpleasantly familiar. "Mine was a sudden business summons. Permit me that offer you and the Sister some coffee or bouillon? Everybody takes it here while we wait for the train to start.' I gave a curt refusal ; but to my chagrin- Sister Marie was much more complaisant. "I must have some, my dear Miss Wilmott. I cannot do the whale journey without something of the kind." And thereupon we bent to the buffet, the man keeping close to my side. I did not like the position at all. I had been warned of the dangers of trayelling alone, and it seemed to me very suspicious that the man should be travelling without luggage. I had nothing of any value on me, but I was afraid of him and kept as close to the g..md Sister as possible, refusing to hear the silly compliments which he whispered now and again into my ear. 'The noise and !,onfusion in the refreshment-room bewildered me and rather added to my fright. At first the man pressed me, to have some wine, and I had to be positively rude to him before lie would accept my refusal. I would not touch a thing. I was longing for a cup of coffee tea, but I would not accept it in his hands; and when he had ordered the bouillon for himself and the Sister, and had left us for a minute, I told my companion what I wanted and she sent me to get it. This was not an easy matter in such a crowd, and when I returned to the table with it in my hand the two had nearly finished their soup and 1. Id only time to swallow my coffee hastily before the cry came for us to take our seats, and lie I had to flurry out.

my great annoyance the man insisted upon travailing in the same compartment, and this again increased My suspicions. He was a rather shahljily- dressed man with no luggage, yet was going on by the mail, first-class, and it was with a feeling approaching consternation that I saw the guard was waiting for him holding the door of a carriage open which had apparently been reserved for us three. ' I hesitated a moment before getting in and looked about for another compartment. "Is there no room .elsewhere ? " I asked the guard, who smiled at my school-made French and shrugged his shoulders, not understanding me. "I would rather not travel with him, Sister," I said, protesting. But her smile was so indidgent and expressive of such good-natured 'astonishment at my reluctance that it made we feel half-ashamed of my youthful_awkwarduess.

"CittiCkly, if you please," said the guard, impatiently. "My friend would rather find another carriage." "There is no time by this train ; we are starting this moment. Will the good Sister wait for the next train."
"I cannot," she said. "But you do as you please, Miss Wilmott," and without more ado she

got into the carriage. Thinking I should be safe with her and knowing ' that I was to be met by the mail train at Paris I ! followed, and the,rnan had barely time to spring in after me when the train started and we were off, . with only one stop, at Amiens, until we reached Paris. I liked the man's obnduct much less in the . carriage than ever. ; The Sister settled herself easily in a corner with • her back to the engine and told me she was going to sleep, and Foliose the seat opposite hr. Ths

man tjok the corner on the sanie.side as my com- panion at the opposite end of the carriage, and ' very soon after the train 4tarled his behaviour began to cause me great concern. It was as though i he had been drinking and 4.tie effects had become suddenly apparent. He lurched and flopped noout in his seat, nodded and rolled as the train moved; and then, with a great effort, he would pull himself together and stare alternately at me and the Sister who was soon sleeping placidly in ber corner,

This Cu frightened me that I tried to wake her, kicking her feet secretly not to attract the man's attention. But my kicking had no effect, except to cause the sleeper to move uneasily ana snore softly. Attracted by one of these snores the man, who had been lolling back against the cushions with his head fallen forward on his chest, started, and making one of his efforts for self-control looked up and across at her with a long, drunken stare. gradually toppling sideways until he rested on his arm, his wbol body swaying fatuously. Then he looked from HI Sister across to me and smirked repulsively as he jerked his head in her direction and asked: "Is she asleep ? " and he lolled, blinking blearilT at me, waiting for my answer. When I said nothing—f::at in my fright., I leant back in my seat and pretended to sleep—he made a big effort to stand up as if to come, to me, muttering some- thin.' I could not make out. If ho came near me I meant to scream and wake the Sister; and I watched him through the narrow slits of my nearly closed lids with a vigilance inspired by the fever of terror which set my heart thumping violently against my ribs, and my pulses beating until the throbbing almost shook my frame with its vehemence. But, to my infinite relief, he could not succeed in rising. The smirk on his face changed to an expression of intense effort, and at the close he sank back in his corner again, breathing heavily 49 if after great exertion. After he had sat n minute or two in this way, he took a note-book from his pocket, and began to write a few sentences laboriously, with great effort and many stoppages. More than once during the writing his head fell now forward on his chest now back against the carriage, as though his drunken sleep had mastered him, and when it was finished he tore the page from the book and read over what he had written, glancing at me frequently tho while.

Then he fumbled in his pocket and took out something, which, to my horror, I saw was a revolver, laid it down on the side furthest from me, azd stopped to think. his fingers playing with the revolver, while his eyes kept wandering from me to . the sleeping woman, his expression all the time furtive, haggard, and half-besotted. I began to fear now that he was worse than _ _

drunk, and a victim to some kind of madness; and the thought that we two women were alone in the carriage at his mercy and that he was armed in this way with the means of killing us, heightened my terror until it was well-nigh-unbearable. Every time I found his eyes upon me I turned cold with fear, and I ransacked my memory for such tags and scraps of knowledge how to deal with the insane as I had heard of or read. But nothing I could think of seemed to have the remotest application to such a crisis as this; and I continued to feign sleep in the one yearning hope that by this means he might be led to take no notice. But this was a vain hope, indeed; for presently he looked more earnestly than ever at me, and then beckoned to me to go to his end of the carriage. His gesture, at first merely earnest and entreating, became insistent, urgent and peremptory, as I paid no heed but kept glued to my seat, while I strove to make my breathing deep and regular like tbst of a sleeper. When I made no response he groaned, and I Aaw his hand go stealing back to his revolver, which he half raised as he glanced across this time at the sleeping Sister, his face dark and threatening, and his lips muttering. But just as I was on the point of rousing the sleeper with a cry of alarm, he laid the weapon down again and turned to me once more.

Then he, slowly unwound from his neck a silk handkerchief, and, gathering all his energies for a great effort, he gripped the arm of the seat, rose, and came towards us unsteadily, staggering and lurching and rolling as the train jerked and bumped in its rapid course. He was holding the kerchief in his hand, and I noticed, to my surprise and intense relief, that he had left the revolver in the corner. When he reached us he stood, holding on to the luggage-rack and leering like one dazed in the Sister's face for a moment. Apparently satisfied with his scrutiny of her, he turned and looked down on me. I kept my eyes all but shut, but he seemed to know I was awake; and I thought now that his face wore a different expression.

"For Heaven's sake f" he whispered. His voice was very indistinct between his stertorous breath- ing, but yet had an accent of entreaty. Then, in a louder tone: "The good Sister sleeps ? " and he laid the white handkerchief over her face and lurched forward until he stood between her and me. "For Heaven's sake, read!" he sailp, putting the paper on my lap. "Read." he urged again, when I lusitated.

I took it then, though almost too frightened to understand it, and while he stood there holding on to the luggage-rack, swaying and staggering and breathing heavily, I rtl,d as follows: • "Help me, ?or He*yen's sake I have been drugged or poisoned. lam Ambrose Goreau, 28, Rue d'Epiciennes, Paris; I have twenty thousand pounds worth of diamonds in my bag and concealed about me. I am either dying or ':;ave been drugged, and shall be robbed if you don't help. It will ruin me. I svepect the Sister is a man disguised. A revolver is on my seat. Get it before lam ;sensible."

A fewful birch which the man gave nearly brought him in a heap to the ground, and hc stumbled and crawled and pulled himself back tc his seat, and lolled there inert and helpless, ane fast growing unconscious. What did it mean ? What should I do?
The tables were now turned with a vengeance. I the Frenchman was right, who was the pretende., Sister Marie? What a position was mine! _
With an effort the -Frenchman held up tho revolver to shew it me.

moved as if uneasily, and then, looking stealthily at the apparently sleeping nun, got up to change my seat. I fancied that the head of the sleeper turned slightly as if to follow my move- ment, and this decided me.

I went to the other side of the compartment, and, standing so that my action could not be seen, took the revolver and put the man's bag on to the seat behind me. As I did so, he fell back with a low moan, utterly unconscious. The moments of suspense that followed were the most trying of my life. I was waiting for the nun to move, and trying to think what to do. I sat with my eyes fixed on the still figure at the other end of the carriage, and my heart beat so fast that it pained me; my lips were hot and dry, and my tongue glued to the roof of my mouth, while my breath came and, went in quick, short gasps of terror. I felt like a terrible coward, and knew I should faint if this strain continued. It was thus a distinct relief when at length the sleeper slimed signs of awaking. She gave a deer sigh, stretched out hands and feet as if yawning, and then took the Frenchman's kerchief from her face, and sat up, stretched again, and cast one subtle, swift glance at me, masking it instantly with a smile.

The crisis was evidently at hand, and I should soon know the worst -now. I was still quite incapable of thinking what to do. My mind seemed paralysed, indeed, with the terror of anticipation. I sat staring at. her and fingering the revolver, which I had concealed in a fold of my dress. 1 was afraid of it. I had never handled such a thing before, and I dreaded lest it should explode and hurt me, and I held it gingerly in lingers that trembled violently. The Sister did not speak, and for a time shewed no intention even to leave hr seat. As I stared at the face I found myself wondering fearsomely whether it was the face 4g. a man or a woman, but it was impossible to determine. The light in the carriage was but dim, -the broad wMte fillet across the brow, the bands under the chin, the quaint, voluminous headgear defied eay efforts to guess the riddle. But the fact that she must see the condition of the Frenchman and yet put no question about him, heightened my suspicions; and then I noticed something which seemed to confirm all my worst fears.

I detected some stealthy movements beneath the ample black cloak, and instinctively jumped to the conclusion that the dress was a disguise, that the Sister was indeed a man, and that he was making I ready to thr.ow off the cloak to execute his sinister purpose. Thia thought seemed to reuse my numbed wits. If I was to do anything, I. nmst do it now; and a glance at the huddled-up corin of the unconscious Frenchman nerved me to act. I felt what my fate would be if his suspicions vo•e correct. At that instant I thought o stopping the train by Means of the communicartion-cord, and blamed my sluggish wits that the simple expedient had not occurred to me before. Taking a tighter grip of the pistol in one band, I grasped the window-strap with the other to carry out the purpose. "Sit still. Move a tihger, and I'll lodge a bullet in your brain." The "Sister's" voice raw, out now clear and stern, and I wondered bow lcould ever have found it .aympathetio and kind, or mistaken it for a woman's. It was harsh and terrorising. But sit still I could not.
The man appeared to be in difficulties with the Dloak, and wv ,—kable to throw it off, and his

Lands were hidden away beneath it. I felt that I might as well be killed standing up and making an effort as sitting still, so I caught the strap, let the window down with a rush, and, thrusting the revolver out into the night, I fired two shots as quickly as I could, and then groped for the corn- muniration-cor4,

Before I could find it, however, I felt myself pulled violently away from the window, thrown back on to the seat of the carriage, the man tower- ing over me, his eyes ablaze with rage and menace. "Another sound, if you dare. Keep still, and no harm will happen to you." _ _ _

Nothing came 'O-f my I:evolver shooting, and I let the weapon fall on the seat of the carriage. I think I half fainted. Tho lights seemed to turn dim, everything appeared to be suddenly far away, and it was thiough a haze, like a dream, that I watclled the man—a lithe, athletic, clean- shaven, determined-looking young fellow—as he bent down and examinee the Frenchman to see whether he was dead. Then he began, to turn out his pockets, and feel all over his clothes, cutting through them here and there in an eager search. Whatever he sought he -failed to find, and I heard the muttered curses rolling fast and furiously from between his thin, tightly-pressed lips. Suddenly a loud and vehement oath broke from him. He stood up and listened. To my inexpressi- ble delight the train was slowing down, and he thrust his head out of the window to ascertain the cause.

As he did this a-very happy thought occurred to me. Taking the Frenchman's bag I hid it swiftly and stealthily under the cloak in the corner where the "Sister had been feigning sleep. That was the last place he would look for it, and when he drew in his head I pretended that I too had lost consciousness.

I believed that saved my life. The train was rapidly coming to a standstill when he cried, furiously: "Where's that bag?" I lay white, still, helpless and flaccid. He hauled me from the seat, searched the place, felt even in my pockets; shook me, bawling the question in my ear; struck me, and even threw me against the back and sides of the carriage. This was partly rage and partly his desire to rouse me. Then he hunted all round about the foreigner, and under the seats; and when he found nothing— for it never occurred to him to look under his own cloak—his oaths were frightful. The train drew to a standstill and he was like a wild beast at bay. He stood over us both with his back to the window, which he had pulled up, his intention being to try and keep anyone from coming into the carriage while the train stood. Then I heard the sound of windows being let down and voices calling to ask the reason of the delay, and someone answered that the signal was against us.

-That was my opportunity. Finding the revolver close.to my hand I sprang up suddenly, clutched at him with all my strength, and fired the weapon through the closed window_; and then sent up scream after scream till lie, struck me down and silenced me. But I had beaten him.

The nest instanbkhe had sprung from the carriage into the night, just as some people came running up and clambered on to the foot-board on my side in answer to my cries for help. The instant my story was told a hue and cry was raised in pursuit of the scoundrel, while a doctor who was travelling on the train came to the assistance of my fellow-traveller. When we reached Amiens, the news was awaiting iis that the man had been caught and recognised as a most daring and original railway thief for whose capture a big reward was offered by the company; and I had the supreme satisfaction a little later of helping to secure his conviction and sentence to a long term at the galleys. More than that, a lame share of the reward was allotted to me, while the firm whose diamonds my easy device of throwing the bag under the thief's own clothes had saved, made up the amount to a really large SUM One point remained. _

Among Canaries the Lancashire Coppy is the giant and the London Fancy Canary the dwarf. A good Coppy has fetched as much as thirty guineas, and the art of breeding is an engrossing pursuit, making great calls on the skill of fanciers. In a talk with a " Sun " representative, Miss Burgess,. sister of a London Canary enthusiast, whose room was full of cages, said that there were times when the work of feeding and caring for them had been too much for her:. "It was about two years ago," she explained, "and if I had not taken Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people I do not know what would have become of me. div.head: TRADES HD LABOUR COUNCIL.
div.p: TRADES HD LABOUR COUNCIL.

Discussion on Educational MattErs, THE SUGGESTED LABOUR CANDIDATE. The monthly meeting of the \V:;rrington Trades and Labour Council was held in 80ld-street ‘Vesleyan schools on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. Podmore, jun„ presiding over a small attendance. CORPORATION CONTRACTS. The SECRETARY (Councillor Stott) referred to Councillor Maginn's motion re the acceptance of the lowest tender which was brought forward at the last Town Council meeting. He. pointed out that the motion did not materially affect the acceptance of tenders, and did not in any way affect the inclusion of the fair wages elause in all Corporation contracts. Therefore he (Councillor Stott) did not object to it. Had Coun- cillor Maginn proceeded with his original intention, which was undoubtedly to have the fair wage clause deleted,he (Councillor Stott) would have most strongly opposed him. Mr. SMITH thought the action of the Trades Council in regard to the matter had frightened Councillor Magma out of his original intention. Councillor STOTT was accorded a vote of thanks for his work in connection with Messrs. Rhodes' and Sons' contract for pails and ashbins. Mr. SMITH said that at one time he heard it said on many sides that Councillor Stott was in the wrong. Since their last meeting' when Mr. Webb, the general secretary of the Iron and Steel Plate Workers' Union, addressed them, he thoight the views of many persons had changed. 'Councillor STOTT said that although his action might not have had much effect in Warrington it had done a great deal of good to workers in the iron and steel plate industry. Several firms ,had so arranged their conditions of labour that they could now be regarded as" fair," and the employees of one firm in ' particular had, without exception, promised to join the Union. He had received a letter from the National Amalgamated Iron and Steel Plate Workers' Union asking the Council to do all they could to see that the fair wage clause was inserted in all Corporation con- tracts for sanitary pails,ashbins, &c. In conclusion the letter stated : "'The objectionable system of sweating which has been practised during recent years on this class of work in our trade we are most desirous of stamping out, .and we feel confident that, with your Council's kind assistance together with that of your labour member in opposing these contracts being given to unfair firms, we can successfully accomplish our object." THE HOUSING OP THE WORKING CLASSES.

Councillor STorr, as delegate to the meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Trades and La- bour Councils, Presented a report of the proceedings. One important matter under discussion, he said, was .the housing of the working classes. Last Sunday he was passing along several streets•in Warrington, .and the need for housing reform was never so greatly impressed upon him as it was then. (Hear, hear). The report was adopted. EDUCATIONAL MATTERS DISCUSSED.

The COUNCIL then proceeded to discus S the report r,- cently presented by Mr. E. Plinston on the work of the Education Committee during the past twelve months. Councillor SToTT pointed out that at the beginning of last year it was estimated that the income from school fees would be about £l,ooo—or equal to about a one penny rate. They would see from the financial statement issued at the close of the year's work, I hat that estimate was considerably lower than the amount actually received, as the income from school fees was something like £3,000, or equal to a 3d. rate. There- fore, if they made education absolutely free in the town, it would cost considerably more than he sugges- ted some time ago. He should certainly claim free seats for his children if he had any goipgto sehool, and ihe thought that if workingmen only knew t was possible to claim free education, many more would do so. Mr. RANDLES asked whether schoolboys were allowed at the present time to go to the baths at a reduced rate.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST.

At the time of writing the West is once snore in uncertainty as to affairs in the East. Again Vie cable has been "interrupted" accord- ing to the official announcement, which deceives nobody. That is to say, it is an open secret that the Japanese Government as our own government did several times during the late Boer War, siezes the cable and witholds all -news till such time as it is convenient to themselves to announce the results of any strategic movements officially and in detail. Anyhow it is certain that these official "interuptions" are never followed by any repairs to the cable itself! The last occasion Upon which the British Government monopo- lised the cable was to cover Mahon's dash upon Mafeking : but it has teen a common feature of the present war. All that is cer- tain is that the Japanese are slowly and surely dosing in their lines of investment 'round Port Arthur and are preparing for an

div.head: MARQUIS YAMAGATA.
div.p: MARQUIS YAMAGATA.

linmediate assault on the fortress, which may ilow take place any day, if it has not already done so: and the conviction is grow- ing upon every side that, though the cost "will be very heavy, the assault will be suc- cessful in elle teeth of all axioms of modern Tailitary science. Another conviction which as growing is that practically all the present movements and dispositions of the Japanese arinies have been prepared at headquarters n Japan and are controlled directly by a "Committee of Defence," presided over ~.13Y the Mikado himself, with Field-Marshal -Marquis Yamagata as chief military adviser. And now it is rumoured that the latter, all the embarkations and dispositions of the troo ps having been successfully cfrried • out, 4s to take the field at once in supreme corn- and of all the armies, which will report direct to him. and be controlled under the one head, thereby acting in unison upon a 'oncerted plan.

div.head: OPEN GOLF CHAMPIONSHIP,
div.p: OPEN GOLF CHAMPIONSHIP,

The Open Golf Champion for he year is ,lack White, of Sunningdale, this honour oeing earned by brilliant plaT, in which he defeated James Braid and J. H. Taylor by one stroke. The issue hung in the balance light up to the last putt of both Braid and Taylor on the home green. Each had a chance of tieing with White if he brought °ff a ten yards' putt, but both just missed the hole. It was soon obvious tha , laSt Year's champion—Harry Vardon—was out of it, and that the winner had to be looked for a• long such men as Braid, Tom Vardon, and white and the others who had been bunched behind him. The concluding stage of the tneeting wilt probably go down in golf history as having furnished the most extra- ordinary finish in a chamiponship tourney. When Harry Vardon had utterly failed in tile morning and James Braid had, on the her hand, put in a 69 for the third round, 'wtre seemed a good chance for the latter.

JACK WHITE. 'l3ut Jack White came in soon after three O'clock with a 69, which meant that Brad had in the last round to do at least another 69 to retain his position at the head of the list. He reached the last tee with 9nly three left in which to do a good 4 hole In order to tie.. His drive was superb, and lay Sixty yards from the green. He ap- proached just a little too strongly, however, and went beyond the hole by twelve yards. ;le in3t missed this long putt and was down a 4. The finish vas quite 'a dramatic one. When Taylor carefully surveying his position, !llade the final stroke the excitement was 11tense. The ball travelled straight, momen- tarily hung on the lip of the hole, and , ted a few inches beyond. Notwith- standing he had failed he was enthusiastically eocteered, for he had done the round in the Pen Championship record of 68. The rloaner's golf was so beautifully true that he dcilt himself little to do on the green, so fjnafdlY were his approaches. His card was: 4. 4,3, 4,2, 3,5, 3, 4-31 ; home: 4,5, 4,4, 4,4, 4-37 . total, 69.

ARCHDUKE FREDERICK OF AUSTRIA'S VISIT. since King Edward's accession London has a.°llstantly been visited by foreign royalties, . the latest of these was the Archduke r.euerick of Austria, who came over to ~13resent his cousin, the old Emperor of b,:tria, and to invest King Edward with his 43n as a Field-Marshal in the Austrian 3'• It had been hoped that the Em- or Francis Joseph would have been able return in person the visit of the King to

_ REDERICK OF AUSTRIA. Ot - last autumn and that of the Prince hear,,ales this spring, but his age and his tryi,'4 did not allow of the long journey and Fre-r7g round of festivities. The Archduke tveriek, a vivacious and grizzled little mr Wed,an eye-glass, arrived at Victor' by 'esday in the afternoon and wa.. Prince of Wales and the Duk ..sizigiZa",..ught, with whom he drove to Buck- Palace. He was received at the •I,—elgres entrance by the King and Queen '-rson. and in the evening their Majesties
UKE

gave a dinner-party to their royal gneatti which was followed by a visit to the Operg to hear "Die Meistersinger." On the follow- ing day the investiture took place at the Palace in the morning, and in return King Edward conferred upon the Archduke the Military Grand Cross of the Bath. In the afternoon a visit was paid to the Military Tournament, which delighted the Archduke immensely, and in the evening a State banquet was given in his honour at Bucking- ham Palace. It was followed by a concert in the Picture Gallery under the direction of Signor Paolo Tosti, and amongst the per- formers were Madame Melba, Signor Caruso and little Franz Vecsey, the boy violinist. On Friday the Archduke, accompanied by the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Con- naught, reviewed the First Army Corps at Alderkhot under Sir John Femch on Laffan's Plain, which afforded a very brilliant spectacle, especially in the march past. In the even- ing the Archduke Frederick dined at Marl- borough House, and afterwards a State Ball was given at Buckingham Palace in his honour. He left Charing Cross the next morning at ten for Vienna after a short but very busytvisit.

The latest addition to the glorious role of V.C.'s, the heroes of the Army, is Lieutenant Clement Leslie Smith, of the .Duke of Corn- wall's Light Infantry, who won the little bronze cross which means so much to a soldier in the recently concluded Somali campaign. The notification was published
in the 'Gazette"
last week, and it
indeed a
thrilling act of bravery which
won the Cross.

div.head: LIEUT. C. L. SMITH
div.p: LIEUT. C. L. SMITH
and endeavour--
ed to carry him

out of action. The orderly was, however, again struckand killed by a second bullet, and the two officers found themselves surrounded by der- vishes. In the hand-to-hand fight Dr. Well- and Was wounded, but Lieutenant Smith 4tuck grimly to him, endeavouring to carry .I.im back to the lines. He, too, was struck again and killed; but the young subaltern seemed to bear a charmed life, and, after emptying his revolver into the enemy, reached his men unharmed. Mr. Smith is a son of Canon Clement Smith, of Whipping, the par- ish church of Osborne, in the Isle of Wight, where the late Queen Victoria used, when in residence, to worship regularly. He entered the Army four years ago, joining the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry, and was soon pro- moted to a full lieutenancy while serving on the staff. At the outbreak of the Somaliland affair he was sent out as a special service )fficer.

div.head: QUEEN VICTORIA MEMORIAL HALL FOR INDIA.
div.p: QUEEN VICTORIA MEMORIAL HALL FOR INDIA.

It must be gratifying to all that sub- 3tantial progress is being made with the great Indian memorial to Queen Victoria at Calcutta. It is only three years since the project was raised, when it then was decided it should take the shape of a great marble hall to be known as the Victoria Hall, and be erected on the Calcutta Maidan. It is to serve primarily as a monument to the great Empress Queen, and in the second place as a national gallery and Valhalla for the Indian Empire. n is being built with the subscriptions of the Princes and the people, the European and the Native communities of India, and the money began at once to pour in. Within the space of three months thirty-four lakhs of rupees ( 227,000) were raised, and the fund now exceeds £350,000. So munificent were the offers of some of the Indian Princes—the Maharaja of Kashmir, for instance, offered fifteen lakhs, the Maharaja of Gwalior ten,

INDIA'S MEMORIAL TO HER EMPRESS. and the Maharaja of Jaipur five—that the Viceroy was compelled to suggest a curtail- ment, and fixed the limit at one lakh. The Victoria Hall is estimated to cost £300,000, and will be of pure white marble in the Italian Renaissance style of architecture. It will stand upon a terrace six or seven feet high, extending in some forty feet in width _lnnings declared. At present the country is domi- nated by Rais- uli, a notorious brigand, who levi es blackmail on every side, an d captures prisoners, whom he holds up to ransom. Only a. few months ago he kid- napped Mr. Harris, the " Times' " cor- respondent; and now in Mr. Per- dicarris he has seized the most eminent Europ- ean in Morocco. In this case he has not only demanded a large ransom, but has laid down certain condi- tions which will leave him practically auto- crat of a large slice of. Morocco, and to these demands the Sultan has found himself forced to yield. The Powers, however, have not bound themselves to let matters rest, America especially holding out, and Raisuli rurip a grave risk of finding himself at loggerheads with an irresistible combination of the chief nations of the world in consequence of his latest action. Muley Ahmed el Raisuli is a man of about forty, of splendid physique and excellent education, and, like many of his predecessors, imagines himself an Ishmael with a grudge against life and his fellow-men. Coming of a good family, he took to petty larceny at an early age; and, meeting with success, Raisuli soon blossomed out into a larger line of business, encouraged particu- larly by escaping from prison by means of a bribe. Following this up, he subsidised the governor of his district and looted with im- punity for years, until he fell foul of the Europeans and was taken prisoner by guile. For six years he was kept at the convict ;ettlement at Mogador, until by dint of whole- ;ale bribery he was freed two years ago. ;ince then he has resumed his brigandage on far larger scale, showing the utmost resent- aft and desire for revenge; and his two .ars' record of murder, pillage, incendiarism, .....attle-lifting, and kidnapping s a very seri- JUS one. His latest exploit seems to be the zlimax of his career, and it is hoped that it will lead to his downfall in the near future.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS Education Expanditura.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS Education Expanditura.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at, Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. A. R. Norman pre- siding. There were also present :—A lmiral J. P. Jones Parry, Messrs. C. Roylance, J. Bolshaw, H. Eves, J. Whitlow, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, J. T. Collier, S. Woodward, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton, C. Horton, J. Fryer, J. Spruce, \V. M. Morris, J. J. Lea, J. W. Temperley, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. Moan- field, A. G. Guest, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), T. Cook, J. Riley and W. R. de Prez (relieving officers) and J. Cunnah (master).
A NEW MEMBER.

The Clerk reported that a pall was taken at Frodsham Lordship on Saturday for a Guardian and District Councillor. and resulted as follows :—John Henry Davies, 130; John Dabson, 81. Mr. Davies was there- fore elected.

div.head: TRAINING OF BOYS.
div.p: THE TRAINING OF BOYS.

The Clerk read a letter from the" Wellesly " training ship, North Shields, enclosing list of charges and stating that boys from 11 to 14 years were trained until 16 for the Royal Navy Mercantile Marine or Royal Navy Band School, and that boys from 6to 11 were trained in Green's Home, South Shields, for transference to the shin " Wellesly " at 12 years. The Clerk said the terms were practically the same as those upon which the Board already sent boys to the "Indefatigable." He presumed that the Board would not desire to change. The Board did not deem it desirable to depart from the present system.

PROTEST AGAINST EXCESSIVE EDUCATION EXPENDITURE. A letter was read from the Wirral Union enclosing the following protest and inviting the Runcorn Board to pass a similar resolution: "Resolved that a protest be made to the County Council against excessive expenditure under the Education Act and Particularly as regards salaries and school buildings. Some buildings of asuit- able character will, no doubt, have to be provided, but in the opinion of the Guardians there is no need for the elaborate and costly buildings erected in some parts of the' district." Mr. Woodward asked if it would not be us well to refer the letter to the Education Committee. If he might speak for that committee, he was sure their sympathies were entirely with the opinion ex- pressed-in the letter. They did not know much in that district of the extraordinary cost of elaborate buildings for they had not built any. With reference to the gen- eral question of salaries, they were following on the lines of every other place of which he knew, and the difficulty was to start a lower scale. If they could have a system by which the payments should be generally comparatfve, he was quite sure the committee would be in favour of the suggestion offered in the letter. It seemed to him that the best thing would be to refer the matter to the Education Committee.
rhe Chairman pointed out that the letter was ad- dressed to the Board of Guardians.
The Clerk said the Educatiqn Committee had nothing to do with the Board.
Mr. tVoodwa,rd : I propose that we express our sym- pathy with the object of the communication. Mr. Spruce se3onded,and the motion was agreed to. _ THE _EXTENSION OF THE WATER. SUPPLY. _

The Clerk produced art agreement with Messrs. E. Timmins and Sons, Ltd., for the connecting of the water mctin to the Workhouse so that a supply will be available for fire etw tinishing p3rpose3. The expen- diture will be .£49 13s. 'lod.
The Council ordered the agreement to be sealed. FINANCIAL.

Mr. Woodward reported that at the List meeting there was a balance in hand of £3,364 10s. 7d. The re. ceipts during the fortnight amounted to £345, and the cheques payable that day totalled £l4B us. 7d., leaving a balance of £3,560 19s. The following parishes had not yet paid the first call which was due on May 12th : Acton Grange, Alvanlev, Aston, Bartington, Budworth, Frodsham, Grappenhall, Halton. Flelsby, Keckwick. Kingsley, Moore, Newton-by-Pro'cisharn,Norley,Preston- o'-th'-Elill, Sutton, Wilton Inferior, and Whitley Superior. Str3tton, Appleton,and Crawley had escaped by the skin of their teeth, the call being paid on the previous day. He moved that the usual application be made to the defaulting townships for immediate payment. • The Chairman remarked that the list was exception- ally long. • The proposition was carried. THE WANT OF TELEPHONIC COMMUNICATION WITH TETE HOUSE.

The Visiting Committee recomtheaded t'ae appoint- ment of Nurse Rhoda Bottomley at a salary of £3O per annum with uniform, rations, &c. In moving the confirmation of the minutes, Mr. Spruce said the Medical Officer had again called atten- tion to the want of telephonic communication with the House. 'fiat was an old subject, but the committee had passed a resolution that the Master be instructed- to mike further inquiries as there was an impression that better terms could now be arranged with the Tele- phone Company. The committee was of the opinion that it would be a great advantage if a second hydrant coal I be fixed near the engine house to be used in case of fire.

Mr. C. E. Linker, jun., slid he was at present in communication with the Telephone Company with the object of obtaining several connection with Sutton. He would also endeavours to arrange terms for the Workhouse.

Mr. Woodward said the matter was very important and should be attended to at as early a date as possible. He was sorry that the negotiations in the first instance fell through. He hoped that if there was the slightest possibility of gaining this much-needed improvement, the Board would immediately take steps to do so. Mr. Spruce pointed out that owing to the lack of telephonic communication an old man of about seventy had recently to he removed from the Workhouse to Frodsham at one o'clock in the morning. The Clerk was instructed to make application to the Telephone Company through the proper channel. It was also decided that the clerk should obtain an estimate for the extension of the water main and the provision of a second hydrant near the engine house.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. The Working Clause and its _Proposed Abolition.

Representatives of clubs constituting the Northern Rugby Union met in strong force on Tuesday night at the George Hotel, Huddersfield, on the occasion of the annual meeting of the Union. The chief item discussed was a proposal to abolish the working clause of the professional laws, which stipulates that players shall have, and keep in bona-fide employment. Upon this subject Yorkshire and Lancashire are very much divided but after an interesting discussion the meeting agreed that in the interests of the game the restriction was necessary unless players were, at the end of their career to become loafers. Mr. R. Collinge, of Rochdale (President of the Union), was in the chair.

The annual report and balance-sheet,•e:xtracts from which have already appeared in the Press, were formally a.dopted,on the motion of Mr. Taylor (Wiaan), seconded by Mr. Gresty (Broughton Rangers.) Next came the usual discussion of the by-laws. First the method of governing the Union came under review, and strong protests were again made by the representa- tives of the Salford and Swinton clubs against the pre- sent plan of selecting the Committee. Mr. Walrnsley (Salford), who proposed the deletion of the existing rule on the subject, argued that it was not fair that some clubs should have representation on the Committee and that others should not. All clubs alike ought to have a share in the management. His object was that a Sub-Committee should be formed to revise the by- laws, providing for the election of a Committee of a representative character, such revision to be submitted to a special general meeting of the Union to be held at an early_ date.

Mr. Worthington (Swinton Club), in seconding, de- clared that the present method of electine. the Com- mittee was unsound, unbusinesslike, and undemocratic. The resolution was, however, lost, 31 voting for it and 27 against. Oldham and District League proposed,and the Salford Club seconded, another proposal which would have the Union governed by3o members, the founders having one , representative each so long as they remained in the front rank of Rugby football,andtho remaining 12 seats being distributed amongst the other members of the Union. This was, however, lost, a Committee of 30 being regarded as too large :!;r1 By a narrow vote the meeting passed a resolution substituting a two-thirds majority in place of a three- fourths majority, as being necessary to effect a change in the by-laws. SNIALLER COUNTIES AND THEIR, FUTURE. On behalf of the Union CO rll nittee, qr. Lister (Brad- ford) proposed that By-law 15 should be altered to read —"Any Union, League, or Combination of clubs in membership of the Northern Rugby Football Union, shall be under the authority of the Union, and shall be required at its formation to submit for confirmation the rules of such union, league, or combination, and subsequent alteration to such rules to the said Union Committee. A county union shall cease to exist when it has less than five clubs in membership. Clubs located in a county where there is no county union may become members of the union of the count,y adjoining." By- law 13 add—" Unless the spe3ial permission of the Union Committee has been obtained, such permission only to be given under specially exceptional circum- stances."

Mr. J. Platt, in seconding the resolution, said county matches were practically a farce when county players had to be drawn from a very small area. Under the resolution it was proposed that counties with less than five clubs should join the county adjoining it, and that the players should take their chance along with those of the adjoining county. The representative of the Runcorn Club, which would be affected by the resolution, urged the unwisdorn of such a policy. It was, he said, desirable to preserve the smaller counties for the sake of junior football. Mr. Worthington (Swinton) also opposed the resolu- tion, which was lost on a division, 32 supporting it and 18 voting against. PROFESSIONA.LTS3I AND THE WORKING CLAUSE. On behalf of the Broughton Rangers Club, Mr. Kirk- ham proposed the abolition of what is known as the "working clause" of the prefessional laws. Mr. Kirk- ham claimed that the object aimed at by the promoters of the rule had not been carried out. One thing sought, was to keep men in bona-fide employment. The con- tention of his club was that with the majority of local players it was not necessary to keep them in employ- ment. They did not need watching and following, but with regard to players brought from a distance he knew difficalty had arisen. "They occasionally work," said Mr. Kirkham, amid much laughter. "At least, some of them do," he added quickly, amid renewed merriment. There was no doubt that if a wealthy club got a player worth keeping they would not let questions of work stand in his way. They would get a beerhouse for him or put him in some other business, and then it was con- sidered bona-fide employment, whether he attended to it or no. He could idle his time away and do as he liked. This did not encourage local men to follow the working clause. Another object of the clause was to place all clubs on an equal footing, so that the rich one should not have an advantage over the poor one: but that had not happened. A rich club was able to put a man into business, but a poor club was not. Mr. Eyre (Hull), in seconding, argued that the work- ing clause had not operated either for the benefit of the clubs or the players. Work was distasteful to many of the players, and when they were forced to do it they would devise any idle excuse to avoid it. Players regularly deceived the clubs. A man would say he had been working, and get a colleague to lend himself to the lie, but when the inspector came round to investi- gate someone gave information, the club was probably lined £5O, and the player was suspended. What good was that to the club? Let us," said Mr. Eyre, "do away with this degradation to ourselves by being asso- ciated with men whom we have. to bolster up, and who defy us at every turn." (Hear, hear.) It was abso- lutely impossible to conduct clubs at the present rate unless a scheme was devised to frustrate the present rule. ~

Mr.lowarth, on behalf of a number of Cumberland clubs, spoke in favour of the resolution. It was needed, he said, in the interests of ksecretaries, who had 110 W-fir d-tys a lot to do in seeing whether players were really at work.

Mr. Porter (Hull) speaking also in support, slid that in two years' time if the resolution were passed there would be no need for club representatives to go scour- ing the country for recruits, for they would be able to fill the vacancies from the junior teams. In addition, clubs would be able to remove from their midst these "loafers.' The majority of imported players were neither more nor less than loafers. (Flear, hear.) A PLEA FOR THE PLAYER'S FUTURE. - .

Mr. J. B. Cooke (Wakefield- 'IC-init.-0 agreed that it was the imported player who was the loafer now, but if the Union legalised open professionalism he was afraid the local player would become the same. He could not comprehend the attitude of Cumberland clubs in this matter. He could understand men earning £3 or tl at football not wishing to work, but in Cumberland and many parts of Yorkshire and Lancashire it was abso- lutely essential that players to live must work. if open professionalism were adopted, secretaries would let themselves in for much extra work. "We do not want, players." he continued, "when they have finished play- ing football, to be idle, good-for-nothing fellows. We want them to feel that they are doing good for them- selves by increasing their income and providing sport for the public, but we want them to feel also that when they have finished playing football they can go on with their work." If a man did without working for ten years he had forgotten how to work; he would be a loafer to the end of his existence. Mr. Coke suggested that much of the opposition to the rule would dis- appear if the rulings of the Professional Sub-commit- tee, now often arbitrary, were modified. _ _ _

M. Hoyle (Huddersfield) argued that a good man at work was a good man at play. - Mr. F. Lister (Bradford) said that what Yorkshire clubs felt was that if anything wanted overhauling it was the rulings of the sub-committee. (Hear, hear). The teachers of Leeds and Bradford had intimated that if the working clause were deleted they would not assist them again. In his hearing, a high authority in the Association game had said that if they had to start again they would have a works clause. Mr. Gresty (Broughton Rangers) said that what peo- ple objected to was not the rile, but its application, re- vealed in some of the arbitrary rulings given. The two years "clause had been the cause of a lot of heart-burning. If the rulings were modified he believed the rule would have general support. He argued that there was more necessity for stringency formerly than there was now, but naively confessed, amid great laughter, that " there were men who did not like work now." "I am not referring to ray own club," he added as the laughter continued. The resolution was lost, there being 28 votes for it and 36 against. The result was received_ with applause..

CHANGES IN THE PROFESSIONAL LAWS. Several other proposed alterations to the profes- sional laws were discussed. On the proposition of the Co m mittee,the following amendments were agreed to : "A player must work three days previous to playing Saturday football, or two days prior to mid-week matches, after being away for sickness etc. Add to rule 1, sub-section c :—" It shall be within the power and at the option of the Union Committee to exempt any professional from the provisions of the works clause when playing for a junior club which makes no payment to any of its players, on an applica- tion being made by such junior club." Professional Rule 3, amend first portion to read "All agreements between clubs and professional players must be in writing, and such agreements must state clearly the terms agreed upon between such clubs and players." Proposed I y the Bradford Club, seconded by the Leeds Club, sub-section 3 of Rule 1 was altered th read after the words "Professional sub-committee," "Except in the case of a mid-week match where a player has been away from work for sickness or injury, but has worked three days when the secretary of the Union shall be empowered to grant a provisional permit." THE FEET-UP RULE. Confessing that the penalty for " feet-up "in the scrummage had been a lamentable failure, Mr. J. H.

Smith moved a number of alterations in the rules of the game, which, it was hoped, would improve scrum mage play. It was agreed to addas additional penalties- " Being in a scrummage lifts a foot from the ground, before the ball has been put in." "If a player lifts his foot in a scrummage when the ball is about to be put in a scrummage, the referee may penalise such player, although the ball has not been put in," or. "Puts his foot across the opening in the scrummage." _ _ _

Law 16-was altered to read—" When a player knocks on or throws the ball forward, any player of the oppo- site side may play the ball, but should he or any player of his own side play the ball it shall at once be brought back to where such knock-on or throw forward took place, and there put down and scrummaged. If the ball or any player running with the ball touches the referee it shall there be put down and scrummaged. A player who accidentally knocks the ball on shall not be penalised if he obtains possession before it _falls to the ground."

div.head: CHALLENGE CUP RULES.
div.p: THE CHALLENGE CUP RULES.
On the suggestion of the Union Committee, a number of the Challenge Cup roles were altered. Amongst them were these :

Rule 7, commence rule :—" The charge for admission to qualifying and intermediate rounds shall be at the discretion of the home club, but for the Cup-ties proper the minimum, etc." Rule 7, delete latter portion of ruleand substitute "All members and ticket-holders must pay the admis- sion charges to ground and stands." (Carried 36 and 23).

Rule 7.—Add at end—" When a Cup-tie is played on a neutral ground, a commission of 10 cent, shall be allowed to the club upon whose ground the match is played, but members of such club must pay the admis- sion charges to ground and stands." Rule 8, add-- Where a ground is larger than the minimum size, and fulfils the requirements of this rule, it shall not be lawful to reduce the size of the playing space for the purpose of a Cup-tie." MEETING OF THE GENERAL COMMITTEE. A meeting of the committee was held during the afternoon, Mr. R. Coiling° (president of the Rochdale Hornets Club) presiding. • The resignation of Mr. W. Jones, of Runcorn, as a member of the committee' was accepted with regret, audit was resolved that a hearty vote of thanks should be given him for his services to the Union. Mr. C. Pownall was elected to the vacancy. _ . _

The Salterhebble Club mule a do—mplaint against the Brighouse Rangers F.C. for approaching J. Baldwin, one of their professionals. It was found that the Brighouse Club had committed a breach of Professional Law 2, and the committee imposed a fine of a guinea. It was also found that the Salterhebble club had com- mitted a breach of Professional Law 3, and the com- mittee imposed a fine of ss. upon them. The Halifax Club was granted permission to present extra cup medals to five players and the secretary, and the Warrington Club was granted permission to present medals to four of their players.

EXAMINER OFFICE,

THE opposition to PIRA.TED MUSIC. the Musical Copy- right Bill is ti quaint instance of misdirected zeal. The Bill, which was read a secoad time without a division, provides that any music registered within tha terms of the Copyright Act of 1842 shall be protected from piracy, and that the pirates shall be punished like any other law-brea,cer. Owing to defects in the existing, law pirated music has been sold in the streets with impunity. It might be thought that a measure to deal with this abuse would be passed with ease and general approbation. Oa the con- trary, an obstinate resistance is made by a considerable number of legislators. The Bill came up on report from the Grand Committee, and Mr. CALDWELL, Mr. HARWOOD, and others cheerfully endeavoured to delay if not to prevent the third reading. They were possessed by the singular idea that the com- posers and publishers of music are oppressors of the poor. The poor man who would like to buy a song finds that it is marked on its face at four shillings. As a matter of form it is sold for two . shillings, but even that sum is beyond the poor man's means. When it is offered to him for three- pence by the street hawker he takes it home joy- fully to lighten the hearts of his sorrowing family. The hawker or his employer is the Robin Hood who plunders the opulent composer and publisher to befriend the poor man. Mr. CALDWELL, Mr. HARWOOD, and their associates uphold the glorious principles of Robin Hood against the • grasping owners of musical copyright. The Bill, said Mr. CALDWELL, is conceived in the interests of property. A watch is property. So is a pair of boots. Nobody can steal them without suffering the penalty: but to steal a copyright song is s meritorious act, because it cheapens music for the people who cannot afford to pay the legitimate market price. In short, music, according to Mr. CALDWELL, is not property at all; and the man who writes it and who is often poor enough in all conscience ought to be ashamed of himself for not giving it away. So deep was the indignation that Mr. ATILERLEY JONES: who is a lawyer, proposed to inflict only a nominal penalty for piracy when it could be shown that the composer and publisher had not satisfied the "requirements of the public." Had this charming proviso been adopted the Act would be a dead letter, for, of course, the public always requires a commodity to be cheaper than it:ever is. It would satisfy our requirements very nicely if coals were sold at sixpence a ton, though we do not suggest that a Bill to prohibit any Robin Hood who wanted to steal coals and sell them at the figure would meet with the approval of members of the House of Commons. But if the poor man cannot have his coals at that rate, why should he not have his music for next to nothing? We can imagine the pathetic appeal which Mr. ATHERLgy JONES. defending the copyright pirates, would make to the jury. He would draw a picture of the working man's home where thrift has provided a cottage piano for the working man's daughter, whose sweet young voice gladders the father's heart after his day's toil. He has bought a threepenny song from the pirate. He is thinking of buying more, when suddenly this spring of domestic joy is dried up by the greed of composers and publishers, who put the pirate in the dock. The working-man's daughter cannot sing now, for her voice falters when she thinks of this injustice; and her father, missing his even- ing melody, seeks consolation at the public-house. This line of argument would not be a whit more absurd than most of the talk against the Bill. Mr. HARWOOD contrived to strike a still more original note by suggesting that the compulsory registration of music would prevent the publication of a "lot of rubbish." Songs which Mr. HARWOOD despises may be rubbish or they may not; but if their publication were to be restricted how would this arbitrary measure justify that beautiful

'schools a police notice setting forth some of the °fiances which are most prevalent amongst the refng generation. He points out how by break- the law boys frequently get into the hands of the police, thus bringing punishment and discredit IlPen themselves, as well as cost and trouble upon their parents. After reading the notice they will be unable to plead ignorance, for the seriousness of offences which to some might seem trivial is fully explained. Mr. Talbot does well to emphasize that the use of bad language is "a very disgrace- and unmanly offence." He endeavours to per- *Made the children to do right, because it is right, llot simply to avoid punishment. He points out 110 W, by exercising thought and self-control, they __would save a serious amount of annoyance, awl warrington " might soon become known as a town ,of Well-behaved boys and girls." We say "hear, "ear,' to these sentiments, and hope Mr. Talbot's .advice will be taken to heart by those for whose goad it is offered.

, One of the most gratifying features of the cele- oration of Cobden's centenary was the tributes displayed by foreign organisations to the memory of the great reformer. Cobden's life work in pro- Moting closer commercial intercourse between the !Istions of the world may not have fulfilled all his ocPes, but it is encouraging to know that through- out the world enlightened men are acting in co- Operation for the attainment of his ideals. Those 'Who have to bear the crushing burden of Protec- tion in Italy,Austria,Germany,and elsewhere know how enviable is the condition of:those who sixty tars ago emancipated themselves from tariff fetters ; and it is with astonishment that they see any indication of a Protectionist reaction in the country which since ic adopted FreeeTrade hai 'flourished so greatly.

That truth is stranger than fiction has time and 'again been proven a true saying. No novelist has .ever told a more remarkable story than that which ,turrounds the personality of the "Countess dells •Lo. rre "—or, to give her her true name, Emma i tilisani—who has just been done to death by her opeband at Apricale. Emma Alio= was a young girl of extraordinary beauty when she married a atone-carver named Pisani. She was ambitious, od to satisfy her ambitions Pisani, before they bad been long married, turned coiner, and, being detected, had to fly to America. His wife, freed *from her marital obligations,set out upon thecareer ff adventuress which has just been brought to itS tragic close. She managed to get into the iSshionable set at Nice, and there, by her excep— tional beauty, captivated the Count delta Torre, 'whose mistress she became, calling herself the %antes& On the Count's death she inherited his wealth, and ambition and social success urged her forward until she had some of the most famous statesmen of the Continent literally at her feet. was the recipient of Cabinet secrets, and was IS constant alliance with the military authorities 4t St. Petersburg for whom she acted the part of agent, receiving in return fabulous sums of money. lier end Cams through her desire to get finally 'free from her husband. He returned to Apricale few weeks ago, after an absence of twenty years, and there murdered her with a stone-mabon's hammer. The pages of fiction can surely present 210 more remarkable tale.

Coming Events. The summer anniversary services will be held at Rill Cliffe Baptist Church, to-morrow (Sunday), when the Rev. S. D. Thomas, of Earlestown, will preach afternoon and evening. Miss Bessie Dutton will address a children's flower service in the morning. Miss Lucy Davies of Hollinfare, is the soloist for the day, and she will sing "Abide with me," and 'Sun of my Soul." Provision will be made for an overflow service in the evening. Prof. Timson will speak at the Spiritualist Hall to- Morrow (Sunday). On Monday evening Mrs. Holden will give clairvoyance, &c. he Secret of Jesus " will be the Rev. H. Dunnico's subject at the Parr Hall to-morrow (Sunday) •evening. , The annual special services for "Old Blues" will be held in the Blue Coat School Chapel to-morrow '(Sunday) evening. The Rev. John Yonge will preach at Wycliffe Church to-morrow (Sunday). The Warrington and District Agricultural Society's 15th annual show will be held in Walton Park on Thursday, August 11th. Prizes, cups and medals to the value of £750, are offered for competition. Personal.
Mr. Thomas S. Steel, snlicitor, Warrington, has been appointed by the Lord Chancellor a Commisioner to administer oaths.

'Sequel to a Chimney Fall. We understand that Mr. Thomas Halton of the 'Cteorge Hotel has commenced an action against the Warrington Corporation, claiming damages for negli- gence attending the fall of a chimney, during a etn.rm, Whereby damage was done to his hotel.

BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art Ehades.—J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Widening of Warrington Bridge. Mr. J. J. Webster, engineer, appointed by the Cor- oration to superintend the widening of Warrington -Bridge by the erection of cantilevers, has been instructed to prepare estimates and quantities for the Vork. As soon as these are received tenders will be invited.

Fatality at Daliam. Mark Dolan, (50), a single man, employed as a lack wheeler at Dallam Forge and lodging in Winwick-road, met with a shocking death on Thursday blaming. He was unloading slack from a railway -waggon, when by some means he was crushed between Ihe waggon and the wall, death being almost instan- taneous.

'POOP Children's Camp. Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co. Limited have 'kindly sent a donation of £5 to this fund and the ,IfVarrington Football Club have also very generously (?Warded a similar amount.
_ A. A gentleman whose name we are not at liberty to umlige,has promised g,lO and two valuable tents for the Poor children's summer camp at Prestatyn.

Temporary Authority. At the Borough Police Court yesterday, Walter Connolly Brooks was granted temporary authority to sell at the Raven Hotel, Fennel street, in lieu of the late William Dillon.

The Stockton Heath Tramway Extension. A special meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee was held on Wednesday to consider the tenders for the permanent way of the proposed tram- way extension to Stockton Heath. The committee ultimately accepted the tender (conditionally) of Mr. J. A. Ewart for ;£2,936. There were eleven tenders. The work will be proceeded with immediately. Relieving Distress. On Monday morning a distribution of relief in con nection with the iron workers' distress fund took place in the G-olborne-street schoolroom. The Relief Committee was represented by Mr. James Payton and Mr. Herbert Hayes (hon. treasurers) and Mr. Charles Algie and Mr. Joseph Elwell (hon. secretaries). About 230 tickets entitling the bearers to parcels of groceries were distributed.

Big Catches of Salmon on the Dee. At Chester on Tuesday, some fishermen netting the Dee had the remarkable luck to take thirteen salmon at one draught and fifteen salmon at another. Many other fisherman landed three or four in a draught. No doubt the big "fresh" in the river accounted for the big catches. .

UNDER the CLOCK for GOOD BOOTS.—Aavt. Ragged School Band of Hope. The final concert of the season was given in the schoolroom on Monday evening before a fair attend- ance. Mr. Albert G. Odell presided, and his remarks were well received. Solos, recitations, and display exercises were given by thii members. Roars of laughter were created by the rendering of" The Haunted Room," by Mrs. Barlow, Misses M.A. and S. A. Titchard, 0. J. Wright and S. Potts, and Messrs. Crozier, Titchard, and the Bros. Wright. Mr. Frank Owen accompanied with his usual ability. The Com- mittee thank Mr. and Mrs. Worrall and friends for their assistance during the season.

Drowning Case. About five o'clock on Thursday morning the body of Alice Jane Albinson (35), a single woman residing at 79,Churcb-street,was recovered from the Old Quay canal at Wilderspool by P.C. Turner and several boat- men. The deceased was a daughter of the late Mr. Joseph Albinson, and it is stated that since her father's death a few months ago she had been rather despondent. She had been missing from home since 6.30 on Sunday morning.

The inquiry. The Inquiry at the Town Hall into the allegations of the Non-Traders, resumed its sitting after the holidays on, June 6, and meetings have also been held on the 9th and 16th inst. Nearly all the evidence has now been taken, and it should not be long before the Inquiry closes, and the Commissioners for each side present their respective reports.

Pawnshop Broken Into. Mr. T. Docnville's pawnshop in Knutsford-road was broken into early on Sunday morning by means of .a back window 71t from the ground. A lamplighter in the employ of the Corporation, named Bailey, was on duty near Litherland's-yard, at half-past two when he heard a noise in the shop. He took no notice of the affair at che time, but later on, talking it over with a friend, it was decided to communicate with the police. This was done, and Mr. Domville was also informed with the result that the premises were searched, and it was found that a small amount of money had been stolen.

ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH•CLASS MINIMA WATERS.—Advt. No War Trophy for Crewe. The Crewe Patriotic Committee, who applied to the War Office for one of the trophies of the Boer War to be placed alongside the beautiful memorial, in the Queen Park, to the Crewe Railway Engineers who served in the campaign, have received a reply from Lord Hardwick° stating chat the limited number of trophies at the committee's disposal precluded any recommendation in favour of towns even so patriotic as Crewe.

FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-strect,Warringion.— -Advt. Warrington Technical Institute Secondary Day School. On Saturday afternoon last, a most delightful cycle excursion took place in which both scholars and teachers took part. place, party of 32 cyclists left the Institute at 1.30 p.m. en route for Delamere Forest via Strettou and Acton Bridge. Norley was reached about 3.4s,where a most enjoyable 3 honrs_.was spent. After partaking of tea, s3me games were played in the adjacent woods. The homeward joarney via Frodsham was commenced about 6.45, the Technical School being reached a couple of hours later. Here the party dispersed, having thoroughly enjoye,l the first of a probable series of similar rides. The best lof weather prevailed throughout. See BOOTR AND SON'S Latest Designs in Children's Boots and Shoes for Walking Day. Also the White Heather and Portland Boots and Shoes for Ladies' Wear. Buttermarket street.—Advt.

Dispute in the Flint Glass Trade. A dispute has arisen in the flint glass trade affect- ing the makers or blowers, as they are now. familiarly called. Warrington forms part of the Man- chestor district, and sometime ago, the masters in the district served notices upon the glass makers of a re- vised scale of pay, in which a reduction had been made on the ground that the state of trade and present prices did not warrant a continuance of the present scale. The men naturally objected to the new scale and on Thursday they withdrew their tools pending a settlement. About 20 or 30 men are affected in War- rington all of them being engaged at the works of Messrs:Robinson, Son and Company, Ltd., Bank Quay. Not a Ghost of a Chance for Mr. R. A. Naylor. In last Saturday's issue of the Warrington "Guardian" appeared a paragraph respecting Mr. R. A. Naylor's candidature for Carv.arvon Boroughs. , One of our most regular subscribers sent this to a ' friend who has long resided in the district concerned. The following is a copy of his reply dated June 15th. "mote the paragraph you marked. Lloyd George is alright. Bangor is the only weak spot and always was. Cathedral and Castle influence, and now the Railway Company have built a number of houses for their employes above station and they try to get their men to vote Tory. But Bangor is better than it was and we certainly will put Lloyd George in. Mr. Naylor hasn't the ghost of a chance."

Warrington Society's , Annual Picnic. Favoured with delightful weather, the Warrington Society's annual picnic on Thursday was a great success. The party, numbering twenty-six left War- rington in a special soloon at 8.40 and reached Bake- well about 11 o'clock. The old church was visited, and afterwards the company had a pleasant walk along the river side and through the meadows to Haddon Hall. Here lunch was served alfresco, and the hall was inspected. A drive to Chatsworth was the next item, and the party spent a pleasant time in the hall and grounds. Again boarding the char-a-bancs, Baslow was viSited, and a capital tea was served at the Peacock Hotel. The gentlemen afterwards indulged in Beveral games of bowls, and driving to Bakewell station the party rejoined the saloon. Warrington was reached at 10.15 after a splendid outing. The company included two of our newly-appointed J.P.'s—Alderman Bennett and Mr. William Richardson—and after tea at Baslow their health was drunk.
