ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS NIDTERAL WATERS.—Advt. Accident to Mr. F. Monks, J P. At noon yesterday, Mr. F. Monks, J.P., was driving to the works at Atherton's Quay, when the horse stumbled near the works' office. Mr. Monks and his coachman were thrown out of the trap. They were both much shaken and sustained some bruises, but we are glad to learn that the injuries were not serious Death of Mrs. Robert Proud. We regret to record the death of Mrs. Robert Proudd who for many years resided in this town. The deceased lady was seized with a stroke on Sunday at Birkenhead and passed away yesterday morning. Wedding of Mr. A. M. Ker and Miss Twiss. The wedding took place at St. John's Church, Walton, on Thursday, of Mr. A. M. Ker, assistant Borough Surveyor, to Miss E. A. Twiss, youngest daughter of the late Mr. Charles Twiss, formerly headmaster of the Warrington British School. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. H. V. Pigot, M.A., assisted by the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, B.D. Mr. Howard Ker officiated as best man, and the brides- maids were Miss Pattie Woodcock, Miss Hilda Ker, and Miss Freda Wilson. After the marriage cere- mony the happy couple departed for London, where the honeymom. is being spent. PuBLIc BENEFIT, UNDER the CLOCK for BEST BOOT; in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. P.S.A. Meeting. Mr. T. S. Steel presided at an open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. Society held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street on Sunday. Mrs. Hannan sang "The last milestone " and" Eternal rest" with very pleasing effect, being accompanied on the piano by Mr. Wadsworth. The Rev. D. R. James (curate of St. Peter's Church) gave an interesting address on "The marks of manhood." He said he made no excuse for attending that meeting, and was very glad to meet that afternoon outside the ties of denomina- tionalism, where he might carry on his work indepen- dently and say a word for the Master, for whilst the Church of England had his first claim, he was broad- minded enough to come outside and help on the cause for which they were all fighting. He specially pleaded with the young people to be temperate in all their doings, and guard against the one great evil, drink. As a model of what true manhood was he urged them to take as a guide the late H. M. Stanley, who lived as n.uch for others as himself, and who left the world the bt.4-ter for his having lived in it. AsirroN's LIFE ToNIC is the KING off TONICS.— 63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Sale of Work. The sale of work in aid of the new Wesleyan Mission which it is proposed to erect in Ellesmere-street, was continued on Saturday. Mr. Jonathan Taylor presided at the opening ceremony, and said that he was specially interested in the Ellesmere-street Mission as having been one of those who were imitrumental in founding it. He was lookinr, forward to the time, and not a very distant date, when they would have a building which would be a credit to the neighbourhood. ' (Applause). With regard to the work at Ellesmere- street he did not think there was a school or chapel that had made such progress as their mission had. They had nearly 300 children in the school, and he was sure they would agree with him that the time had come when they should have more accommodation. (Applause.)—Miss Isaac then declared the sale open, and wished the workers every success in their en- , deavours.—On the proposition of Mr. Joseph Mather, seconded by Mr. E. Horton, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and Miss Isaac. The proceeds for the two days amounted to £2l 14s. id. FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street. Warrington.—Advt. Militiaman Falls from a Train. On Monday afternoon the men of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire (Militia) Regiment left Warrington for their training at Chipping (Preston) camp. The strength of the battalion was 430 officers, non-com- missioned officers, and men, and they were under the command of Lieut.-Colonel M.H. Hall, D.S.O. The majority of the men returned from active service in South Africa in August, 1901. Headed by the band of the regiment the men marched out of Orford Barracks at about a quarter to three, their departure being witnessed by a fairly large number of people, and left Warrington by the 3.10 p.m. train from Bank Quay Station. There are already at Chipping camp 230 recruits. During the day a serious accident occurred. Was. Stanley, a plate- layer, Liverpool, and a member of the Liverpool Militia, joined the 10.30 Liverpool to Manchester express at the Central Statioa, Liverpool, with the object of proceeding to the Orford Barracks. With him in the carriage were two other members of the same battalion. When the train had attaincd a good speed and was approaching Hale- wood, Stanley is stated to have opened the door and fallen out. The man must shave struck the ground with terrific force and for some yards he was rolled along the ground in the same direction as the train. The man was picked up and promptly removed to the Great Northern Hospital, Liverpool. It was found that he had sustained a fractured skull in addition to other injuries of a most serious kind. At Warring- ton after being closely questioned as to the event, the injured man's two companions were allowed to join the militia. BaCE BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt

Since it became known that a list of names had been submitted to the Chancellor of the Duchy as suitable persons to be placed on the Commission of the Peace for the Borough, speculation has been rife as to the gentlemen who were to be honoured. All surmises were set at rest on Wednesday when the County Seal- keeper at Preston, acting under instructions from the Chancellor of the Duchy placed the names of the following local gentlemen on the Commission of the Peace for the Borough of Warrington. : Mr. Arthur Bennett, chartered accountant, Market Gate Chambers. Mr. William Bolton,brewer, Mill Bank,Wilderspool. Mr. Charles Sawkins Burgess, produce merchant, Winmarleigh-street. Mr. Charles Jackson Holmes, estate agent and in- surance broker, Barnacre, Latchford Without. Mr. Alfred John Jolley, 16, Arpley-street. Mr. George Pilling, Oak Bank, Ackers-lane, Latch- ford Without. Mr. Lewis William Reynolds, tanner, Millington House, Thelwall. Mr. David Tinnion, spelter and chemical manu- facturer, 18, Winmarleigh-street. Mr. John Wilkinson, velvet manufacturer, 14, Bewsey-road. Mr. Edwin Woods, wire manufacturer, Rock Villa, Latchford. _
Mr. William Richardson,coal merchant,Uolly Bank, Walton-road.

Mr. William Roberts, boot and shoe manufacturer, Harleydene, Grappenhall-road, Latchford Without. The list is a long one, and it is the first time in the history of the Borough that 12 magistrates have been placed upon the Bench at once. The last additions were in 1900 when sevn local gentlemen were placed upon the Commission. Politically, four of the new magistrates are Liberals and eight Conservatives. The Liberals are Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. Councillor Tinnion, Mr. William Roberts and Mr. Councillor Wilkinson.

His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) presides I over the Bench at the present time in virtue of his office, but henceforth he will sit upon the Bench as one who is also appointed by the Chancellor of the Duchy. Alderman Bolton has had a long and honour- I able association with the Town Council. Appointed in 1882 he has been continuously in office since, and his long services were recognised by his colleagues last November when he was unanimously elected to the Mayoral chair. He has been connected with the town all his lifetime. On leaving school, he joined the reporting staff of a local contemporary, afterwards sub-editing an agricultural pap'. called "The Farmer." Later he became associated with the brewery in Mersey street, and in 1872 he visited the United States. Returning the following year, he took over the control of the brewery, of which he is the proprietor. In 1882 he became a member of the Town Council and was elected an alderman in 1894. He has attained a wide reputation as a grower of flowers. Whilst in Mersey street he grew auriculas and roses to such perfection as to secure the chief prizes at many otthe leading shows. His attention at present is devoted to the cultivation of orchids, of which he has one of the finest collections in the world in his extensive houses at Mill Bank. He generally favours each member of the Town Council with a buttonhole on Council night—an act which is greatly appreciated. His Worship is a connoisseur of medals coins, cameos and old china, of which he had a choice collection.

Mr. C. Jackson Holmes has never been connected with the Town Council, but he has performed much useful public work. Many years ago, before much attention was paid to technical instruction, he was the first secretary of the School of Science held in the rooms above Arpley Station. He was a member of the committee of the People's College under the old regime, and is the corresponding secretary under the new. Formerly hon. treasurer of the Liberal Associa- tion, he now discharges the more onerous duties of hon. secretary. He is a trustee of the Warrington Savings Bank, and the hon. auditor of the Warrington Infirmary. As a member of the Society of Friends he has filled many prominent positions. He was formerly clerk to the quarterly meeting of the Society of Friends of Lancashii6 and Cheshire—a position somewhat similar to that of a president of a Wesleyan Ildistrict Synod. He is treasurer of Penketh Friends School and for several years has acted as clerk to the Hardshaw-East monthly meeting of the Society of Friends which includes all the districts between War- rington and Manchester. Mr. Holmes's father was Mayor of the Borough in,1863-4 and 1869-70. On his retirement he was made an honorary freeman of the Borough, in recognition of his long and faithful public serv. ces.

Councillor Tinnion came prominently to the front on becoming a member of the Town Council in 1895. The extension of the Borough had then been con- firmed and on St. Austin's Ward being created he became one of its first representatives. He carries on the business of a chemical and spelter manufacturer and his works are situated at Bank Quay. During

his 81 years' continuous service on the Town Council he has performed much useful work, and has promin- ently identified himself with the Gymnasium and the work of the health, sanitary works and paving and sewerage committees. As a Liberal, he has never shirked the work of the party. At the last general election when the local battle was a hopeless one, he stood loyally to the cause and was one of the hardest workers. _ He is chairman of the

Liberal Association, and as a vice-president of the Liberal Club, he has done much to place it on a sound financial basis. He is!. keen sportsman. Formerly a footballer himself, he has followed with interest the career of the Warrington Club from its inception. He

is a great advocate of physical exercise for young people and has taken a leading part in popularising the gymnasium amongst the schools of the town. Councillor Tinnion is also connected with the War- rington Cricket and Bowling Club of which he is the hon. auditor. Mr. William Roberts has not been as prominent in the public eye since his retirement from the Town Council. He sat as a member for St. Austin's Ward, but on his term of office expiring last November' he did not seek re-election. He was formerly hon. secretary of the Warrington Temperance Federation, and did much to give vitality to the movement in this town—perhaps the most difficult town in the Kingdom to move on behalf of temperance. Despite much opposition and discouragement, the Federation has performed much useful work at the licensing sessions, and in this particular Mr. Roberts', was always to the fore. He conducts the business of a boot and shoe manufacturer, which his respected father, the late Mr. Richard Roberts established in Bridge-street. In addition, Mr. William Roberts also discharges the duties of secretary to several local companies. Councillor Wilkinson joined the Town Council in 1900, when he became the representative of Orford Ward on his father's death. He is one of the most promising of the ‘younger members of the Council, and has shown an aptitude for public work. He is one of the vice-presidents of the Liberal Club and takes an interest in all that appertains to the Liberal party. He is connected with the velvet manufacturing trade, and holds a prominent position in the Association which was recently formed in con- nection with it.

Alderman Bennett is one of our best-known public men. He touches local life in most of its phases, and takes a deep interest in all that affects the welfare of the town and its townspeople. He has served the rate- payers in the Council Chamber since 1893, and has endeavoured to foster an insthetic taste in a distinctly utilitarian community. By establishing a monthly magazine of progress entitled "The Dawn," and forming the 'Warrington Society he has partially suc- ceeded in his efforts. In politics he is a Conservative, with imperialism as a major note. Mr. Charles Sawkins Burgess at one time took a prominent part in Liberal politics but latterly he: has been associated with the Conservative , party. He is a son of the late Mr. Charles Burgess, formerly a tradesman in 'this town and a nephew of the late Alderman Burgess of this:Borough. Alderman Burgess, of Liverpool City Council, is his Ibrother and another brother is associated with Messrs. Robert Davies and Co, solicitors. Mr. • Burgess carrie4 on the business of a produce merchant at Liverpool. He has for many years been identified with S. James' Church and has held various offices in connection with it. He is the correspondent for St. James' schools and one of the co-opted managers of the People's College under the new Education Act. Mr. William Richardson is a local coal merchant and is also interested in the tanning trade.He is a director of the Longford Wire Company Limited. He has acted as correspondent of St. Ann's school in which he has taken a great interest. Last year he was presi- dent of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club. Mr. E. Woods is the managing director of the Long-

ford Wire Company Limited. In politics he is a Con- servative, and takes an interest more especially in the work of the Junior Conservative Association. He occa- sionally finds time to write to the local press on political and social matters. He has recently written on the fiscal question and declared himself a Pro- tectionist. _

Mr. LW. Reynolds is a son of the late Mr. William Reynolds who established the Mersey street tannery. He comes of a musical family,and as hon. treasurer of the Warrington Musical Saciety he has performed an onerous, and at times, thankless task. The society is just now emerging from a long period of indebted- ness, and to Mr., Reynolds especially, this must be very gratifying. Mr. A. J.. Jolley is best known as a Poor Law administrator. He has held all the offices open to a member of the Warrington Board of Guardians and by careful study of every department of work he has become an authority on poor law administration. He is Chairman of the Local Assessment Committee and was recently a member of a deputation that waited upon Mr. Long, with reference to the Valuation Bill. For several years he represented Fairfield Ward in the Town Council, but was defeated on seeking re- election. He has filled the position of Mayor's auditor and is one of the Commissioners appointed by the Town Council to conduct the inquiry into the trading transactions of the Corporation. He is a useful mem- ber of the Education Committee and occupies the position of Chairman of the Finance Committee. He also discharges the duty of hon. secretary to the Hos- pital Sunday Committee. , Mr. George Pilling is another new magistrate who . , interested in poor law work. He sat on the War- rington Board for a number of years, but was defeated at the last election by Miss Broadbent. He is still a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians and the Rural District Council, sitting as the representative of Latchford Without. He is a Conservative in politics and has filled the position of secretary of the Conserva- tive Club with ability. MAGISTRATES SWORN IN.

All the new magistrates, with the exception of Mr. A. J. Jolley, were sworn in at the Police Court yester- thy morning by the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle). The Commission of the Peace with its impressive legal phraseology was read and the magistrates then made the usual declaration to "faithf illy and impartially" execute the office, and also swore allegiance to the King.

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB DINNER. Presentation of S.W.L Cup and Medals.
div.p: FOOTBALL CLUB DINNER. Presentation of S.W.L Cup and Medals.

There WIV4 a r vresentative gathering of the Warring- ton Football Club at the Lion Hotel last evening when a dinner was held and the presentation made of the South-West Lancashire cup and medals. Mr. T. Bowers (chairman of the committee) presided and he was supported by members of the committee, officials and players. An excellent bill of fare was submitted and full justice was done to the good things provided. The players especially were in fine form and kept up "the attack " with a vigour that must have dismayed even Mr. Lee's energetic assistants.—Mr. Ashton an- nounced the receipt of a letter of apology from Mr. W. R. Neil, the president, regretting his inability to be present as he was confined to bed and had been there a week or more. Regret was expressed at Mr. Neil's absence and the cause of it. After the loyal toast had been duly honoured, Fish complied with a song "A Broken Melody," and scored as he usu- ally does.--in presenting the medals, Mr. Bowers said he would have been more pleased if he had been able to present the gold medals of the Northern Union. It was a matter of the wheel of fortune, he said, that he had not that pleasure. but he hoped on another occasion to have the privilege. Hallam led the way to the table to receive his medal, closely followed by Fish. Isherwood came in for a cordial reception on receiving his. but perhaps the best ova- tion was reserved for Fairhurst, " silver " evidently being- a favourite with the players. Thomas was seen in a new role, when he gave a robust rendering of "The Belle of Tennesse." The proceed- ings would have been incomplete without a word from " Lawyer " Barnes, and he was heard at his best in an oration on the doings of the club during the past cason. and the greatly improved play that was given. International caps were banded to Dickenson and Fish by Mr. 4shton, and Harris, Boardman, Naylor and , Frank Lkeesom added to the harmony of the evening.

An official return issued on Thursday shows that the number of children under eight years of age committed to industrial schools in the decade 1893 to 1902 inclu- sive was 3,440 and the number of children over eight and under ten years of age 6,439. The numbers in the later years are below the average of ten years. During an inquest on a cyclist who was killed as the result of an accident on Dale-hill, Sussex, on the Brighton-road, a witness stated that she had known fourteen serious accidents to occur there during the course of four hours.

div.head: CHARGE WITHDRAWN.
div.p: A CHARGE WITHDRAWN.

The only prisoner in custody was George Smithies, a stranger,who,the Chief Constable explained,was charged with having been found on enclosed premises with intent to commit a felony. At 6.30 prisoner was seen loitering in a suspicious manner about the premises of Mr. Charles White who is away from home. P. C. Phillips questioned him and he said he was looking round to see what he could steal. On being taken into custody he became very violent, and had to be hand- cuffed. Prisoner had been discharged from the army as medically unfit and did not appear to be quite responsible for his actions.—ln order to mark the auspicious occa- sion the charge was withdrawn, and prisoner was sent to the Workhouse for 14 days in order that his mental state could be inquired into.

div.head: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD'S CANDIDATURE.
div.p: MR. A. H. CROSFIELD'S CANDIDATURE.

Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, the hon. secretary of the Liberal Association, has received a letter from Mr. A. U. CrOsfield, in which he says : "I need not tell you that when the time comes I shall accept without hesitation this handsome invita- tion. It is a great honour, and in years to come may, be a .great responsibility, if we are to succeed in wiping out the big and adverse majority at the next election—a pretty large order as you and I know, with the powerful organisation and vested interest against us in Warringion."

div.head: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON. The Social Problem.
div.p: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON. The Social Problem.

[By THE FREE CRITI, .] I acknowledge with thanks the criticism of " One Interested" and also the remarks of the Rev. H. Dunnico on my article of two weeks ago in your paper. " One Interested" states "If my intuition serves me well I rather fancy Free Critic's' great concern is for the Liberal Party—especially the Liberal Party in Warrington." He also goes on to say " Free Critic' would do well to leave out of his future articles any reference to ' God ' and Beneficent Creator' in connection with the Social Problem.' " I thank him for his well-meant advice, but as my reason both guides and lconvinces me, along with the study of history that the Social Problem cannot be solved without taking into consideration God and his works through nature, "One interested" will see that in this respect lam unable to follow his advice. lam con- vinced too as most other students of Socialogy are convinced also that the Social Problem can only be solved by man living and working in conformity with 'Nature's or God's laws. Any other way is doomed to I failure. We hold that all the evils that we are suffer- ing from are in consequence of our living and working in contradistinction to the Divine will. That no man or woman can offend one of Nature's or God's laws without bringing suffering in some way or other upon themselves or upon their fellow men is a truism we believe, as sure as twice one 'makes two. I know this doctrine is not followed in its entirety by some theologians but thanks to science and a more intelligent, theology the truth is gradually dawning upon think- ing people. However, to the question of the moment so far as Warrington and its relation to the Social Problem is concerned, let me say to "One Interested" that I am not so much concerned for the Liberal party of Warrington as lam for the people of Warrington. It is for the people as a whole that I am concerned about and here it is that I see that "One Interested" and myself are on the same platform. We both at heart seek the welfare of the people. The matter therefore resolves itself simply into a qu ?stion of methods or i policy—through what political party can the people ' receive the most benefit? A political party can only be judged by its aims, achievements and works. It cannot be gainsaid or denied for a moment that most of the liberties, principles of self-government, the obtaining of the power of voting, the improved methods and cheapness' of living through the abolition of the Corn Laws, the freedom of trade, and the improvement in our Land Laws have all been, brought about by the agency of the Liberal party, but of course much- remains to be done. Now what about the Conservative party? Well they are the natural protectors of the landowners, the landed proprietors, the House of Lords, the Church, the liquor traffic, and titb so-called rights of property, which in the end all tend to the keeping down of the people and thus prevent them from enjoying the whole of the fruits of their own labour, as they have to carry upon their shoulders the landlords and the so called aristocrats of the country, and other expensive and foolish systems in our midst. _ _ _

Now what about the Independent Labour party? Their aims after all in most matters are iden- tical with those of the Liberal party but so far as a Party they have not been able to achieve much in the way of legislation, for the main reason that they have not had the chance. And it is necessary for the House of Commons to be captured before they or any Party can carry some of their aims into effect. The natiiral enemies therefore of both the Liberal Party and the Independent Labour party,both the true friends of the people, are the Conservative Party and therefore ' it behoves these two parties to be on their guard and to use their common sense against the common enemy. Well what is to be done in Warrington ? It is obvious. Both the Liberal and Independent Labour parties must combine and work together. That party, viz., the Liberal or Independant Labour party,which at the moment commands the least votes must merge itself at the time of the General Election into the other. But the policy should be at once announced, in order that the decks can be cleared for the forth- coming political fight. "One Interested" advises waiting. I say that no time should be lost in the parties coming to a decision. If they do not, then they will be caught napping and confusion will arise and the Conservative party smile. If the Committee appointed at the recent conference at Parr Hall, brought about through the agency of the Rev. H. Du.nnico can bring the two parties to an agreement on this matter, they will have affected a good Work.

div.head: BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of "Search Lights on Land, Labour
div.p: BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of "Search Lights on Land, Labour
and Social Problems."
THE UNEDUCATED WORKMAN.

"My people are destroyed for lack of know- ledge."—Ts i PROPHET HOSEA.. If you were to ask me why so many workmen have to toil so hard, and earn so little money,and fare so badly, I should say it is because they know no better. They are not exploited by capitalism, and they are not killed by their environments, but they are destroyed for lack of knowledge." One of the most common causes of poverty is ignor- ance. It does more to exploit men's labour, and im- poverish them, than all the capitalists in the world. And it is one of the most difficult social diseases to cure. You can give a man food and clothes,and employ- ment, but you cannot give him brains. You can make a bad man into a good one, but you cannot make a born fool into a wise man. 1 I.—THE UNEDUCATED WORKMAN IS HANDICAPPED Blr IGNORANCE. He goes into the world's labour market seeking a job and he fondly imagines that all men are equal, and he ,is as good as the best of them, and that he ought to have as much wage as any other man. But the man who starts life with these wild notions in his head is only airing his own ignorance. These theories are not true, and all human experience exposes their fallacy. 1 There are wise men in the 'world, and there are fools. There are strong men, and there are weak ones. There are traiird, educated workmen, who are worth their weight in gold, and there are clumsy, awkward, helpless duffers, who are neither use nor ornament to anybody. I What is the great dividing line between these differ- ent class of workers? It is the possession of knowledge 1 and the ability to use it for their own advantage. The man who has this gift will agree with Lord Bacon when he says, "knowledge is power." And he will understand Solomon's proverb: " A wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge increaseth strength." The man who has been born in ignorance, and desires nothing better, does not understand these things. He will turn a deaf ear to the Hebrew prophet's complaint that his "people were destroyed for lack of knowledge," and go blundering through life in helpless, hopeless ignorance. . Let us follow these two men to the labour market. Emplcyers of labour seldom "buy a pig in a poke." They usually examine and sample goods before they buy them. If they find a man capable, and honest, and in- telligent they are not long in picking him up, and pay- ing the full market price for him. If they come across an uneducated workman who knows little and can hardly do anything they pass him by as dear at any price. So you see knowledge puts money into one man's pocket, and finds him employment, while ignorance im- poverishes the other man, and leaves him stranded, and helpless. But in his efforts to save himself the ignorant man inflicts infinite mischief on wiser and better men. IL—THE UNEDUCATED WORKMAN PULLS DOWN WAGES. I have shown you how heavily he is handicapped by ignorance, and that when he goes into the labour market he must either accept a job that nobody else will have, at starvation wages, or he must join the ranks of the unemployed, and become a tramp or a loafer. In either case he is doing a great injustice to his fellow-workers and to the community. If he accepts lower wages than anyboly else, he is helping to pull wages down all round. If he takes to the life of a tramp, he quarters himself on his fellow-men for life, and makes a living out of every one of us without giving us anything at all in return. Sometimes he does even meaner tricks than these. Instead of "bucking up," and pulling him- self together, and sharpening his wits, and turning out better work, he tries to climb by pulling his rivals down. He offers to work for less money, and he is happy if he can undersell better men. He does not always succeed, I am thankful to say, but every attempt of this kind has a tendency to lower the price of labour and make the educated worker suffer for the sins of the ignorant workman. Trades unionism has much to fear from workers of this type, who will not bring themselves up to any reasonable and fair standard of efficiency, and yet they are anxious to undersell labour in the market by pulling down wages to their own level. Lord Bacon says: "I hold every man a debtor to his profession, and as men do seek to receive counten- ance and profit from that profession, so ought they to be a help and ornament thereunto." If Bacon's golden rule were universally observed the ignorant workmen who are levelling down wages would have some lively times, and the honest and intelligent workmen who are levelling them up, would soon belong to the aristocracy of labour. Look for a moment at the crowds of untrained, unskilled workmen who are always out of a job, and in the market. Whose fault is it that so many of them are in this condition. In ninety-nine cases out of every hundred it is their own fault. When they ought to have been at school they were in the streets, graduating as hooligans and loafers. You ask them why they are poor to-day, and they would probably own up that they knew no better. If they knew a more excelleut way they would take it. I spent a Sunday in one of our large Midland towns some time ago, where free breakfasts are given every Sunday morning to all tramps and casuals, who care to call. As these waifs and strays of humanity were putting heaps of bread and butter and buns out of sight, I questioned them as to how they had spent their earlier years. The majority of them could neither read nor write, and for years they had successfully dodged our school attendance officers,and schoolmasters. Only two or three of them had ever served any apprenticeship to any trade, and they were "jacks of all trades and masters of none." More than half of them had been in the army, where they had learned to do as they were told, and ask no questions. They had become mere human machines, of no earthly use to anybody in any emer- gency, and their services to me would be dear at any price. Now I should like to know what you are going to do with a motley crew like that? The root cause of all their trouble is ignorance, and if you could send them all to some training school; or farm colony, and put some new ideas into their heads, you woul.l do them far more good than giving free breakfasts, and casual relief. HESE UNEDUCATED WORKMEN INFLICT MUCH NEEDLESS SUFFERING ON THEM- SELVES. They do not harass and impoverish themselves for pure cussedness, but because they have not wit enough to act wisely. Their suffering is not caused by want of heart, but by want of thought. If they have any brains they never use them, and theynever look an inch beyond their noses. If they lose one job, they either sit still and expect another to drop down from heaven, or they go to seek one in the most unlikely places. Some of them have a perfect mania for trying new situations. You can find them the best job in the world, and they will get tired of it in a few weeks and ' throw it up and go on tramp in search of another. You have to come into personal contact with these restless, uneasy mortals, and hear their stories from their own lips before you can fathom the appalling depth of their ignorance, or understand their crass stupidity. Many years ago I picked up a wrinkle from a young navvy that was a revelation to sue. He was a clean, smart, well-groomed fellow, but he was very tired and footsore, and he was sitting on the bank of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal one hot summer's day, bathing his torn and blistered feet in the cool water. He was suffering intense pain, and seemed completely exhausted by carrying all his worldly goods on his back so many miles. He told me that he had been working at Roch- dale reservoir for a few months, and earning on the average four shillings a day. But he thought he would like a change, so he gave up his situation, and started off to Settle to work on the new railway. He had been there before, and was always sure of a job, but when his old spirit of restlessness came over him he threw it up again. So he was always playing shuttlecock with him- self from one situation to another, and spending a good deal of his time on the road. I I asked him why be did not travel by train on these long journeys. And he asked me if I thought he was fool enough to put his money into the railway com- pany's pockets. He was walking to save his fare, and walking was ever so much cheaper than riding. I told him that was not true,'and that he had not saved a penny by his long tramp, but he had lost a pound or more. He had been taking money out of his own pocket, and pleasure out of his own life, in trying to save three or four shillings. He stared at me in blank amazement, and could not tell what to make of me for a little while At last he asked me to explain how he could have lost anything by walking than he could have got by riding, so I did my best to enlighten him. I had to explain to him that every day he worked he earned at least four shillings, and every day he tramped on the road he earned nothing. But he was spending eighteenpence or two shillings every day on the road,in board and lodgings so if he tramped a whole week he would be four shillings_per day worse off than if he was working all the time. If he had knocked off work on Saturday at noon,and taken train to Settle,he would have had a pleasant ride,and hewould have landed there with nearly a week's wages in his pocket. By tramping all the way he had savedhis railway fare, but he had lost about a golden sovereign, and he had got knocked up, and made footsore into thebargain. What do you think he said when these elementary truths dawned upon him? He simply sat and swore the most miscellaneous collection of polyglot oaths I ever heard in my life. He swore till he nearly made my hair stand on end, and he cursed himself for "all the blanked fools that ever was born." It never dawned on him that time is money, and a week spent on the road is a week's wages lost for ever. I have beard all sorts of language in my time, but that navvy's reproaches against himself took the cake. I do not suppose that he has forgiven himself to this day. ' It took him a long time to realise that his sore feet, and his aching limbs,and his diminishing funds were the

div.p: toll he had to pay for his dense ignorance, and his want of thought. Before I left him he thanked me in his rude wayl and with many swear words for my informa- tion and advice, and he told me I was "a real gentle= man to explain things to a poor devil like him.' I know it is the fashion to sympathise with half- witted fools of this type, and feed them when they are hungry, and nurse them when they are sick, and help them out of every fool's trap they fall into. I do not believe in that silly sentimentalism. If a merciful Providence has given men brains they should use them, and I am under no obligation to provide umbrellas for people who have not wit enough to go in when it rains.

div.head: EDUCATION IN —WARRINGTON. Business of the Next Committee Meeting.
div.p: EDUCATION IN —WARRINGTON. Business of the Next Committee Meeting.
A meeting of the Education Committee will be held on Monday evening. The business will include the following:—
THE RESPONSIBILITY OF HEAD TEACHERS

A report by the district auditor of tg Local Govern- ment Board on his recent audit of the accounts of the Education Committee for the year ended the 31st March last, was submitted to the Finance Committee and, in a discussion which followed as to the method of paying the teachers' salaries, the committee recognised that considerable responsibility was placed upon the head teachers with reference to their returns of the attend- ance of the teachers at school, and, it being reported that inaccuracies and oversights had takes place in sending in these returns, it was resolved, that the director be instructed to notify the head teachers that any oversights or inaccuracies in the returns of the attendance of all the teachers engaged in the schools will be reported to the committee, and, unless they are satisfied that there is reasonable ground for excuse,each case will be referred by them to the Education Com- mittee for consideration.
THE SECONDARY CLERK.

The Finance Committee resolved.that the resignation of Mr. Herbert Parkinson as secondary clerk be accepted as from the 30th June, 1904. It was also resolved that Mr. Ernest Haigh, at present committee and minute clerk, be appointed 9.5 secondary clerk in place of Mr. Parkinson, resigned), at his present salary; also, that a committee and minute clerk be appointed in succession to Mr. Haigh, at a commencing wage of 17s. 6d. per week; and that the appoint- ment be left in the hands of the Director.
RESIGNATIONS AND APPOINTMENTS.

The resignations of the undermentioned teachers have been accepted by the School Management Committee: —Miss E. C. Wallington, head mistress of the infants' department (Thewlis-street) of the Warrington British school as from the 31st August; Miss Margaret Whittle, assistant, Warrington Parochial Infants' as from May 31st; Miss Maude Nield. assistant, Fairfield National, Upper Girls', 31st May; Miss Jane E. Payne, Certificated assistant, Heathside National, Girls', 30th June ; Miss Margaret E. Taggart, Certificated assistant, Ladies' School- of Industry, Girls', 31st July; Miss Martha Chesworth, Art 50 assistant,Latchford National. Mixed, 31st July; Miss Margaret Caldwell, Certificated assistant, St. Alban's, Mixed, 30th .Tune; Miss Mary A. Lee, Art 50 assistant, St. Alban's, Infants' 31st May; Miss Georgina Barlow, Art 68 assistant, St. Ann's Infants' 31st July. The following appointments are recommended:—Fair- fieldlNational,Upper Girls', Miss Maude Nield, assistant (temporary); Fairfield National Girls,' Miss Ellen Gandy,Certificated assistant; Fairfield National:lnfants' Miss NellieLongbottom,Certificated assistant :Hamilton- street, Girls'' Miss Catherine M. Saxon, Certificated assistant; Hamilton-street, Infants', Mrs. Katharine Sutton, Certificated assistant (temporary);St. George's Mission, Infants', Mrs. Harriet Dakin,Certificated assist- ant (temporary); Silver-street Wesleyan, Infants' Mrs. Margaret D. Carter, Certificated assistant. 'War- rington British Infants' (Thewlis street) Miss Mary Williams, head mistress; Heathside National, Infants' Miss Mary B. Hatton, Certificated assistant; Trinity National, Mixed, Mrs. Florence G. Clibborn, Certifi- cated assistant; (supply); St. Alban's Mixed, Mrs. Mary Montgomery, Certificated assistant • St. Mary's, Latchford, Infant;' Miss Annie Allen, Certificated ass's- tent; St. Mary's, Latchford, Infants' Miss Alice Kitchings, Certificated assistant; Warrington British, Mixed, Mrs. Clara Bowen, Certificated assistant, (supply).

THE FAIRFIELD SCHOOL STAFF. A further letter from the Managers of the Fairfield National school, asking (a) for reconsideration of their request for permission to appoint an additional certi- ficated assistant mistress in the upper girls' depart- ment: and for permission to appoint an additional certificated assistant mistress in the girls' department, wassubmitted. With reference to the application in.., respect of the upper girls' department, it was resolved that a sub-committee, consisting of the chairman of the committee (the Rev. Morley Stevenson), Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. J. Fulton Smith and Mr. John Upson, be appointed to confer with the managers of the school, with a view to considering the advisability of reorganis- ing the upper girls'and girls' departments. With refer- ence to the application in respect of the girls' depart- ment, the committee were of opinion that the staff of that department required strengthening, and, in order that advantage might be taken of the fact that teachers would be soon leaving college and would be available after the midsummer holidays, it was resolved that per- mission be given for the appointment of an additional certificated assistant mistress : and that the decision as to the department to which this teacher should be finally attached be deferred until the receipt of the report of the sub-committee appointed to confer with the managers of the school. Permission was given for the appointment of a certificated assistant mistress at Wycliffe British in place of Miss Critahley,resigned. An application from the managers of the Beathside National school for an additional teacher was not acceded to, and it was decided that the vacancy caused in the infants' department of the St. Ann's school by the resignation of Miss Barlow should not be filled.

• TRINITY SCHOOL. An explanation from the managers of the Trinity National school,- together with a letter from H.M. Inspector with reference to entries made by the latter in the log book of the mixed department of that school, was considered, and it was resolved by the School Management Committee that a copy of H.M. Inspector's letter be forwarded to the thanagers of the school and to the head mistress, that their attention be called to the chief points therein, and that an intimation be con- veyed to them that the committee expect the managers and the head mistress to take such action as will ensure that the conduct of the school will meet with the approval of H.M. inspector. HEAD TEACHERS AND THEIR SCALE OF SALARIES. At the meeting of the School Management Committee, a letter from the Hon. Secretary of the Warrington Head Teachers' Association, asking for an explanation of resolution No. c 445, paragraphs (b) and (d), the former referring to the salaries of head teachers above the minimum of the scale,andthe latter to the increases in the salaries of head teachers whose present salaries are above the rate for their years of service,wa.s submitted, and the director was instructed to explain that the term "years of service " in this resolution relates to service since the Ist April, 1903. THE SECONDARY SCHOOL.—FRESH APPOINTMENTS. It having been reported that applications had already been received for the admission of 100 scholars (whose parents are either ratepayers or residents in the Borough) to the Secondary school and to the preparatory pupil teachers' classes, it was resolved that, in order to accom- modhte sixty additional scholars, rooms Nos. 8 and 9 be divided by means of glass screens; and an assistant master, qualified to teach chemistry, physics and general subjects, and an assistant mistress who can teach draw- ing, French and general subjects, be appointed to the Secondary schooll at salaries of £l2O and £llO per annum, respectively. THE PREVALENCE OF INFECTIOUS DISEASE. SUGGESTED CLOSING OF SCHOOLS. A letter, dated the 28th May, 1904, from the Medical Officer of Health, suggesting the desirability of closing all the public elementary schools in the Borough at once until the date already fixed for their re-opening after the midsummer holidays (15th August) owing to the continued prevalence of infectious disease, was submitted to the School Management Committee and it was resolved,that having taken into consideration the fact that twenty-one departments have already been closed during the present school year for periods rang- ing from two to four weeks at a time, and that, during the ten weeks ending the 26th March last, 1,125 (or eight per cent.) of the children have been excluded from attendance at school by the direction of the Medical Officer of Health as suffering from, or being in • contact with, infectious disease, this committee is not Isatisfied that the suggested closure of the schools will have the desired effect.

- _ _ THE ACCOM MOD AT lON QUESTION. In accordance with the decision of the Sites and Buildings Committee at their last meeting, the com- mittee visited various proposed sites for new schools, and instructions were given in certain cases for alterna- tive sites to be obtained.--Letters were submitted from the managers of the Heathside National, Silver-street Wesleyan and Warrington British schools, with refer- ence to the annual cleaning and decorating of the schools, and it was resolved that the managers of all the saki's be asked what action they propose to take in this matter, and that it be left to the Chairman and the Director to call a special meeting of the Committee as soon as this information is obtained. Plans of the alterations proposed to be carried out, in accordance with the request of the Committee, at the Heathside National and Warrington Parochial schools, having been submitted, it was resolved that the alter- ations in question, as set forth, be appioved, and that Plans be forwarded to the Board of Education for their approval. A letter was submitted from the Managers lof the Wycliffe British school, submitting their pro- posals with regard to the alterations and improvements to that school, and it was resolved that the proposed alterations, in-so-far as they were submitted, be approved, but that the managers he asked why they do not propose to carry out the remainder of the alterations required by the committee. A resolution of the School Attendance Committee, with reference to the urgent need of additional school accommodation, was sub- mitted, and the Director was instructed to inform that committee that every possible effort is being made to supply the accommodation required as speedily as possible.
