div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A SUSPICIOUS CHA.RACTER DETECTED BY A. GIRL.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court onMonday,a rough-looking man who gave the narne of RiehardJones, and said he was a cotton operative, was charged with having been a suspicious character found loiterilg in Paul-street and Enstance-street at 9.25 on Saturday night, for an unlawful parpose.—The Chief Constable,in .applying for a remand until to-day Saturday) said that on the night in question Miss Davies,the little daughter of Mr. Thomas Davies, of Paul-street, was left alone in the house. Her parents had gone out to complete their day's marketing, as men of the prisoner's class very well knew. The little girl had just seen her younger sister safely to bed, and was looking out at the bedroom window when she saw the prisoner going along the houses at the opposite side of the street. He tried the doors of the houses, and when he failed to get an answer he peeped through the keyholes. The girl very intelligeatly kept the prisoner under observation, and then went downstairs. When she reached the bottom of the stairs she heard the bell ring. She did not answer the door at once, but heard a noise as though someone was trying to insert an instrument in the key- hole withhich to open the door. The girl then went to the door and upon opening it cautiously was con- fronted by the prisoner who immediatelyasked her why she did not open the door when he rang. Being frightened the girl went away from him, and just then her parents came upon the scene. The girl pointed out -the prisoner, and he was 'afterwards taken into custody by P.C.Sweeney. Prisoner could give no satisfactory account of himself, but merely stated that he was a cotton operative. , There were too many of that class of men going about, and he (the Chief Constable) asked for a remand in order that prisoner's antecedents might be inquired into.—P.S. Sweeney deposed to having arrested the prislmer,and a remand was granted until to-day Satur- day).

div.head: DRUNKEN FREAK.
div.p: A DRUNKEN FREAK.

Two respectable young men appeared at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court on Saturday morning as the result of indulging in a lark with a bicycle which did not belong to them. The prisoners were Joseph Taylor, 10, Neston-street, and Alfred Rose, 13, Catherine-street, and they were charged with having stolen a bicycle in Bewsey-street, the previous night, the property of William Butler Smith,painter and decorator,43, Bewsey- road.—Prisoners admitted being in possession of the bicycle, but denied that they took it with felonious intent.—Superintendent Monaghan said that at about 10.25 on Friday night, prosecutor went into lqalkin's chip potato shop for some refreshments, leaving his bicycle outside under the window. Upon coming out he found that the machine had been taken away,and a man named James Gibbons told him he had seen the prisoners going down the street with it. Prosecutor immediately went after them, and came up with them in Foundry- street. He told the prisoners, both of whom had hold of the bicycle,that it belonged to him, but one of them replied, "We have it now." Taylor then ran away up Foundry-street, and Rose pushed the machine to prose- cutor, told him he could have it, and ran up Bewsey- street. For nearly an hour Drosecntor followed on his bicycle after the prisoner, and eventually watched him near Froghall Bridge. where he was handed into the custody of P.C. Hamblett. While being followed Rose threatened " ANhat he would do " for prosecutor. At the Police Station,prisoner refnsed to give any informa- tion about the man Taylor, but the latter was subse- quently arrested.—Corroborative evidence was given by prosecutor. and the man James Gibbons,a labourer, re- siding in Haydock-street, deposed to having seen the two prisoners take the bicycle away.—For the defence prisoners stated they" had had a drop of drink and thought they wouldhave a ride." They were only "lark- ing" with the machine—The magistrates imposed a fine of 20s. including costs.

div.head: CYCLIST Arr.tc KED NE kr:, WARRINGTON.
div.p: CYCLIST Arr.tc KED NE kr:, WARRINGTON.

- - - -- At the Warrington Occasional 'Court, yesterday. before Mr. F. Monks and Mr. F. A. Frost, John Coneannolv and John Snay, two farm labourers, were charged with assaulting Thomas Hughes of Kingswond. Frodsham, at Little Legh on Sunday night.—Thomas Hughes stated he was returning to Little Legh in comppany with a Mr. Grice on his bicycle. When near the Legh Arms near Acton Bridge he saw four men in the road. On approaching them he was knocked off his machine and was struck a severe blow in the eye, by one of the men. He did not recognise the man who struck him.— Mr. Grice, farmer. Kingswood, Frodsham, said he was in company with Mr. Hughes. When near Acton Bridge, Mr. Hughes was knocked off his bicycle. He saw the two prisoners there. The prisoner Concannoly rushed at him with a bottle and threatened to strike him. When charzed, both prisoners denied the assault.—The magis- trates dismissed the assault, as there was not sufficient evidence to convict.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Gases.

MoNDAY.—Before the Mayor, Alderman Bolton (presid- ing), Aldermen Smethurst and Hutchinson, Councillor, Thornton, and Messrs. T. Birchall, J. W. Hayward and E. Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For these offences the following were fined :—John Dolan, 51, Foundry-street, s. 6d.,- John Whittaker, 3. Jolley's-court, 10s. and costs; Thomas Cullen, 34, Rose and Crown-street, 10s. and costs; George Johnson, no settled abode, 10s. and costs; William Coyne, 34, Rose and Crown-street, 10s. and costs; Thomas Morris. 31, Dolman's-lane, ss.—For having been drunk it charge of a horse and trap in Sankey-street, on Sunday night, NVilliam Lythgoe, engine driver, Martinscroft, was fined ss. and costs; Charles Straw, 70, Winwick-street, was fined a like sum for having been drunk in charge of a pony and trap in Battersby-lane on the Bth June. WITHOUT A LIGHTED Lip.—Robert Brown, "boots" at the Patten Arms Hotel, was fined 2s. 6d. for riding a bicycle without having a lighted lamp attached at 10.10 on June 2. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—A fine of 2s. 6d. as imposed on Thomas De. ,n' I, Peers-court, for havirg allowed the chimney of 1. s dwelling-house to be on fire on June 8.

TtiESDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) und Hutchinson, and Mr. J. R. Young. IMPUDENT THEFT.---Jobn Edwards, last from Man- chester, was charged with stealing from the backyard of an unoccupied house, 37, Bewsey-street, on May 25th, -1903, a leaden pipe of the value of 20s.—Superintendent Monaghan said that on the date in question Mr. Barlow, who resided next door, heard the noise of knock- ing at the house in question, and on going to the back saw the prisoner in the act of cutting the pipe from a wall. He spoke to him about it,and prisoner went away. Later in the evening he returned with a handcart for , the pipe. Mr. Barlow ordered him away, so he left the pipe and went off. Inquiries were made by P.C.Clough, but prisoner had left the town and was only arrested on Monday by Detective Meacock. When charged he said "I wish I had taken two instead of one."—Prisoner

now stated that he was in drink at the time, and he was very sor:y.—Superintendent .Nlon ighan said prisoner made his 40th appearance and was nothing but a prowl- ing .thief.—fle was sentenced to two months' hard labour.

FRIDA Yi.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst and Bennett,Co unc i 110 rs Roberts, Thornton, Tinnion, Wilkinson, Messrs. H. Roberts, Hepherd, W. Roberts) C. S. Burgess, L. W. Reynolds Edwin Woods, G. Piling, C. J. Holmes, and W. Richardson. DOGS WITHOUT LICENCES.—The following were fined in the costs (75.) for keeping dogs without licences : Joseph Brierley, 277; Knutsford-road; Percy Bate, 50, Elaine-street; John Waring, 39, St. Mary-street; Thomas Gresty, 12, Admiral-street. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—James Barton, 63, Laira- street, was summoned for working, a horse whilst in an unfit state on June llth.—John Barton, 101, Birchall- street, was summoned for causing the horse to be worked.—The evidence showed that the horse was attached ton lurry laden with coal. On turning out of Bewsey-street into Horsemarket-street, the animal fell down. On examination, P.C. Gibbs found a large wound, full of matter, under the saddle.—Defendants %ere fined 20s. and costs elf.h.

div.head: WIRRAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: WIRRAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.
A Great Stock Exhibitioa.

The 62nd annual show of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Society, which opened on Tuesday, is now one of the most important in the country. Its open classes attract exhibits of high merit from all parts of England: Toe "district" properly so called of the show stretches from Preston on the north to Stoke-on-Trent on the south, and from Dewsbury on the east to Colwyn Bay on the west, and includes some rich agricultural areas. Two years ago the Society acquired a large perm-inent shewground at Bebington, which has led to an iacre Ise in the prestige of the show. From the point of view of the casual visitor. it is an attractive one. Passing through a pretty gabled building at the entrance,ihe finds himself in a sort of big bazaar, with bright stalls all round full of everything that has the faintest con- nection with agriculture, from motor-cars down to horse medicines. Further on is the show-ring, a very extensive piece of turf, where the big horses parade before the judges and the jaunty turnouts are displayed The entries this yearnumbered3,72l,compared with 3,309 in last year's show. The increase is accounted for by a striking development in the exhibition of dogs. A curious circumstance attends this show, inasmuch as the weather is almost invariably bad on the first day. The fine morning on Tuesday made it seen likely that the old custom was going to be broken, but in the afternoon the rain came down heavily. High praise may be given to the general quality of exhibits. There were about 650 horses and a noticeable feature was the widening of the area from which the horses came. Many of the finest animals came from Scotland, others from Yorkshire, and a fee from South Wales. In many classes, how- ever, the Cneshire horses won a good share of prizes, especially in the section of hunters. In these classes first prizes were won by Messrs. E. Powell (Chester), A. C. Carr (Broxton), G. Denison (Chester), F. Gibbons (Salop), and J. H. Stokes (Market Harborough). Among the hackney horses, Mr. Carr and Mr. Joseph Taylor (Birkenhead) were prominent prize-winners, and in general the beet horses were those sent in by Yorkshire exhibitors—Messrs. A. A. Hayley (Melton), T. P. Robinson (Wigeington), Stephen Cliff (Wortley, Leeds), and F. NV. Battle (Driffield). The excellence of the Yorkshire exhibits was notable in this department. In the open competition for hunters, the Macgregor Laird Commemoration Challenge Bowl for the best hunter mare with foal at foot was won by Mr. Austin C. Carr, and in the hackney section the Record Reign Com- memoration Challenge Vase for the best flackney mare with foal was won by Mr. A. A. Haley. The shire horse class3s were all large ones, and con- tained many admirable exhibits. The winners of first prizes included Earl Egerton of 'fatten. Sir P. A. Muntz M.P. (Rugby), the Hon: V. C. W. Cavendish, M.P., Messrs. C. Bell (Norley), W. F. S. Humphreys (Montgomery- shire), E. Davies (Partington), and .T. Lewis (Garthmyl, Monmouthshire). The district classes for agricultural horses were also excellent. The riding, turnouts, and harness classes all gave rise to close competitions. There were 139 entries of cattle. Among the prize-winners for shorthorns aay be mentioned Messrs. R. Taylor (Carnoustie),H. S. Leon (Bletchlev), G. Harrison (Dar- lington), Captain W. B. Harrison (Lichfield), R. W. Rothwell (Preston), and F. Miller (Birkenhead). The classes for cows and two-year-old heifers were especi- ally good. The dairy CCAVS, though excellent were not perhaps up to the very high qu ility usual at this show. Mr. S. S. Rain.gill (Alt inehain) won first prizes. The Channel Islands cattle were first-rate. Captain %V. B. Harrison and Captain L. G. Gishorne (Derby) won the chief awards. In general the cow classes were notice- ably excellent, and the balls in the yearling class were singled out for judicial recemmendetion. The 1,381 dogs, of every conceivable breed, included many winners of championships well known to those interested in the subject. Champion prizes for sheep Were won by Messrs. R. P. Cooper (Lichfield) and Mr. F. Miller (Birkenhead) There were also exhibitions of pigs, poultry, and agri- cultural produce. The implement section was promin- ent,and there was quite an imposingarray of meter-cars. The judging began on Tuesday morning, but it was far from completed at the close of the day, and a good deal was left over to the remaining two days of the show. There was a big crowd to watch the judging and the spirited leaping competitions. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Walton Hall, Warrington, secured the champion prize for the best pig class 3, middle white boar, (not exceeding nine months), while he also carried off the following awards : Class 1, large white boar, first prize; large while sow second prize, middle white sow 1 and 2,and sow of any breed 2 and 3. Messrs. Ga,rtons,Limited,seed growers and merchants, Warrington, were well represented, and exhibited their new and improved breeds of farm plants, including their famous Excelsior, Storm King, and Improved Abundance oats; the Maltster, Invincible, Stand well and Eclipse, six-rowed barleys, also their new and im- proved breeds of grasses, clovers, swedes, mangels, turnips, &c., Sze. Other local exhibitors in this depart- ment of the show were Messrs. P. Dobbins, of Chester Messrs. Day and Sons, of Crews; Messrs. Henry and Julius CTsar, Knutsford, and Messrs. J. A. Lawton aeid Company and McHattie and Company, of Chester. There was a consensus of opinion that a better lot of yearling's, heavy, massive, and sound, have rarely been seen at a show. The yearling fillies were very fashion- able, and Mr. Gould had not the best luck to be this, and again in e fine class of two-year-olds Lymm Bloom was certainly close to the daughter of Sir Alan Hender- son's Champion, sho.vn by Mr. Lewis. A famous old grey mare headed the class for those with foal at foot, and then came Lord Egerton's Lord Warden Gem, a heroine of many rings, but not showing her best form. Mr. Kenworthy won the Lever challenge 50 guinea bowl for the best stallion belonging to a member with Dela- mere %Var:ior, shown in useful form. His cup, value 50 guineas.went to Mr. Bell for his mare with foal at foot. Mr. Gould's Lymm Champion won on his merits in the district yearling stallion class, and he was again at the top in fillies with Lyme' Bloom. The Band of H.M. 2nd Life Guards was inattendance, and discoursed an excellent selection of music under the conductorship of Mr. Charles Hall, and practical lectiires in beekeeping (including demonstrations) were given by the Rev. T. 3. Evans, and proved highly instructive. The leaping of hunters over hurdles and water, and the parade of motor cars in the large judging ring attracted considerable attention. An enormous c rowdassembled on Wednesday afternoon in the horse ring, to witness the trotting in harness and the leaping. The feature of the harness class was the really fine collection of pairs in class 78. The animals did some very pretty work, and first honours went to Mr. John Kerr, M. P., for a superb pair of bay geldings A slight accident happened to Mr. W. J. Milton's team owing to the spiritedness of the leader. The leaping competition again afforded much enter- tainment, a good deal of which was due to the peculiar horsemanship of Mr. John Taylor, of Ormskirk,and the antics of his black naare,Lady Somerset. After a thorough trial the judges awarded the first prize to Rufus, a chestnut gelding owned by Mr. F. V. Grange, Farndon ; the second to Mr. B. Robins's hay gelding; and the third to Mr. George Ledsona's Pioneer, which was similarly placed on the previous day. The third and final day on l'hursday of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Show was a big success, the attendance and recei ts being considerably in advance of the corresponding day last year, owing in a large measure to the fact that the Birkenhead half-holiday on this occasion coincided not with the second but with the last and most popular day of the show. Despite a boisterous element, the weather was delightful, and in the afternoon the visitors crowded every part of the yard. Some disappointment was expressed at the removal on the previous night of the dogs, poultry, and pigeons, but for that the officials were in no way to blame. Dog-owners will not exhibit at any outside show for more than two days, and owing to the show being held in the breeding season the owners of the feathered exhibits had made a similar stipulation. Thursday's principal awards were as follows :—The George Harding Cup (replacing the W. H. Lever Cap which was won outright last year by Mr. Kenworthy) for the best shire stallion. Sir P. A. Muntz, M.P. ; re- serve Mr. Kenworthy. Warwick Fowle Challenge Bowl for the best tradesman's turnout, T. G. Rowe' Greaeby; reserve, %V. J. Milton, Birkenhead. • Lawton Challenge Cup. for the best horse and gig, W. J. Tatem, Cardiff. The trotting in harness and the leaping again proved very attractive. The prizes for leeping went (1) to Mr. F. V. Grange, Farndon (Hardcash) : (2) to Mr. B. Robbins, Rickmansworth (bay gelding) ; and (3) to Mr. Arthur Jo' ileg Llanddanial. The consolation prizes were won (1) by Mr. Arthur Jones (bay gelding) ; (2) Mr. F. G. Liddle, Hull (Little John); and (3) Mr. James Dodwell, Dumfries (High Life.)

div.head: PROSPEROUS INSURANCE COMPANY.
div.p: A PROSPEROUS INSURANCE COMPANY.

It is satisfactory says the Observer to see that Eng- lish Fire Insurance Companies continue to flourish in spite of some big lopes at home and abroad. The recent report of The Royal Exchange Assurance Corporation is alike gratifying to the proprietors and insured since after adding a substantial sum to the Reserve Fund, the directors are able to contemplate with equanimity their lopes from the Baltimore Fire which are indeed nearly met by the increased receipts from premiums last year.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 18 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 18 1904

forward the aims of the Unions and their, Assessment Committees VI this connection. It was, therefore, at length agreed to meet in London on June 17th. It was also agreed to send copies of the three resolutions adopted by the National Conference to eveiy Union in England and Wales, and to every member of Parlia- ment, and to request every Union which has not already done so to pqition the House of Commons against or for the drastic amendment of the Bill. The question of the method by which the expenses of the committee, engaged in this arduous and important task of defend- ing the interests of Unions throughonl the country, should be defrayed was discussed. It 'was at length agreed that it should be dealt with by the National Committee as the Lancashire Committee had no real authority to settte the matter. Continuing, Mr. Jolley said it was pretty clear that the bill was rather a serious blow at the authority and influence of Boards of Guardians. It looked as though the bill were a step in policy which might easily lead to a great deal of trouble.- It was a bill calculated to bring about the gradual extinction of Boards of. Guar- dians and the substitution of paid officials for the voluntary local work, which on the whole he ventured to think had been admirably done by the representa- tives of the people in the past. (Hear, hear.) In view of that he thought they were perfectlyjustified—and he hoped they would be quite unanimous—in petitioning against the Bill. The resolution was carried unanimously and it was decided that Colonel Pilkington M.P., be requested to present the petition.

div.head: WARRINGTON DAD OF GUARD:ANS. The Congested State of the House.
div.p: WARRINGTON DAD OF GUARD:ANS. The Congested State of the House.

A meeting of —the Warrington Board of Guardians was held in the Board room at the Workhonse on Wednesday morning. Mr. A. Brooks presided and there were also present : Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Rev. Father Mercer. Dr. Murray, Messrs. J. W. Knowles, J. Clarke, S. Davies, J. Payton, R. Balton, A. J. Jolley,J. Billinge, IT. Ritchie, %V. Flannagan, %V. Houghton, G. Thompson, G. Mather, J. 'Parton, E. Forshaw, P. Longton, with J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master) and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schools). SHALL THE BOYS WEAR TWEED SUITS? The Pa,dgate Schools Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Singleton for the purchase of pigs, now fit for consumption, at Bs. 2d. per score be accepted also that the purchase of store pigsbe left to the chair- man. It was further recommended that the chairman be requested to arrange with the contractors for the new boiler, and to make such arrangements as may be , necessary to ensure a temporary supply of water while the new boiler is being fitted in its place. After con- sideration of the minutes of May 17th, which had been referred back for further consideration it was agreed that tweed suits be provided for wearing on Sundays and when walking out, for the boys in the homes. Mr. MATHER moved the confirmation of the minutes. . Mrs. WILKINSoN seconded. Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON said if the Board agreed to the minutes respecting tweed suits they would be go- ing in for an extravagant .and unnecessary annual ex- penditure at the schools. He moved that the resolution referring to tweed suits be the subject of a special notice to the members for the next meeting. There was not a full meeting of the committee and the recom- mendation was only carried by a majority of one. There was so much to be said on the matter—not only on financial grounds but on others—that the change ought not to be made until the recommendation had been placed on the agenda for the next meeting. The CLERK.said the matter was very fully discussed at the last meeting and much of what Mr. Houghton had on his mind was referred to. Mr. CLARKE seconded Mr. Houghton's amendment. On a vote being taken, the amendment was carried,and the minutes were then confirmed with the exception of that referring to tweed suits. THE ACCOMMODATION QUESTION. TARVIN AUTHORITY TO BE COMMUNICATED WITH. The printed report of the sub-committee appointed to deal with the congested state. of the House was sub- mitted, in which the following conclusion was recom- mended:—" That a building suitable for the aged and infirm inmates intermediate in character between the Infirmary and Workhouse proper, and of as inexpensive a nature as possible be provided, to accommodate at least 109 persons. and so arranged as to allow for , further extension needed." Mr. A. J. Jolley moved the , adoption of the resolution and Mr. Mather seconded. , Mr. Jonner-Fust, Local Government Board Inspector, also addressed the committee in favour of the sub-cona- , ruittee's recommendations, and pointed out that the crowded state of the House had been reported to him on more than one occasion, and that if Guardians had not moved in the matter it would have been his duty to have directed the attention of the Local Government Board to the needs of the Workhouse. MR. FORSHAW proposed as an amendment that the committee recommend to thoGnardians the following : "That the consideration of this matter be postponed until the Clerk can make representations to the Tarvin Guardians as to whether they are prepared to receive a number of inmates from the Warrington Union, and if so; at what cost per head per week." Mr. Thompson seconded and on being put to the meeting, the amend- ment was declared carried, 8 members voting for it out of 15. The Master reported that the lodge had been ransacked by some person yet unknown and the belong- ina's of two vagrants stolen. The two men in question had preferred a claim for compensation for their losses, and the Master was instructed to pay to each, the sum of 10s. from his petty cash. At, a subsequent meeting four tenders were dealt with for a supply of a 30 gallon beef tea extractor, and it was resolved to accept that of Messrs. Summerscales, of Keighley for the inclusive sum of £.2i. The question of intproving. the training of the probationer nurses was adjourned for a fortnight. Mr. Mathias, borough electrical engineer, having reported favourably, it was decided to accept the estimate of Messrs. H. Wood and Company, Man- chester, for putting down a new cable from the power station to the laundry for £2l, and for wood troughing and bitumen to lay.fthe cable at 3s. 2d. per yard, approximate distance 80 yards.—A deputation from the Health Committee, consisting of Councillor James Evans and Barton visited the Workhouse on May 31st, for the purpose of inspecting the new laundry and were very kindly received by the Master. The• deputa- tion afterwards visited the hospital and other parts, and found everything in connection therewith in a very excellent state of efficiency. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved, and Mr. G. Mather seconded the confirmation of the minutes. The minutes were passed without comment. A discussion then ensued as to the instructions to be given to the Clerk in his inquiries respecting the reception of inmates at Tarvin Workhouse. Mr. A. J. JoimEvsaid he sympathised with the Clerk in his desire to have something definite to go upon. It was a farce for any member to think that the Tarvin Union would accept the Warrington inmates in the winter only. The Warrington Board would have to be prepared to send them permanently. , • Mr DAVIES pointed out that the Beard had spent considerable sums on building schemes during the past few years. The hospital was built with the object of relieving the pressure on the workhouse accommoda- tion, but now there was a cry for more room. The accommodation was made to suffice in the old days, before the new hospital was built. -He deprecated any building scheme at the present time. Mr. BILLINGS said he agreed with the statement of Mr. Jolley at the committee meeting that the passing of the• Workmen's Compensation Act had thrown many old and infirm men out of employment, and conse- quently on the funds of the Union. He thought perhaps the Schools Committee might send some of the older boys and girls out to work. Mr. MATHER said there were no boys or girls ready to go out. It was decided that the Clerk have an interview with the Clerk of the Tarvin Union, and see upon what terms I inmates would be accepted from Warrington. THE VALU ITION BILL. The CHAIRMAN and Mr. A. J. JOLLEY (chairman of the Assessment Committee) reported noon the proceed- ings of the conference of Boards of Guardians held at ICaxton Hall. Lcfndon, on June 3rd, and upon an inter- view with Mr. Long, president of the Local Govern- ment Board. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Jolley and he attended the conference, and considering the very short notice which was given, the meeting was an emi- nently successful one. Over 150 unions were repre- sented. The meeting passed off not quite unanimously but almost unanimously. Any lack of unanimity was tending to more stringent resolutions than those which the Lancashire committee had put before the London meeting. A deputation yas sent from the meeting to meet Mr. Long the president of the Local Government Board, and as Mr. Jolley was one of the deputation, he (the chairman) would ask Mr. Jolley to take up 'the • matter from that point. In the meantime he would move that the following petition to Parliament be approved: •" That whilst cordially approving the principle of uni- formity of valuation, the Guardians of this Union dis- approve of the bill now before Parliament, being satis- fied that in its present form the bill will fail to secure the desired parpose and will in effect aggravate exist- ing anomalies and inflict injustice upon aggrieved rate- payers ; the Guardians therefere petition the House of Commons to reject the bill." I Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded the proposition. The resolutions drafted by thelLancashire Committee, three lin number, he said, were carried unanimously with the ' exception of three dissentients to the second; and their , only objection was that the resolution as drawn was not quite strong enough. A deputation consisting of the Lancashire Committee and 20 others from various parts of the country was then appointed to lay these resolutions before the President of the Local Govern- ment Board. •Mr. Long had limited the deputation to two speakers, and Mr. Brown, of Dewsbury, and Mr. Bevan, of Cardiff, were chosen to voice the sentiments of the representatives of England and %Vales, which they did with clearness and force, urging that though ; the avowed purpose of the Bill—uniformity of valuation—was admirable, the Machinery proposed to be sat up was unworkable, and would aggravate instead of removing existing anomalies and inequities. Mr. Long, in his reply, was conciliatory and complimen- tary, and expressed his willingness to give most careful consideration not only to the three resolutions sub- I mitted to him, but to any further proposals they, might formulate and which they might think likely to facilitate the attainment of the purpose or to improve the machinery proposed to be slt up by the Bill. On the Conference resuming, at 2 p.m., Mr. Brown reported the result of .the interview with Mr. Long. After a full and, at times, heated discussion, it was agreed unani- mously that in view of the Government's evident determination—to proceed with the Bill—despite Mr. Long's professed readiness to consider amend- ments of detail—a committee should be formed to organize opposition to the Bill, in accordance with the three resolutions agreed upon and communicated to the President of the Local Government Board, to try to secure amendments, and, if deemed necessary, to again convene the Conference. This committee was to consist of the Lancashire Committee with the 20 who had been added from other districts to form the depu- tation to the President of the Local Government Board. On June 7th he (Mr. Jolley) attended a meeting in Manchester of the Lancashire Special Committee; this had been informally agreed upon by the Lancashire members at the conclusion of the National Conference lon .Tune 3rd. Mr. Brown, of Dewsbury, had been con- sulted, and quite concurred in their again taking the initiative, and further expressed his willingness to accept their decision as to the time and place of meeting of the National Committee to 'formulate definite pro- posals for submission to Mr. Long. It WAS felt to be inexpedient to convene the first meeting in Lancashire, lest any feeling of irritation or local jealousy should be aroused. Leeds and Birmingham were suggested as possibly suitable, but it was felt that London was the most suitable place for the first meeting, and also as ' affording, at this time, opportunities for approaching members of Parliament and in various ways helping

div.head: REV. H. DUNNICO AND THE LICENSING BILL.
div.p: THE REV. H. DUNNICO AND THE LICENSING BILL.

Notwithstanding the intense belt, a good congrega- tion assembled in the Parr Hall on Sunday evening when the Rev. H. Dunnico gave an address upon the "Licensing Bill." If there was one subject more than another upon which the Christian minister should speak in no uncertain tone he said, it was upon the liquor traffic. Therefore, he (the preacher) made no apology for dismissing such a question as the "Licensing Bill." He newer had and never would drag party politics as such into the pulnit or on the religions platform Questions which affected merely the commercial or material interests of the intion might be left alone by the religion's telcher, but those questions bearing upon the moral welfare of the people ought not to be rinsed . over in silence by the watchmen of God, and it was hecamse this question had an important bearing upon national life and charac- ter that he appealed to them irrespective of creed or party to listen to what he had to say. The drink trade was the greatest hindrance to the spread of the gospel in the land; it was the source of more evil, tyranny, vice, suffering and degradation than all other causes put together, not excepting our present competitive system

A POLICY OF BRIBES. - The present Government stated that this Licensing Bill had for its object temperance reform, but such a statement was sheer hypocrisy. It had introduced it because it dare not do any other, and hoped to remain in power. He believed with Dr. Clifford that the House of Commons was just now the theatre of the most despicable and disgraceful proceedings that had ever disgraced English public life. The Conservative party was an ancient party. On more • than one occasion it had rendered good service to the State, possibly it would do so again, but the present party had outraged every canon of morality. By an outrageously iniquitous Education Act it had sacrificed the liberties of the English people to the plans of a scheming priesthood and thus bribed the priests and the majority of the parsons. By the legislation of Chinese slavery it had bribed the South African Rand Owners and now by the introduction of this bill it sought to hand over to the rich brewer a present of £300,000,000 and thus bribe the magnates of the mash tub. Mr. Balfour had stated that this bill would promote temperance reform but Mr. Balfour had told them so many things which were not true that he preferred to analyse the bill for himself and draw his own conclusions.

WHIT TILE BILL PROPOSES. Well what did this bill propose? In the first place it sapped popular control by depriving tie magistrates of discretionary powers with regard to the renewal of licences and transferred that power to Quarter Sessions. Secondly it created a vested interest in that which hither- :to had been a yearly 'fleasehold. Thirdly, it arrested the necessary suppression of licences by limiting that sup- pression by an unjust and illegal form of compensation. Let them consider the first proposal, that which deprived the magistrates of discretionary power.

div.head: NOT AN IDEAL LICEN-SCNG BF:NCR.
div.p: NOT AN IDEAL LICEN-SCNG BF:NCR.

He did not for one moment contend that the present constitution of the licensing bench was an ideal one, still one of the most hopeful signs in our national life of late had been the awakening of the conscience of the magistrates. They had begun to realise that they were there to protect the poor and humble and those who suffered from the ravages of strong drink rather than to protect those who profited by the sale of it. Conse- quently they decided to &duce the number of unneces- sary licences because they must bear in mind that for a many years these licences were scattered free as from a i pepper box all over the country. How many did the magistrates close? They thought that possibly they might close say one in 300 without plunging the • nation into chaos and ruin. What was the result? ! —this Bill which sought to deprive them absolutely of ; their power. The greatest Statesman of the last I century. Mr. W. E. Gladstone, had said that the supreme I purpose of legislation was to make virtue easy and vice difficult, and this the magistrates in a slight degree had been inclined to do, but this was the treatment meted out to them by the degenerate politicians of to-day. Well, waving aside the snub which this Bill administered to the local justices, was there any sense or reason in taking this power out of the hands of the local justices who were daily,if not hourly, passing to and fro in the neighbourhood and transferring that power to the men who sat on the Quarter Sessions bench and who in all probability knew little,if anything,about local circum- stances and local requirements.

div.head: MAGISTRATES DEPRIVED OF POWER.
div.p: MAGISTRATES DEPRIVED OF POWER.

But what in his opinion constituted the most serious objection to this clause was not so much the actual , number of houses that might be closed by the magis- trates if unhindered,but the depriving them of the power to close them. It was the knowledge possessed by the 1 publican that his licence was granted for one year only, land that its renewal depended upon the decision of the local justices that acted as a check to evil, and placed in the hands of the local authority . the only power whereby they could exercise any ' control whatever, and impose such conditions as should secure the good conduct of the house ,In Liverpool, for instance, long before the passing of the Bill prohibiting the sale of drink to young children ' the Liverpool magistrates in virtue of this power had , been able to put a stop to this practice. In like manner such practices as giving sweets to children, selling ! drink on credit, giving the long pull and many other things had been stopped simply because the power of renewal was in their hands. This bill,howeve-,proposed to put an end to it. Moreover at the present time the local justicas met not as a strictly judicial court but as a committee to take into consideration the needs of the neighbourhood and to act accordingly. They were corn- pelled to give ear to all public objections but the present bill took away that privilege. No one,not even the police would be allowed to oppose the granting of a licence before Quarter Sessions. The whole bill was a piece of tubtle trickery. LEASEHOLD PROPERTY TO BE MADE FREEHOLD. Again this bill sought to create what had hitherto been a yearly leasehold into an unlimited freehold to endow the rich brewer at our expense. This was a most out- rageous and iniquitous propos il. As early as thd time of Henry VII. it was found necessary to place restric- tions on the sale of drink. The powers that were" decided that licences should be granted not for the sake •of enriching the holders but in order that the public might be protected from what experi- ' ence had proved to be a dangerous trade. Certain men who were considered trustworthy were solicited to keep these ale houses, and the Act of 1552 , was passed prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquors wherever it was thought to be inconsistent with the public good. The licence granted was not a property, it was simply a limitation of a troublesome trade. It could not be sold or even transferred by the personl holding it. It was granted for one year and no longer, at the end of that time it died a natural death, it carried with it no claim of renewal, in fact it could not be , renewed. The person holding it might make applica- tion for a new licence and if the magistrates deemed it expedient they might grant it, if not, refuse it. For , nearly 400 years that law had held good and now this Government by one f mil stroke proposed to make this yearly licence into a property, and thereby presented to the trade at our expense a free gift of 400 millions at least. What did the trade present the nation with in return—lunacy, misery, crime, degraded manhood and disgraced womanhood.

: NOT OPPOSED TO A SENSIBLE SCHEME OF COMPENSATION. With regard to compensation he was not opposed to a reasonable and sensible scheme of compensation but such compensation must not come either directly or indirectly from the State. Further it must be organised in the interests of the publican and not the rich brewer , but this scheme proposed in this bill would not benefit 1 the licensee in the slightest, only the owner, and when they remembered that 80 per cent. of I on licences were tied houses they would Neat a glance Onto whose pockets the money would go. Another serious objection to this proposal was that it arrested a ' very sensible and honest attempt to reduce the number of unnecessary licences by making it dependent upon a sum of money which could be raised by an altogether inadequate tax. Take Manchester as an example. The maximum amount tint could be raised would be £31,000 and taking a very moderate estimate it would take 40 -years to bring ,Ilanchester down to the level of Liverpool, and Liverpool was far in excess of the number recommended in Lord Peel's report. In conclusion Mr. Dunnico appealed to all present to resist to the very utmost the passing of this measure, because if passed it made the trade secure for all time. To recognise a licence as a property was a shameful endowment of a pernicious trade. Every man, be he Conservative, Liberal, or Labour, ought to put the welfare of the people above the gains of a trade: Let them however toil on, and when the Lour of victory came, as come it must, they would have the glad consciousness that in this great struggle between Heaven slid Hell they had hit hard in the name of the Eternal god.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
THE PAST SEASON REVIEWED.

Very few nlembers of the Warrington Musical Society attended the annual meeting held in Cairo-street school- room on Monday evening, when the past season's work was reviewed, and the officers elected for the ensuing season. The President (Mr. J. C. Parr), presided and there were present: Hr. NV. E. Atkin (hon. secretary), Mr. L. NV. Reynolds (hon. treasurer), Mr. J. Newcombe, Mr. F. H. Crossley (conductor). Mr. NV. H. Wallington, Mr. John Dewhurk, Mr. F. Hickman, Mr. Newall, Mr. Fieldhouse, Mr. R. Whitfield, Mr. A. IL Burgess.

div.head: HON. SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: THE HON. SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. ATKIN, in his report, stated that the season corn- 'mencina with the first rehearsfil on September 22nd, 1903, and ending with the final concert on March 23rd, 1904, was slightly longer than the previous one. A slightly later start was made with the active work of the season but it was impossible to avoid a Lenten concert, and it would be remembered that the previous season ended in February, 1903. The chorus members were called to 27 rehearsals during the season closed, 17 of which were with the orchestra and 10 with the pianoforte accompaniment only; whilst the orchestra, in addition to the practices with the chorus, had nine separate meetings. Thus the mem- bers of the orchestra met 22 times, and the members of the chorus met 27 times. The committee were able to carry out the prospectus in fulland the past season was without a failure of any of the soloists promised in that prospectus. This risk of failure to appear was one which they had to face year by year, and the immediate future of a concert date was an anxious time on that account. The usual three concerts were given, viz., on November 18th, February 10th, and March 23rd last. He expressed great regret that the financial result was again most unsatisfactory. The heartiest thanks of the society were due to the section of the members who so ably performed tie " Yeomen of the Guard" in October, and also to the conductor and the Opera Com- mittee. By this means a handsome sum was handed over to the treasurer,and the finances helped sufficiently to avoid an actual debt. It was disappointing, how- ever, to feel that great success had been followed by loss on the concerts later, and the idea of forming a nucleus of a reserve fund (to which he referred at the last general meeting) by the proceeds of the opera was rendered entirely impossible. The books showed for 1903- 4 :—Sopranos 56,being three less than 1902-3 ;contraltos 43. being three less than 1902-3 ; tenors 20, being four less than 1902-3 ; basses 34, being same as 1902-3 ; or a total of 153 as against 162 chorus members for the pre- vious season. The orchestra membership is 33, the same as the previous season. The committee had met only four times during the season, but its work had been important, and the tremendous speculation in- volved in concert promoting rendered its task a diffi- cult one, and it would seem to point to a still greater economy being necessary (if possible by any means) if the society was to pay its way by its concerts. His thanks were due, and he begged to tender them most heartily, to all the officials of the society, from whom, one and all alike, he had received much help and willing co-operation. _

A.TKIN made one or two verbal additions to the report. The ladies he said, came to their help in February, and a little dance was got up. Financially it was not as successful as the previous ones had been, but they did make a little money. The balance sheet of the society was satisfactory, inasmuch as they appeared before the meeting without a debt, but they ought really, if they had made the concerts pay, to have had considerably more in hand. Steps should. be taken to avoid a loss. It would be a difficult problem to solve, but the committee had already considered the point. Thera was a suggestion to work one concert at very much less Axpense next year if possible. There had been a great falling off in the receipts with regard to the number of tickets sold to other than subscribers —that MS to the general publicp-and the loss was very considerable. The committee had been moderate in their expenditure, and the total was less than during the previous season. They had had an eye to possible loss, and, as far as possible, had reduced their expendi- ture. The falling off in receipts was owing almast en- tirely to fewer tickets being sold to those who were not subscribers. The society was not alone in that respect, as there was scarcely any society or concert promoter who had been able to make both ends meet. There was only one society that he could name that had made a profit. Trade had not warranted people in spending very much money on concert going. THE BALANCE SHEET.

Mr. L. W. REYNOLDS entered into a detailed state- ment with reference to the a3counts. It appeared that there had been a loss on the season's concerts of £69 19s. 3d. The year commenced with an adverse balance of £l6O 2s. Bd., to which had also to be added interest on banking account of £2 4s. 3d. Against this the society had received 2129185. 11d., the surplus from the organ trust account, £134 2s. Bd. net proceeds of the opera" Yeomen of the Guard," and £6 10s 9d. net proceeds of the dance, making a total of £270 us. 11d. At the close Of the year, there was a balance of £3B ss. 9d. carried forward to the succeeding season's accounts.

div.head: Tfll: CHAIRMAN'S OBSERVATIONS.
div.p: Tfll: CHAIRMAN'S OBSERVATIONS.

The PRESIDENT said he was afraid things were not quite as bright and roseate as they would like to see them, but it was satisfactory to know that they were without a debt, which in years gone by they had had to face. Of course, the absence of the debt had been brought about by the transference of the organ into other hands, and the receipts from the opera, the "Yeomen of the Guard," so that they had a balance in hand. He hoped it would stimulate all to do their utmost to keep up that condition of their balance sheet and that they would rs cognize the hint the treasurer had given them that it would require a keen effort on their part to keep free from debt. He regretted the concerts had not been the success they should have been, considering their merit. Whether it was that the people of Warrington found so many other attractions, or whether the classical programme was above the heads of the people, he did not feel competent to say, but the concerts were not a paying asset, and they must, therefore, try all the means in their power to make them a success, because it would nut be satisfactory for a society to go on from year to year and find a debt growing up after the one they had discharged. He was sorry to find that the falling off was largely in the sale of tickets. It looked as if the public generally were not sufficiently alive to the importance of the society, and the very excellent work it was doing, because, as he had often remarked before it was not only catering for the public amusement, but was really an educational institution. (Hear, hear.) I He thought that those who were not already subscribers should recognize the society and give it their support., 'He hoped all the members would do their utmost to make the merits of the society known, and to create an interest in it. (Applause.) Although they had handed over their organ to the Corporation, which personally he was glad of because he thought it ought to be part and parcel of the hall ag it was such a useful adjunct, the society had obtained certain privileges res- pecting it. He would like to recognise the energy, ability and untiring devotion of the conductor. cApplause.) He should not like the meeting to be con- cluded without recognizing, as they all did, the import- ant work he carried on, and the stimuli's he was able to give to the society. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN DEWHURST, in moving the adoption of the report and statement of acolunts, thought it. would be a disgrace to Warrington if it allowed a society like this, which had been established for so many years, to go down, owing to want of support. He was an out- sider, and one of the public. IVith such a chorus, band, organist, and conductor, it would be a disgrace if the society did not prosper. He was delighted with the opera given in October, and he was glad to learn that another opera was to be given this year in aid of the funds of the society. It should be borne in mind that the Warrington Musical Society served to train the choirs of the churches and chapels of the town, and the result of that excellent training was seen Sunday after Sunday. Therefore the respective congregations ought to give the society their warmest support by purchasing tickets lavishly. Mr. FRANK HICKMAN seconded, and pointed out that there was a loss of about £25 on each concert. Would it not be possible to have an absolutely choral concert and an absolutely orchestral concert, which would about cover the deficiency? Mr. ATKIN : That has been considered. What will come of it I don't know, but there is a suggestion to give an orcheqtral concert. - The motion was carried. RE-ELECTION OF THE PRESIDENT.

'Mr. W. H. WALLINGTON moved that Mr. Parr be again asked to accept the position of president. (Applause.) He (Mr. Wallington) was very sorry they could not 'beet under happier circumstances. He had the interests of the society very deeply at heart, but the statement they had had laid before them that night was not by any means satisfactory. He had had to deal with the society far a good many years, and with the exception of one or two seasons, they had never been able to report a victory. They were not hopelessly bankrupt. They had a small balance in hand, but this state of affairs was due to extraneous circumstances. He was only sorry that their Government did not include musical societies in their educational system. (Laughter) Then they might have got something from the rates. It was rather unfortunate, but he did hope that if and applause.)' Mr. the loss of v another Education Bill was introduced musical educa- tion Would be included. In conclusion, he hoped the success of the the last one. (Hear, Mr. FIELDMOUSE crconded. coming hesaear. s The SECRETARY inisupporting the re-election of Mr. Parr as president, said Mr. Parr had always taken a deep interest in the society. The motion was carried unanimously. • Mr. PARR, in acknowledging the compliment, said he ,thanked them very much for the honour they had done him in again electing him president. He had very great pleasure inagain occupying the position, with their kind consent, but he felt it would be under much happier circumstances if the suggestion's made had been carried

out, and the society was paying its way. As president, it might partly be his fault that things were not as suc- cessful as they might be. (Cries of " No, no.") If a more energetic president could be found they might possibly turn over a new leaf. In the event of a more energetic person being found for the position he was quite willing to give way. Until they found one he would accept the office, and do his best to stimulate as far as in his power lay, the position that society ought to take, not only as catering for a musical taste, but as a great musical establishment for the teaching of music to their friends in Warrington. (Applause). VICE-PRESIDENTS AND OTHER OFFICERS.

On the proposition of Mr. NEWALL, seconded by Mr. FIELDHOUSE, the following vice-presidents were re- elected :—Fhe Mayor (Alderman Bolton), Messrs. Ziba Armitage A. H. Crosfleld, James, John and R. T. Fair- clongh, F. A. Frost, F. Monks J. Monro, R. C. Parr, C. E. Parker, R. Pierpoint, Md., Colonel Ridgiray, L. W. Reynolds, H. Roberts, and John White. The committee were re-elected as follows :—Messrs. H. Bond, G. Johnson, J. T. Knowles, J. Newcombe, P. C. Price, W. Scotson, R. H. Silcock, W. H. Wallington, R. Whitfield, with the addition of Mr. A. H. Burgess. Mr. W. E. Atkin was re-appointed hon. secretary, Mr. L. W. Reynolds hon. treasurer, Mr. Johnson hon. librarian, and Mr. J. Newcombe hon. auditor and registrar.

div.head: THANKS.
div.p: THANKS.

On the proposition of the SECRETARY, the thanks of the meeting were conveyed to Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., o:ganist ; R. Afr. H. Pearson, leader of the orchestra ; and Miss Fairclough, for hr services in connection with the dance. Tile secretary tendered his personal thanks to the conductor, Mr. Crossley. Referring to his re-election as hon. secretary, Mr. Atkin said circumstances might arise which would compel him to give up the position, but he would not give it up on the ground that the work was too much. Nevertheless he hopect the committee would be on the look out for someone to step into the position if he were compelled to leave it.

THE CONDUCTOR AND NEXT SEASON'S WORK. Mr. CROSSLEY said he was very grateful for the kind acknowledgment which had been made of his services. He was inclined to think people were taking too gloomy a view of the present situation. The present was only the second time there had been a balance on the right side for the past 14 or 15 years. They had therefore something•to be thankful for. He hoped the next opera would be successful. He had already attended 12 rehearsals for "The Gondoliers." and there was no doubt the next performance would be fully as good as, if not better than, the nerforman3e of the" Yeomen of the Guard " was. But op3ra was not the end of their existence. (Hear, hear). It was nice to help themselves but opera was not what a musical society was intended for. (Hear, hear). Mr. Crossley then read a letter he had received from a lady member of the chorus. He said he did not know who the writer was but she said she was grieved to see from the report such a heavy loss on the season's concerts, and, with a view to economize next year's expenses, she suggested that at the first sub- scription concert" Faust "should be given entirely by their own members, band excepted. This would effect a saving of £3O. She also suggested that the prices for admission to the unreserved portion of the hall be re- duced a little in price. That was a practical suggestion but it had been considered by the committee before. " Faust " had been done twice during the past four or five years. and it was perhaps inadvisable to repeat it so early. The writer brought under their notice the possibility of pro- viding their own member, with a little more solo work. Mr. Hickman had also made the suggestion that they should have one choral concert and one orchestral con- cert. The society's orchestration was not very ex- pensive. If they got up an orchestral concert them- selves they would save perhaps £2O. Of course it would necessitate an entirely different class of music from ' that which they had been giving. They could not do anything in the way of work on the lines suggested. The committee had considered the advisability of making an orchestral concert a special feature, and possibly doing that without any professional singing whatever. The committee thought such a concert might be provided and engage an intrumental soloist. That, he thought, was practicable. Another idea was that they should give "The Messiah "at Christmas. They had not performed it for three or four years, and it might come a little fresh now. As the seasons went on it became more difficult to choose music that would be attractive. Last season it was thought that Hiawatha's "Wedding Feast "would be a popular piece, but it did not draw very well. "The Redemption" was another strange thing. The first time the society performed it it was quite a success. They did it again and there was a very poor audience to listen to it. It was very awkward to know what to do. Star " vocalists were very expensive, but yet when they went round touring with a party they did not get half the fees they charged the society, and it was difficult for musical societies to engage them. No doubt the remarks which had been made that even- ing would help the committee in making some new arrangements. He concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Parr for his excellent services to the society. (Applause.) Mr. NE WALL seconded, and the motion was heartily agreed to. The PRESIDENT acknowledged the compliment, and observed that the suggestions made showed that the members were taking a deep interest in the work of the society.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Latchford.

At this church on Sunday evening the Rev. J. F. Matthews delivered a special sermon to young men on, the subject of "A genuine sixth sense." Special music was creditably rendered by the choir, including an anthem "Arise, shine." Mr. W. T. Wilkinson con- ducted, and Mr. Peter Harrison presided at the organ.
Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church Bible Class.

Mr. J. W. Elaywa,rd presided at an open meeting in connection with the above class which was held on Sunday afternoon. The address was given by the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who took for his subject the words "Who am I, what am I, whither am I going?"

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday. The chair was occupied by Mr. Joseph Owen, who delivered an address on "Success." The attainment of success, he said, was nothing more than doing what could be done, well. Whilst they might not hope for the success that crowded some lives, they might each do what they could, well, remembering that without failure there was no gain. There was a success in life which might be reached by every human being. The building up of a noble life was a work far more important than the accumulation of wealth. and to all was given power, if opportunity was embraced, and exertion made, to make life a success.-111r. William Hickman made a welcome reappearance as a sneaker, after a long absence through illness and bereavement. He spoke upon the subject of the Resurrection and referred to the great hope and consolation which the Christian had through his faith in the resurrection. He showed that the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead was the key-stone of the arch of Christianity, and advanced arguments in sup- port of the Christian's belief.—Miss Griffiths very efficiently sang as a solo" The Good Shepherd."—The service was also taken part in by Mr. B. Farrar and Mr. F. Morrall.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

One of the adjuncts of dress which has this season advanced to a position of some impor- tance among the most popular modes is the shoulder cape or scarf. On all sides we see the deep stole or scarf of several tows of soft marabout feathers in black or brown or dyed to harmonise with the predominating colour in the toilette it completes. Some, indeed, of these pretty scarves (for wraps they really are not in any sense) are of pale colour such as pink or blue shaded from the faintest degree of colour to a deeper tone. It cannot be said that they are easy to arrange or when once arranged kept in place except by the aid of neatly fastened and carefully concealed safety pins, otherwise a very slipshod and untidy- looking result is obtained. These Weather stoles are becoming rather too much in evidence on all and sundry with no apparent connection in many instances with the costume they complete and I therefore recommend the discerning of my readers whc
PRETTY COAT.

may contemplate • the purchase of some such complement of the toilette to select in preference a dainty shoulder cape of silk chiffon and embroidery, which will wear longer and is really more of a novelty than the feather stole. There are many varieties of these ruffles or capes to be bought ready made while with a little taste and the careful study in some shop window of a French model of this sort of thing any girl can evolve out of lace and silk, chiffon and satin, a charming and com- paratively inexpensive little wrap. For those who do not find that this style of wrap proves becoming another equally useful mode will be found in a loose coat of tussore silk lined with soft white silk or satin and trimmed with embroidery or piece lace and dainty cordings and tassels of white silk in the manner depicted in my first sketch. The sleeves are made loose and therefore suited to the protection of the blouse or bodice underneath and are dainty trimmed at the cuffs. The little shoulder cape of lace or em- broidery gives a more finished appearance to the garment. A little coat of this description can be worn with any sort of skirt and the colour of the latter is a matter of no impor- tance. Of course .a warmer and more lasting
A SPORTING CAP.

garment would be obtained if putty-coloured box-cloth (or any cloth of a light colour and weight) were used, but the silk is very durable and cleans well and is less likely to show any marks. It is also cooler for summer wear during the long hot days to which we eagerly and hopefully look forward. Serge, either navy blue or white, is a material which really never disappears from its sphere of usefulness from one year's end to another. Cream serge is used in this instance to form the sporting cap shown in my second sketch. It is piped at the seams with green silk as is also the loose coat which it completes. This shape was, of course, originally designed for motoring but it proved such a success that it is worn by the fashionable girl when engaged in any kind of sport, whether cycling or golfing. It's flat crown is too low to catch the wind and its brim shades the face from rain and shine. One must be careful in selecting a cap of this description to choose one of just the right size to suit the face and height of the wearer as a short girl looks most absurd in a very large size while a stately maiden does not appear
'EAT

properly hatted if she adopts a mall size. They can be bought in all sorts of tweeds and cloths ready made. For motoring, of course, & leather cap of this shape is the most correct and serviceable headgear one can adopt. My last sketch shows a neat costume of light brown holland or crash suited kik early morn- ing wear. It is simply made with a white pique collar and revers finished with twists of white cord. The toilette is completed by a coarse straw toque trimmed with bunches of shaded red geraniums which prove a most effective touch of colour, especially when emphasised by a sunshade to match. I recommend those, who invest M a costume of this material to complete it by a pair of nice brown shoes as this colour looks much better than black with a dress of holland or linen. A material of this kind wears well and is most useful and smart-looking for morning wear in summer with pretty shirts or blouses. In- deed, its value has been so appreciated that there are few well dressed girls who do not possess some such costume. The material which looks best for this purpose is not the stiff, hard fabric of some years ago but a soft, pliable material which does not require to be starched and therefore does not crush readily and so preserves its look longer. It is a great improvement on the old-fashioned variety al- though, perhaps, it is a little more expensive. COQUETTIrj

div.head: BRITAIN'S DECLINE.
div.p: BRITAIN'S DECLINE.
ARE WE LOSING OUR TRADE?
STARTLING SYMPTOMS.

AT the Alexandra Palace there is to be seen stowed away in a corner of that vast building an interesting reminiscence of the late Queen's Diamond Jubilee. It is a screen upon which is pictorially represented the growth of the Empire, its trade and commerce, during the reign of Queen Victoria. During the Jubilee year similar pictures on a smaller scale were scattered broadcast over the country. They showed that the British Empire was the greatest in area the world had ever seen, that its trade had increased by leaps and bounds, that its people were richer, happier, and better than they ever had been. This view Of the British nation was, at the time, generally accepted. The danger of those days was to be too contented with our lot, and to despise our neighbours.

Sudden Change. IT is not long since the Jubilee of 1897, and at that time one of the most confident men in the whole Empire was Mr. Joseph Chamber- lain. Why, then, the sudden change of the last twelve months P If we are to believe the Mr. Chamberlain of to-day rather than the Mr. Chamberlain of the Jubilee year,. all the joyous declarations of the wonderful progress of the past sixty .years were but a vain delusion, the empty boastings of a bankrupt people, whose trade was fast leaving them and whose Empire is tottering to its fall.

Trade Practically Stagnant. MR. CHAMBERLAIN has endeavoured to give the nation a rude awakening from its happy confidence. He has told us: • During the last thirty years our general export trade has remained practically stagnant. Instead 01 extorting manufactures in 'exchange for food and raw material, we are expor ing more and more raw material in the shape of coal, and impotting more and more foreign manufactures. • Putting aside our Colonial trade, our trade with foreign countries had decreased in amount and deteriorated in character. We are no longer first among manufacturing nations, we are third, and shall he fifth or sixth unless we take steps to reverse our present policy of Free Trade. Further, the only hope of retaining our trade is to develop commerce between ourselves and the Colonies, and if we do not do this we shall not only lose our trade, • but the Empire will fall into disjointed atoms.

The Reason Why. BRIEFLY stated, the above is Mr. Chamber- lain's view of our trade and Empire. The first thing that strikes us about this sudden descent from the optimistic heights of the Jubilee year to the pessimistic depths of the present day is that, if the last view is right, then the previous view must have been wrong. And as, according to Mr. Chamberlain, these evil conditions have been growing for thirty years, how is it he has not only not pointed them out before, but has actually been among the foremost men to delude us as to the strength of our trade and Empire ? Finally, if matters are in these desperate straits, why did Mr. Chamberlain plunge the nation into a war which drained the country of £300,000,000 of money, and reduced its securities to the lowest point we have known for fifty years ? Taking these questions into consideration, Mr. Chamberlain's sudden revelations seem to lack veracity. We must indeed look elsewhere for the reasons for this startling rightabout. Mr. Chaplin has told .us that the Government's withdrawal of the shilling duty upon corn in the 13udget of 1903 forced Mr. Chamberiam-s hand, and compelled him to declare himself before he was prepared to take the field on behalf of Preference and Protection. From this we gather that but for Mr. Ritchie's action in refusing to continue the Corn Tax Mr. Chamberlain would have tried graCually to :lead the country into accepting Protection as inevitable, as he previously led them into war.

Facts and Figures. IF Mr. Chaplin's statement is correct, it explains a. good many of Mr. Chamberlain"s subsequent blunders. • His scheme had all the appearance of being hurriedly considered, and the countless inaccuracies as to the facts and figures of our trade are explained. Still there are certain points in Mr. Chamberlain's care that it is necessary to answer, and to answer repeatedly. These points are:
1. Is our trade stagnant? 2. Are we suffering from the importation of foreign goods? 3. Is our Colonial trade worth more to us than our foreign trade?

Mr. Chamberlain would decide the first point by considering our export of goods only. For many reasons, that is not a correct method Of estimating our trade. It is impossible to compare values of 1870 with Values of NCO. It is necessary to consider our shipping and other services as a part of our exports. it is also necessary. to remember our internal trade but, unfortunately, we cannot calculate the amount. For these and other reasons, the only safe method of judging whether ' our trade is stagmat is to consider our total turnover. These iigures are as follows:
There does not seem to ie very much stagEa- Con about those figures.

1 Foreign Imports. THE notion that we suffer from what we buy f is somewhat absurd upon the face of it. it is still more absurd when we come to consider what it is we buy. An examination of the g ports reveals the fact that four-ti-th: of them are necessary for our food or indnstries,and that 1, any attempt to shut them out would inciease 11 the cost of food or be a direct injury to some part of our trade. The amount of mann- ; •factures we import, which are not used in cur industries, is exceedingly small.

Colonial and • Foreign. MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S plea that our trade with the Colonies is worth more to us than our trade with the rest of the world is the main foundation of his schemes. But, while he treats India, the Straits Settlements, and the West Indies as Ccbmies when he wishes to reckon up the trade of the Empire, they are totally ignored in his proposals for givii:g preference to the Empire. He proposes to treat Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa as the taroured Colonies to whom a preference is to be=given, while the rest of the King's dominions are to he treated as foreign countries, and their produce taxed accordingly. If we weigh the trade of the favoured Colonies against the rest of the world we should have a result some- thing as follows. The, figures are for 1902: Total trade with Favoured Colonies Total trade with other British Possessions Total trade with Foreign Countries
£595,000,000 Thus we are asked to risk the whole of our trade for the sake of £126,000,000. If our 2ommerce really were stagnant, that would ardly be the way to improve matters.
