div.head: NOTICE TO CORRESONDENTS.
div.p: NOTICE TO CORRESONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in al cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and 'pent in, if possible,not later than Thursday.

div.head: An Apology Required.
div.p: An Apology Required.

Sir,—ln your issue of last week there is a report of the Liberal meeting of the 6th inst. In this account, Mr. E. Osborne is reported to have said he had asked the question of the President of the Trades Council in Warrington "How is it you cannot accept a progressive like Mr. Crosfleld " and the only reason he could get in reply was "that he was not a trade unionist." Sir, that statement is not true! Mr. Osborne also continues. "It was further said that Mr. Crosfleld was a capitalist" and he was told' There is not a good capitalist in England." This statement following after the previous statement in reference to me has been, and is being, imputed to me. Now, sir, I wish most emphatically to say that this statement if applied to me is also not true. In fact both are abso- lutely false. I demand from Mr. Osborne, if he is an honourable man, a public apology in your paper for ascribing statements to me I have never made. Yours, JOSEPH PODMORE, Jun., President, Trades and Labour Council. 9, Rylands-street, Warrington, June 15th, 1904.

div.head: Novel Subscription for Lancastrians.
div.p: A Novel Subscription for Lancastrians.

Sir,—l wish to bring under the notice of the public a letter which I have received from Lord Derby with reference to the new class of cruiser which is being added to His Majesty's Navy, and which class is being named after certain counties. _

The counties so selected have in each case gladly identified themselves with their namesakes by present- ing them with momentoes. The name of "Lancaster" has been bestowed upon one of these nem ships and it is suggested that the County Palatine should not fall behind other counties in a desire to show its appreciation of the honour. It is proposed that a Silver Ship's Bell should be purchased and the balance used to endows "Lancaster" cot in one of the great naval charitable institutions. I have been requested by Lord Derby to open a sub- scription list and I shall be glad to forward any sub- scriptions which may be sent to me.—Yours faithfnlly. WILLIAM BOLTON, (Mayor.)

div.head: " Social Brotherhood" Idea.
div.p: The " Social Brotherhood" Idea.

Sir.—Again I take the opportunity of addressing you on the above topic. Now that wehaye a letter from Mr. Dunnico on the aim and purpose of the Brotherhood it would perhaps be as well to consider its chance of success and its prospect of doing good. The primary aim of the proposed Brotherhood is the" Re-adjustment of the present social order." This is rather a tall order of the accomplishment of which, as you remark in your editorial comments, one may be rather sceptical. Yet we must not forget that the Rev. H. Dunnico uses it as an apt phrase—the "Re-adjustment of the present Social Order "—which contains the ultimate end and purpose of the Brotherhood but which does not disclose the pre- sent programme and the immediate plans of the com- mittee formed to take the matter up. That the present system needs improving there can be no doubt what- ever. In fact the industrial and social order requires changing—gradually it will have to be done certainly— but it must and shall be changed entirely. However, as we know quite well, to talk of changing the social system is one thing—changing it is another. The Brotherhood must first turn its attention towards municipal affairs and here for some time I think will be its best chance of making itself felt and its oppor- tunity to prove a success. A good strong Brotherhood composed of Liberals, Tories, Labourmen, Ste., all will- ing to drop party politics and unite in one purpose—the common good of the greatest number—cannot help but be a success. Its influence in town life, and town I government ought to be great. The right men should find their way to the Town Council- men with business capacity yet not lacking a desire and I an earnestness to improve the moral and intellectual standard of the town life. We can have too much business capacity at times,especially when it develops a tendency to self-interest. But at the same time I do not plead for very pious church and chapel goers to be placed in the Council. Chapel piety when bordered by a narrow and limited intellect also tends to self interest. Let us by all means have good sound common sense men, men who will not toady men not afraid to speak up men not frightened to show up the wrong no matter whom it may affect or offend. We want men with individuality, men with an eye to justice and purity in all affairs, and in all departments. We want no crazy extremists—ranting total abstainers or other- wise. We've enough sources of amusement already. Extreme views any subject usually border on the ridiculous. Here then we find work for the Brotherhood.—Can se trust them to find the right men and to act themselves from pure motives in so doing. No picking Mr. Liberal so-and-so because say, Mr. Dunnico, a great man in the Brotherhood, leans towards Liberalism. I trust there will be none of that kind of thing. No favouritism or self interest. Provided then that the Brotherhood will act straightforwardly and always for what it conscien- tiously believes to be right I think that all the signs are for a success. You know we are getting rather un- orthodox—we are turning away in a sense from party— we are sick of this sect and that sect (religious and ' political) and desire something rational, broader and sounder. The Brotherhood for this 'reason ought to be a sympathetic meeting place for all shades of opinion, I men ought to be drawn together by a fellow feeling of determination to do something, instead of for ever wrangling and barking from a party standpoint. I am somewhat of a wanderer so must be excused for mentioning Mr. Dunnico's reference to the Brotherhood being "content to use the party,be it Liberal or Labour that is most likely to promote civic righteousness." I don't like the sound of this some way or other so if there's any warning note needed let me sound it. There maybe danger—so forewarned is forearmed. I shall not go into detail but simply say this—that the danger is that one of the parties may be inclined to use the Brother- hood iipstead of the Brotherhood using the party. Mr. Dunnico is connected with the Liberal party and I can- 1 didly confess that this idea of "using the party" bears a likeness to the proverbial two-edged sword. Ido not wish to impute any unworthy motives to the Rev. H. Dunnico. He may mean well, but his position is rather a peculiar one, and to be connected with the Liberal party and the Brotherhood (although the Brotherhood will not be political) at the same time may land him unexpectedly in a double and false position. Mr. Dunnico will, I am sure, take this in the right spirit. and as from a friend. He knows that a good many will look upon this Brotherhood as an endeavour to capture more votes for the Liberals. People are suspicious. Ought Mr. Dunnico, therefore, to sever his connection with the Liberals to ensure the success and progress of the Brotherhood he so wishes to form ? The most manly course would be to resign, and then devote himself heart and soul in the cause of right and social progress which he himself pathetically says wil I never be advanced oethe social problem solved by any one party but by a combination of all parties, and that combination in Warrington will be the Brotherhood. The Brotherhood therefore let him serve._ _ - - -

Personally Ido not object to Mr. Dunnico being a member of the Liberal party and the Brotherhood at the same tinie. lam charitably minded enough to think that he will act straight but I cannot help also thinking that he will do the Brotherhood harm if he keeps in the Liberal party. We all want to be Sherlock Holme's and as a result we have a habit, of deducting things so I will leave Mr. Dunnico to "deduct "what other people will "deduct" from his position in the Liberal partv,and his endeavour to form a Brotherhood.A letter from Mr. Dunnico might be of some use on this point. In con6lusion I may say I object to the last three words of the Rev. H. Dunnico's letter but nevertheless I thank him for the letter.
ONE INTERESTED.

tolerant views if he cannot realise what good friends political " enemies " often are. I don't deny that election times are not without their jealousies and bitternesses, but to attribute all this to the political clubs is, well, rot! The clubs in Warring- ton—at any rate the two principal clubs with which lam acquainted—are well-conducted in every respect, and in themselves have never yet been the cause of any estrangement, political or otherwise. 'lona "seems to have been longing for a cheap sneer at political clubs and party politics generally. There is no more foundation for his charge of gambling in the clubs than for the other wild statements which he utters from behind the shelter of anem-de-plume. As a matter of fact there is probably less betting or gambling in the Warrington political clubs than in any place where men do congregate. With your correspondent's animadversions on I religion and party politics generally, lam not much I concerned, but I should like to point out that after I roundly condemning political parties" Iona" proceeds I to interfere in the forthcoming election by advocating the claims of the Labour party. Evidently in his eyes, I the sinfulness of a party—and maybe a club also— depends upon its colour !—Yours etc., CLUB MEMBER.

Sir,—ln your last issue appeared an able, interesting and important letter on the above subject, and I only wish some very worthy gentlemen well-known in connec- tion with "Social Brotherhoods" Conferences, Chapels, Churches and Sunday Schools &c., would kindly take to heart the lesson "Iona" wishes to teach. I sincerely trust some of these gentlemen read "lona's" letter. I had better confess that I have had the misfortune to attend at one of these clubs several times although only for a modest game of billiards and perhaps a • meat- pie." I'm not a Conservative or a Liberal nor yet a Labourite so I cannot be accused of being a traitor to my own. Having opened thus in a personal manner and having caught the attention of the above "worthy gentlemen" let me point out to them one or two things "Ions" says in such a straight, impres- sive and eloquent manner. In the first place listen to this. " lona " asks "Whose mind was ever enlightened, or whose sympathy enlarged by the harangues of political partisans denouncing their opponents as something un-English and dangerous to the community." Our friends at the Liberal and Conserva- tive clubs might answer this—our friends whose minds are for the most part bounded on the north by"cards" on thesouth by "stout and bitter etc. "on the east by "pot the red" and on the west by "work and bed." How their minds must "be enlarged"—and their heads. And what do a good many of them know about Conservatism and Liberalism? Not much I'm afraid. Let's see. There's Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. Draper, Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Mr. C. E. Parker,and they're notat their respective clubs very much—hence the enlargement of their minds. Yes, these four—and one er two others are the only ornaments of any value, only these know in what they believe. And the other members "the great majority" what good are they? Sir! its no wonder we hear the cry for "Protection." We need it badly. Turning to "lona's " letter again I see he refers to gambling. Yes Ido believe there's gambling at these clubs. Most respectable Sunday School superintendents and such like enjoy a modest gamble for a few pence. How noble, what liberal principles. And why should those Liberals who gamble grumbleat " Joe's Gamble." Its enough to make Methuselah turn in his grave to think that we've so many good, pious and intelligent gamblers, wine bibbers. and political jackasses. We talk about principle. Why there are some of the per- sons who "frequent" these clubs" frequently" who ought to be ashamed of themselves. Do they everthink of their "principle," or is it, not often of their " interest " they think? And now listen to this. " lona " says "The making and retaining of political disciples, which is, I presume, the object of the club, is deemed a good and desirable work, but who overheard of intoxicating liquors being used as helpmates to a praiseworthy cause. Yes, who ever did hear of such a thing? I wonder how many "political disciples are made" at these clubs. How many times indeed are political questions touched upon at all ? In many cases no doubt it's fi case of my grandfather and father etc., were Liberals or Tories,and that's good enough for me.

With regard to the sale of intoxicants I agree with " lona " that it is unfair to the publican that these clubs should be allowed to remain open so long and so late at night. Tne publican has enough competition to contend with already, although I fancy the "poor publican" finds plenty of customers from somewhere, and does not do at all badly. If the clubs would only make some endeavour to edu- cate the people in political questions and subjects we might tolerate them, but unfortunately they do not. They're half asleep and likely to remain so. I am afraid that these clubs in Warrington at any rate,are not doing much (if any) good but on the contrary as lona "sug- gests may be doing a lot of harm, for who knows what the drinking and gambling habits of the club will lead to? Let me ask our Liberal friends whether John Morley would find a delight in drinking and gaming at a club continually. Herbert Spencer we know used to play billiards now and again as a recreation but even he did not live at a club as a good many do. We talk of education, but what education are the Liberal and Tory parties giving to the people? Have they given us any education in Warrington? The people might get too clever, perhaps they think, and that will never do—they might find out what progressive parties we are. The clubs are established to keep men's minds free from politics or anything that requires thinking about. It is dangerous to dank, so we must not do it. The Christian religion at one time would not let people think, but it could not stop the few earnest inquiring spirits seeking for knowledge and truth, neither also will these clubs and parties long keep in check the few gallant agitators for a better state of things. I do not approve of the religious sentiment in"lona's" letter, neither do I consider his reference to infidels to be good taste. Let "Iona" keep within his sphere and not go out of his way to "love" his enemies—the "insult- ing infidels." If I mistake not,"lona" himself insults the infidel. In conclusion, I should like to ask what is "lona's" policy grounded on. Religious truth? The religious truth bothers me, I can't for the life of me think what it is, there are so many religious truths. Is " lona " going to ground his policy on the Athanasian Creed or on a moral ad ethical basis? Nevertheless with most of" lona's "letter I am in agreement, and I sincerely hope and trust that some of the aforesaid "worthy gentlemen "—chapel and social conference men—will read and inwardly digest all that the letter contains and suggests, and may it reform one or two of them, for they urgently need it. I know most of these men are Christians and they follow:their Master—to the club-room for a drink and a game of cards.—Yours "ANONYMOUS."

div.head: NEW APPOINTMENT FOR MR. GOW. Important Position at Blackburn
div.p: A NEW APPOINTMENT FOR MR. GOW. Important Position at Blackburn

Mr. Alexander Gow, principal of Warrington Secon- dary school has obtained the more important appoint- ment of principal of Blackburn Technical school, at a salary of £5OO per annum. There were 93 applicants for the position. Mr. Gow has had a comparatively short stay in Warrington. He was appointed principal at the Warrington Secondary school on August 18th from 106 applicants,at a commencing salary of £250 per annum. .He had then just completed three years' resi- dence at Cambridge University. He holds a first-class certificate in part one and a double first in part two of the Natural SciEince tripos. He was trained two years at the Borough-road Training College, Isleworth where he obtained first class in certificate examination. For three years he was science master at the County High school, Isleworth, and had the organisation and control of one polytechnic, one art school and four subsidiary schools. During his stay in Warrington Mr. Gow has devoted himself assiduously to the work of conducting the Secondary school and technical classes and has gained the goodwill of the staff and students

div.head: WARRINGTON'S HIGH DEATH RATE.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S HIGH DEATH RATE.

In the mortality returns of 76 of the most important towns in the United Kingdom, Warrington has again the misfortune to come out on top with the highest death rate for last week. The rate for Warrington is 25 per thousand, whilst the average in the 76 great towns is 14.1 per thousand. From inquiries made, we learn that the high rate in Warrington is attributable to an abnormal infantile death rate. The recent epidemic of measles has left many of the children very weak and susceptible to other illness. Whooping cough is very prevalent just now and responsible for a number of deaths amongst. children. With the view of minimising the prevalence of infec- tious disease, the Medical Officer of Health communi- cated with the School Management Committee, suggesting the desirability of closing all the public elementary schools in the Borough at once until the date already fixed for the re-opening after the mid- summer holidays (15th August). The Committee did not accept the suggestion as it was nbt satisfied that the suggested closure of the schools would have the desired effect. There seems reason to believe that many children under five years of age are sent to infant schools when they are suffering from infectious diseases, and in this way assist in spreading disease amongst others.

Political Clubs. Sir,—l have often glanced more or less amusedly through the effusions of your correspondent "lona," especially when he .has been fulminating against war, or priestcraft, or inquiring into the history of the papyrus tree. Usually his remarks are of the kind that do no one any harm and, at least, please their author. but last week he ventured on new ground with the result that his footprints are decidedly obstrusive. " lona's" diatribe was against "political clubs." Why they should suddenly have come under the lash of his criticism I am at a loss to know, but this, Mr. Editor, I do know—that "Iona" is for once "off his horse," to use a colloquialism. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 18, 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 18, 1904
Whitecross Wire Works v. Cheshire Lines ; referee Mr. IL Williams.

Although L.and N.W. Railway figured in the final last year, they will have all their work cut out to beat Pear- son and Knowles No. 2. Houghton's are likely to beat Orford Tannery, as in last year's contests they were beaten by only 6 points by L. and N.-W. Railway. A close game is anticipated between Whitecross and Cheshire Lines, and there is much speculation as to the result.
The Committee have decided to hold a works handi- cap at the close of the present competition. Last year the event was a great success, the entries numbering nearly 300.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington have every reason to be proud of this season's record. Saturday's match with Sale—which resulted in a decisive victory—was the tenth in which the eleven has engaged, and of this number, eight have been won and two drawn.. We are beginning to look upon Warrington as quite an invincible combination. At any rate our cricketers are deserving of praise and congratulation for the consistently good form which they have exhibited with such splendid' results. The interest of the townspeople appears to be increasing, and there was a large attendance to witness Saturday's engagement at Arpley.

Sale were defeated in no half-hearted way, and the satisfaction of the home supporters knew no bounds. Mr. Connor won the toss and Warrington went to the wicket first. The feature of the innings was P. B. Hawtin's brilliant display. He and Lynes were the first to try their skill, and when the closure was applied Hawtin was not out. He never gave the visitors a single chance, and not a faulty stroke marred his exposition. He knocked up the fine total of 77, his chief hits in- cluding seven fours and six threes.

When the Warrington aggregate had reached 185 with only 6 wickets down the closure was applied. In addition to Hawtin's innings, a well-compiled 31 by T. Wright is worthy of note. Until the commencement of this season, Wright had figured in the second eleven, but several creditable performances have already fully justified his inclusion in the senior organization. Captain Coke was responsible for a capital 17, and G. Übsdell also gave a good account of himself, knocking up 16 not out.

Sale made a poor show, their efforts being produc- tive of only 72. The start was sensational, three wickets being down with not a single run on the board. The batsmen could make little headway against the deliveries of Lynes, who was in his best form, and is to be com- plimented upon capturing eight wickets for 20 runs. H.gramshaw was the top scorer,his innings realizing 25.

Without Lynes the bowling would have been some- what weak, neither Connor nor Podmore securing a single wicket. Übsdell did a little better, two wickets falling at a cost of 20 runs. Another good change bowler would be a decided acquisition to the team.

The second eleven were well on their way to victory and Sale did well in averting defeat. The Warring- tonians batted brilliantly and closed their innings after compiling 186 for the loss of seven wickets. J. W. Bibbrplayed in grand form, and made a splendid 80 not out. His chief hits included eleven fours. A. Thewlis and L. R. Connor also rendered good service, their scores being 23 and 26 respectively. A steady stand by J. Makinson and R. T. Rylance helped Sale to make a draw, the match ending with five wickets down for 76 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills found Moore and Daresbury too hard a nut to crack, and had to admit defeat by 18 runs. There was no very high scoring on either side, Antrobus who made 22 for the winners, giving the best perform- ance of the afternoon. Hawthorn (11) was the only Wire Mills player to attain double figures.

Latchford Baptists made no mistake about their victory over Moss Side Baptists, for they piled on a majority of 70. J. Hallam wielded the willow in capital style, and placed 25 to his credit. W. Hallam was responsible for 21. Mr. " Maras" with 13 headed the Moss Side list.

The Secondary school team met more than their match at Widnes, and returned from Chemicalopolis beaten to the extent of 26. Joynson's bowling was largely responsible for the collapse of the visitors, six wickets falling at the small cost of eight runs.

Crosfleld's tried conclusions with Lostock, and although a draw was the result of the encounter, matters stood greatly in favour of Lostock. Maudsley was the most successful batsman, knocking up 50 and carrying out his bat. Warren (14) accomplished the best per- formance for the soapery representatives.

St. Paul's gave the" Guardian "printers a drubbing, thanks mainly to the bowling of Lawless who took five wickets for 5 runs. Mason (22),Dawson (18) andParkes (12 not out) did creditably with the bat.

St. Helens Cable Co.triumphed over Little Sankey by 36 runs. Manning bowled very effectively, capturing seven wickets for 14 runs, whilst Evans (19), Smith (18), and FaHews (13) figured well in the batting depart- ment.
St. Mary's made a poor show against GolborAe-street, not one of their players scoring double numbers. For the winners Speakman knocked up 20.

There was a close encounter between Cheshire Lines Engineers and Bewsey-road Wesleyans, but the engineers came out victorious by the small margin of 3. Hogard and Whitehouse each contributed 30 for their respec- tive elevens.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Saturday was another glorious day for bowling—as indeed, for all outdoor sports—and enthusiasts made the most of the opportunity of enjoying themselves. The widespread interest which is being taken in the pastime is little short of remarkable, and only goes to show what gratifying success can be achieved by organ- izations with zealous and capable officials. Both the Works Association and the Warrington and Dietrict League have fully justified their existence, and all who have the interests of the game at heart will wish them a long continuance of prosperity.

div.head: WORKS' COMPETITION.
div.p: THE WORKS' COMPETITION.

- To show how keenly enthusiastic the workingmen are, it is only necessary to state that the crowd which assembled to witness Saturday's matches was the largest seen on the King • and Queen green this season. Three capital matches were down for decision, but the one in which the greatest interest was centred was that between Smith's Wire Works and Greening's Wire Works. An exceptionally keen contest, it was indeed worth going a good distance to see. So evenly matched were the teams that Smith's claimed the victory by one point.

As may be readily imagined excitement ran high. Smith's were leading by 136-130 when the last game was entered upon, so that clever play by either bowler would have turned the scale. R. Lomax started well for Greening's, and it looked as if he would pull the game out of the fire. At the seventh end he was lead- ing by 7-2. Then his opponent, W. Dodd, scored a single, immediately followed by a double. Lomas- was, however, in fine form, and at tile seventeenth end the score stood at 13-8 in his favour. Then Dodd secured a double, and immediately afterwards the same advan- tage fell to Lomax, who thus ran out winner by 150E0. Dodd just managed to save the game, and Smith's may. account themselves fortunate in triumphing by 1 point.

There was a close contest between G. Shaw and W. Smith. The players never drew level, but at the fif- teenth end Shaw was one point in arrears, the score being 10-11. Shaw then delivered his woods so well as to secure a couple of doubles. Then Smith gained a single, and Shaw, obtaining a point from the next end won a good game by 15-13.

Another well-fought game was that between F. Rath- bone and NV. Patrick. At the eleventh end, each had placed 7 points to his credit. Rathbone then gained the lead by 3, but allowed his opponent to draw up, the result being that Patrick won by 15-12. H. Daintith,the captain of the winning team, tried conclusions with T. Edgington, captain of Greening's, and easily beat him by 15-6. At the ninth end, the position was 5-5, but afterwards Edgington never had a look in, only increas- ing his score by a single.

R. Whitfield defeated J. Lomax, but not with out a keen encounter. Several times the contestants drew level, and at the seventeenth end the score stood at 10-10. Then Whitfield forged ahead, and ran out winner by 15-11.

Crosfield's No. 1 were unable to account for Rylands's No 1 who ran out winners by 28 points. Several close contests were watched with interest. J. Wilcock beat G. Bottomley by 15-14 after a capital game. At the eleventhend the score was 7-7, but Wilcock quickly piled on points and gained the victory. J. Jackson,the soapery captain, defeated F. Miller by 15-13. The players were evenly matched and several times drew level. At the twentieth end each had scored 13, and two successive singles gave Jackson the upper hand.

Stubs's File Works had to admit defeat at the hands Waitl3rlsi wh3 gtinAl Au uij on ty. An exception- ally close game was that between William Shaw and Tom Lawton, the first-named winning by a single. div.head: LEAGUE.
div.p: THE LEAGUE.

The encounters under the auspices of the Warrington and District League provided some good games, although there was not, perhaps, the intense interest which characterized the -previous week's matches between Cemetery and Bull's Head. The Liberal Club trundlers appear to have struck a bad vein. They cer- tainly expected to. gain points on their own green on Saturday, but disappointment was in store. The doughty Cemetery organization beat them by 19 points, and Horse and Jockey administered a heavier defeat, the majority being 36.

Several close games in the match with the Cemetery team are worthy of note. G. Ball defeated A. J. Jones by one point, the encounter in the latter stages being particularly close. At the outset Jones held the upper hand, and at the seventh end had scored 9 to his oppo- nent's one. Ball then had a turn, and the scoring to the close was :-3-9, 4-9, 5-9, 5-10, 5-11, 6-11, 7-11, 9-11, 11-11, 1141, 13-11, 13-12, 14-12, 14-13, 14-14, 15-14. J. Allison tried conclusions with R. Marrow, and he too won by a single. Allison was the first to score, and led to the tenth end when the position was 9-7. Marrow then secured a double which put the players on equal terms. Allison got two singles in succession;and after- wards the scoring was-11-10, 11-12, 12-12, 12-14, 13-14, 15-14. H. Diintith had the best of his game with R. Bothwell, but the scoring was close. At the eighteenth end each player had placed 14 to his credit, and a single gave Daintith the victory.

In the Horse and Jockey match the closest game was between J. Houghton and 6. Higham, Houghton winning by 15-14. R. Marrow beat T. Hackett by 15-12, and the same majority fell to T. Davies in his game with E. J. Mitchell.
Bull's Head had no difficulty in defeating Fearnhead by 47. J. Worsley, jun., played a close game with George Weston and won by 15-14. W. Andrews beat
Albert Gleave by one point. The following is the league table up-to-dite
P. W. L. For Agst. Pts. Cemetery Bull's Head Chapel House Horse and Jockey 7 ... 4 ... 3 -.1079 ... 880 ... 8 B rooklands Penketh Fearnhead Liberal Club
To-day's matches, to be played on the greens of the first-named are : Fearnhead v. Cemetery. Chapel House v. Bull's Head.

A well attended meeting of the league was held at the Bull's Head on Thursday evening. The chief business was to fix the venue of the match with the Widnes, Runcorn and District league on July 7th. As the re- sult of the draw the match will be played on the Horse and Jockey green. The team will consist of two mem- bers of each league club. The matter of presenting medals to the runners-up will be decided at a meeting on July 6th.

The suggestion that the arrangements for the open- ing of the new public bowling green at Victoria-Park should be left in the hands of the Warrington and Dis- trict League has been f tvourably received by the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee. Many people have noticed that the green is without the usual gutter, but I understand that the defect will be remedied before the opening in August.

div.head: OTHER MATCHES.
div.p: OTHER MATCHES.
Warrington met Leigh Railway in a Lancashire and CbBshire Association match, but sustained defeat by 39. There were several exciting games.

Fifteen members of Messrs. Richmond's office staff combined pedestrianism and bowling on Saturday after- noon. They had a pleasant walk to Halton, and played an interesting main on the Castle Hotel green, the princi- pal winners being :-1, J. Aikenhead ; 2, G. H. Anderton; 3, W. Rigby.
Warrington Conservatives entertained the Altrincham Conservatives, and defeated' them by the handsome majority of 154.

The opening main of the season in connection with the Brooklands club was a very successful affair, the entries numbering close upon 60. The handicapping was very good and resulted in some tight games. The prize winners were:-1, J. J. Millington; 2, T. Rigby; 3, J. Jackson; 4, J. E. Jefferson.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

On Saturday the weather was again all that could be desired for cycling, and the roads were in grand con- dition. The Warrington Club's run to Oulton Park proved an attractive fixture. Nearly a score of mem- bers turned out, and the spin across the fine Delamere Forest was thoroughly enjoyed. Tea was provided at the Red Lion, and after a stroll round the pretty park and mere, the party turned their faces homeward. The journey was made via Whitegate, Hartford, Northwich, and Marbury, Warrington being reached in good time after one of the most successful outings of the season. -- Owing to the wet weather, Tuesday evening's run to Tabley had to be abandoned. On Wednesday evening the first round of the bowling main was continued at Sankey Chapel House, and there were some interesting games. The entries number about forty, and it is expected that the main will be concluded on Wednesday week.
To-day's destination is Mouldsworth,and on Tuesday the club go to Little Legh.
Sankey Wesleyan Club journeyea to Tarporley on Saturday, and the run through tbe heart of picturesque Cheshire proved highly enjoyable. To-day's run is to Rostherne Mere.

Thomas Summerfield, a quarryman, of Weston, near Runcorn. borrowed a free wheel bicycle in order to attend his sister-in-law's funeral at Warrington on Thursday. He did not understand a free wheel, and failed to turn the awkward corner at Delph Bridge, Runcorn. He went full tilt into the wall. The machine was completely buckled up, and Summer&ld was badly shaken and his face much cut. He was sent home in a cab instead of attending the funeral.

Between 7,000 and 8,000 spectators assembled at Fallowfield on Saturday to witness the N.C.U. Champion- ship races. The mile final was a sensational race. A. L. Reed came in first, being only afoot in advance of Ernest Payne, who beat J. S. Benyon by a wheel. The time was 2 mins. Benyon, Reed, and H. D. Buck figured in the quarter mile final. Benyon gained premier honours, easily beating Buck by three lengths in 33 secs. Reed sat up after going a furlong, and pedalled slowly to the winning post. Asked the reason for sitting up, he responded simply "I was whacked."

Local Successes.

Several Warrington competitors figured at the Winnington sports on Saturday. In the mile bicycle race C. Berry gained the 2nd place from the 110 yards mark. W. Price, of Warrington A.C., came in first in the two miles walking race, but Was disqualified. J. J. Kite, of Thelwall, was first in the 440 yards fiat race.

At the Cheshire Lines sports at Knutsford, K. B. Mellor, Warrington. was third in the 150 ye,rds handicap for youths under 16; H. K. Jepson, Warrington, was third in the half-mile flat, and third in the 600 yards obstacle race • and C. Sinclair, of Warrington was third in the 120 yards handicap.

• lam pleased to hear that A. E. Howard, of Sankey, who met with a serious accident at Liverpool last week is progressing favourably, and his friends are hoping to hear of his discharge from hospital at an early date. Mounfleld, another well-known Nrrington rider, had a nasty spill at Winnington on Saturday, but was not seriously hurt.

The prospects for the coming season are excellent. The following are the dates of the contests in connection with the local angling societies.

Locally a "benefit" match will also be fished at "London Bridge" Stockton Heath on June 25th. A .competition open to all England will be promoted in the Waters of the Bridgewater Canal on July 23rd, prizes £lO in cash. A contest in aid of the Nursing Association will be organised for October 2nd.

The first outing in connection with the Latchford Angling Society Club was undertaken on Saturday last, genial summer-like weather prevailing. Thirty-six members put in an appearance, and the picnic was a great success, due to the admirable arrangements which had been made by the committee of the club. The drive to Stretton was taken via Lymm, High Legh, and Apple- ton Thorn the Cat and Lion hostelry being reached at half-past four. Here on arrival an excellent repast was ready, which had been prepared by the genial host, Mr. Joseph Broady. Full justice was done to the good and appetising viands provide.l. After tea, bowls were indulged in, the President's (Mr. Harry Taylor's) team playing the Vice-President's (Mr. H. Houghton's)team. The President's team in the doubles" scored 89, and the Vice-President's team 95 in the "singles." The President's team scored 148 and the Vice-President's team 158, thus giving the victory to the Vice-Presi- dent's team by a margin of 16 points. A pleasant drive home. via Stockton Heath, concluded a very enjoyable day, the headquarters of the club, the Brook Inn, Latch- ford, being reached by about 945 p.m.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

The Warrington team scored another victory on Tuesday when they journeyed to St. Helens to play a league match. Both sides were well represented and there was a good attendance of spectators. The War- rington team was as follows :—C. Woods, goal; NV. Ashton and A. Boscow (captain) backs ; C. Ashton,half- back ; A. Ashton, J. Peers, and W. Sutton, forwards. Boscow was unlucky in the toss for ends and the wirepullers had to defend the shallow goal. The home team were taken by surprise, as right from the swim up, A. Ashton scored. Goals were registered in quick succession by W. Ashton and J. Peers. The visitors were far and away the better team and their passing and shooting were very accurate. Three more goals were scored before half-time which arrived with Warrington leading by six to nil.

In the second half the Warringtonians relaxed their efforts a little, but their opponents could do nothing against the strong defence of Woods and Company. T. Peers had an open goal but failed to score from an easy position. Give and takeplay followed until the whistle sounded, with the score:—Warrington, G goals; St.. Helens, nil.

As I briefly statedjlast week, Warrington journeyed to Burslem and suffered defeat by 5 goals to 1 in a friendly match. Further particulars are now forthcoming. Both teams were at full strength, the visitors depending upon the same ten that drew with Everton. Warrington won the toss and defended the deep end. The Btirslem forwards at once showed their superiority, and quickly scored. Give and take play followed until Ripley, the old St. Helens crack, raced away and landed another goal. The interval arrived with the home team leading by 4 goals to nil. In the second half the visitors attacked vigprously and the Burslem goal was frequently assailed. From a pass,C. Ashton scored with a long shot,and shortly afterwards the home centre placed a fifth goal to the credit of the pottery men.

A friendly match with Southport was decided at that pretty resort on Thursday evening, Warrington being represented by :—G. Bayley, goal: C. Ashton and W. Sutton, backs; R. Allen, half back; J. Warren, J. Peers (captain) and F. Howard, forwards. I hear that the visitors did not exert themselves very much, and they were beaten by five goals to two. Warren and Allen scored for Warrington.
A squadron race of 9 aside between Warrington and Southport men formed an interesting feature. The Warringtonians won by a length of the bath.
On Tuesday evening next the second team play their first league match at Birkenhead.

The first team's re-play with Everton in the Lanca- shire Cup Competition has been fixed for June 23rd at the Margaret-strelt baths. It will require an extra effort if Warrington are to meet Lancaster bathe second round.
Football. The annual meeting of the Northern Union was held on Wednesday at Huddersfleld,and an interesting report of the proceedings will be found elsewhere.
A determined effort was mide to do away with the works clause, but this proposal was again defeated,i ant glad to say.

Wartingtpniani will ba disxppointed to learn that members will, in future, have to pay for admission to cup-ties. Though the, Warrington representatives, Messrs. Ashton and Pernaerto.n voted against any alter- ation of this rule, it was earned by 36 votes to 22.

Icommend to the notice of my readers several altera- tions to playing rules which should tend to better foot- ball. In particular the scrummage rules have been amended and there should be, in future, less of the style of scrummaging which won the N.U. cup during the past two seasons. A more commonsense interpreta- tion of the knock-on has also been put on the books.
A report of the F.C. dinner last night, and presents- tio.l of the South-West Lancashire Cup and medals, will be found in another column.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

A few sanguine motorists are of opinion that the motor-cycle is the very vehicle to commend itself to a doctor, and, projecting their prophetic souls into the future, assure us that the day is close at hand when practically every member of the medical profession will cover his rounds by the assistance of the motor cycle. Tne motor car is certainly to be recommended and already has very many staunch adherents amongst the desciples of the art of healing; but, save for the use of those whose patients are scattered over a wide area away in the country, the cycle is not really popular amongst the doctors. The real reason is probably much the same as has prevented the pedal-propelled machine being greatly adopted by them—it is impossible to cycle in correct professional attire. And if this has been found to be the case where the ordinary type of machine is concerned, how much less would a motor cyclist convey the idea of the tradi- tional family doctor! One can hardly imagine the feel- ings of a patient whose up-to-date medical attendant suddenly discarded his top hat and frock coat and arrived one fine morning in leather breeches and jacket, a rakish cap on his head and goggles preserving his eyes against the assaults of flies!

A thoughtful article appears in a contemporary, draw- ing attention to the superiority of the motor omnibus for public conveyance, as opposed to the more popular tram. The greatest grievance that every user of the road has against the tram, whether horse-drawn or self- propelled, is the fact that the road is cut up for the construction of the rails. These rails are a continuous source of danger to the public, and when the cable system is employed there are six instead of four of them to reckon with: Of course, the best plan to adopt is the over-head trolley system, so long as side poles are used. The centre poles are objectionable for ordinary traffic.

But another grave drawback to the tram is that it cannot be stationed, and, therefore, any other vehicle must ma way for it. Its presence demands that the, rule of the e road shall be ignored when it is to be over- taken for a tram, like a led horse, must be passed on the inside. In the latter case the reason is that the man in ell walks on the inside,and the overtaking vehigeg se usaliY houuldpass between him and the pavement. In the former it would be unwise to pass outside, for another tram might be advancing from the opposite direction, and being unsteerable, a collision would be inevitable. But motor omnibuses possess none of these drawbacks and would be equally serviceable for the public. It is to be hoped, therefore, that they will eventually find favour with the various authorities.

An enthusiast has just discovered that motoring is the finest cure in the world for lunacy, and argues that the " exhilaration resulting from a 50 to 60 miles spin tends to reawaken the brain," and so makes the first move in steps towards a mental cure. It would be interesting to know whether professional chauffeurs, as a class,regard the proposed cure with the same enthusiasm. According to the letters which are appearing in two or three of the trade journals just now, they always have a to ventilate ; but if in the future long list of grievances they are to be expected to drive a two-seated car for the sole passenger they may instance, for one of these little 50 miles spin and 4ith an exhilarated lunatic as
well consider that their cup of bitterness is to be filled to overflowing.

It is rather amusing to note the trouble some motorists take to start their engines, for, as a rule, it is merely knack and not brute force that is needed to get them going. One often sees a driver monotonously winding his starting crank round and round and bringing as much common-sense to bear upon the operation as if he were turning a mangle or the handle of a barrel-organ. A single-cylinder motor is .admittedly harder to start than one of the multi-cylinder type; but the same modus operandi applies to all. If the care has been standing some time, flood the carburetter, see that the timing lever is quite retarded and then, holding the starting crank firmly give it a short, sharp,upward pull. Some engines are far easier starters than others, but in justice to the majority, it must be conceded that very few indeed really require a gymnastic display which the amateur driver frequently indulges in before the first welcome "kick" is heard.

One of the easiest starters is the 4 cylindered Deena- yule. A sharp half turn of the crank gets her going at the commencement of the day's run,and after that,when temporary stoppages are made during the journey she will invariably start up from the switch. This is a great convenience especially to a lady driver, who is abso- lutely stranded when, alone on her car, she has switched off the engine whilst making a call or doing a little shopping, and is quite incapable of getting it going again. With one that starts so easily as the Decauville she can drive alone in perfect comfort knowing that whatever halt she may choose to call it will start again directly the current is switched on, and she will not be put to the trouble and annoyance of alighting from the car and draggling her gown in the dust or mud of the streets whilst she wrestles with the starting crank of a, refractory motor and the crowd gives advise gratis con- cerning old iron and the advisability of being towed home by a horse.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH ELECTRIC LIGHTING.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH ELECTRIC LIGHTING.
Warrington Corporation's Offer.
PARISH MEETING TO BE HELD.

Warrington Corporation's offer to supply Stockton Heath with electricity was under consideration at a meeting of the Parish Council held in the National Schools on Thursday evening. Mr. J. H. Clarke presided and there were also present:—Messrs. H. J. Westbrook, J. W. Bouchier, F. Pearson. J. Whitley, J. Fairhurst, J. Hallows, T. Williams, F. Warburton, S. F. Welsby and E. Bradshaw (clerk.)

div.head: STOPPAGE OF A FOOTPATH.
div.p: STOPPAGE OF A FOOTPATH.

The Council confirmed a resolution passed on April 15th sanctioning the stoppage or diversion of a foot- path from Fairfield-road to Mill-lane. THE ELECTRICITY QUESTION. REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF GAS WANTED.

The Clerk read a letter from the Town clerk stating that the Electricity Committee of the Warrington Corporation were prepared to supply electric light and energy at the same prices as those charged within the borough, but they were not prepared to consider, as it was outside their province, the question of a re- duction in the price of gas. Mr. Bradshaw then read the first letter on the subject received from the Town Clerk which read:—" The Corporation have been approached on the subject of supplying Stockton Heath and adjoining districts with electric light and energy. To do this the Corporation will require Parliamentary powers, and before considering the matter further, they will be glad to hear the views of Stockton Heath Parish Council." The Chairman said that before dealing with the elec- tricity question he would like to point out the position of Stockton Heath in regard to the supply of water and gas. The Warrington Corporation had the monopoly of supplying the district with water. The residents were debarred from purchasing it from any other source and they paid exactly the same rate as the people in Warrington. The charge was very heavy, and if War- rington Corporation would free them from the tie that was now upon them, it was possible that they would be able to devise a scheme to obtain their water at a very much lower cost. As regarded gas, they were also bound to deal with Warrington. If they were free from the bonds of Warrington, there was no doubt that they would be in a position to construct works with modern apparatus to produce gas at a far lower cost than Warrington could produce it. Moreover the people of Stockton Heath had been in the unenviable position of having to pay 6d. per 1,000 cubic feet more for gas than their neighbours in Warrington were asked to pay. It was true that the power of charging extra was con- ferred upon the Corporation by Act of Parliament, and perhaps at the time it was justified. The times and cir- cumstances had now altered. Ueder the Act it was stipulated that only a certain profit should be made. It was implied that after a certain percentage had been paid to the shareholders the price of gas should be re- duced if the profits allowed. The gas profits at Warrington last year amounted to £lO,OOO and that sum, or part of it, had gone to the reduc- tion of Warrington rates. That was not carrying ,out the spirit of the Act. The people of Stockton Heath, as consumers, were justified in claiming a share of the profit. He further maintained that so long as they were charged one fraction more than the consumers across the canal, they were unfairly treated and would be dissatisfied. The matter of electricity was purely and simply a trading transaction. Warrington people wanted to sell them electricity and they at Stockton Heath were not obliged to buy. They were willing to come to terms with the Corporation, but they maintained that they should be treated like other consumers in regard to gas and electricity. So long as they were treated unfairly in regard to one com- modity, it was unreasonable for the Corporation to expect them to trade in regard to another. He was not sure whether they would not in a few years be able to put down plant and supply them- selves with electricity. If the Warrington Corporation were going to make a profit by supplying them, he felt that it would probably pay Stockton Heath to become producers. What they were going to do now would fas- ten them for all time. Now was the time when they ought to make a proper bargain. The Corporation de- sired to treat them in regard to electricity, as if they were part of Warrington. Assuming that was fair, then it was equally fair and equitable that they shouid be similarly treated in iegard to gas. Alluding to the circularzing of the village by the electricity manager,Mr. Clarke said it was hardly treating that Council with the respect they were entitled to expect,to issue the circular without consulting them. If the circular had contained the terms the Council had already named to the Corpora- tion—that the price of gas should be on the same basis as the electricity charge—he did not think the Council's approval would have been withheld. As it was, people were asked to sign in ignorance of those terms, and he f eh" it was his duty to protect the interests of the parish by sending out a printed notice to the ratepayers. Mr. H. J. Westbrook said the Council was indebted to Mr. Clarke for the prompt manner in which he took steps to counteract the Corporation's circular. He pointed out that under the old acts, the gas and water companies—now represented by the Corporation—had a prescribed area of supply. So long as they supplied the district under the maximum price fixed by the Act, no , other company could come into the area. Before they could come into Stockton Heath with their electricity supply, the Corporation were bound to get the Parish Council's permission. When once they had got there they would have a prescribed area and Stockton Heath would be just as much in their hands in regard to electricity as they were now in regard to gas. He did not think it was unfair or un- equitable, neither did he think it was looking at the matter from anything but a broad and fair basis, that they should offer no opposition to the Corporation seeking Parliamentary powers, on condition that the Corporation would put them on the same terms as War- rington in regard to gas. Would not the Parish Council be neglecting their duty if they allowed the Corpora- tion to get another monopoly in the village? The Cor- poration had had to put down plant which would pro- duce more electricity than they really wanted,so they were seeking customers outside their area. He moved that a sub-committee be appointed to draw up a circular setting before the ratepayers the Council's position in regard to the gas, water and electricity supplies. He agreed that seeing that negotiations were pending between the Council and the Corporation, it was a most undesirable thing, to say the least of it, for the elec- tricity manager to circularise their constituents. He had not been able to find one person in the village who wanted electricity. Certainly the people would not want it. unless it was going to be cheaper than gas, Mr. Warburton seconded. Mr. Hallows moved an amendment that a parish meet- ing be held. He was completely in accord with all that the previous speakers had said, but if they did not hold a meeting it might be thought that they were fighting shy of the matter. Mr. Bouchi er seconded. A parish meeting, he pointed out, would give the inhabitants the opportunity of ex- pressing their views. He could not help feeling that the Council was making a mountain out of a mole hill. If the electricity was for sale, and if it was cheap enough, the people would buy it. If it was not then ' they would not take it. The fact that ratepayers might sign a form stating that they were willing to consider, did not bind them to take electricity for ever from the Corporation. If the Corporation could produce elec- tricity cheaper than it could be produced at Stockton Heath—and he maintained they could—and they gave a guarantee that the price should never be more for Stockton Heath than for Warrington, he did not see that Stockton Heath was in a very bad position. They could never buy electricity at anything like the same price from Knutsford and Northwich as they could from Warrington, owing to the increased cost of trans- mission. He did not think it was altogether policy if a nroposal was put before the Council, to at once assume that that proposal was in the interest of the Corpora- tion, and not at all in the Council's interests, and to treat it purely in an antagonistic spirit. They must not forget that Warrington had voluntarily given them a 3d. reduction in the price of gas, and they were in exactly the same position as every other consumer of

gas outside the borough supplied by the Corporation. Mr. Westbrook: We are in the position of having some reason for demanding preferential treatment. Mr. Bouchier pointed out that the water supplied by the Corporation was the best they could get anywhere in the country. So long as they could get water of that quality at the same price as Warrington consumers, he did not think they need grumble very much about it. He also contended that it would cost -Stockton Heath fully as much as they were paying now to supply them- selves with gas. Mr. Pearson supported the amendment. He point out that on the extension of the borough, the Tovrtu Clerk proved to them that the Corporation could not legally make a sixpenny reduction in the price of gas. The Chairman: I think we have an answer to that already. They are reducing it by 3d. Mr. Pearson: That is made by way of discount.. Continuing he said the tone of one or two speeches was• not quite as friendly as he would like. He did not think anything could be gained by them. The Corpora— tion were stronger to gain their point, than the Parish, Council were to resist them. Ultimately it was decided that a parish meeting be held on Monday, June 27th, and that a circular be dis T -- tributed, setting forth the own Clerk's letter and the Parish Council's reply.

SUGGESTED ST-06KTON HEATH FIRE BRIGADE. A letter was submitted from the Town Clerk, c,alling attention to the Warrington Fire Engine Committee's decision that the fire brigade be not allowed to leave? the borough, unless the rural authorities were prepared to contribute to the expense of the department. The letter was referred to the Council by the Runcorn Rural District Council. _

Mr. H. •J. Westbrook thought that considering the- admirable fire engine at the brewery, which was always' available, Stockton Heath was in a position of greater independency than other outlying districts. It seemed to him that if they could get better terms from Waders' pool, they ought to listen to them first. The Chairman: I don't think you will have any pro. posal of that kind coming from Wilderspool Brigade. My feeling is that if the Warrington Brigade come here- with their engine, this is a fair proposal to put before us. I don't think we ought to rely upon the Wilders-• pool Brigade. They are a voluntary brigade, and ther are not obliged to come out at all times in the night. It was decided to ask the Corporation to submit s' scale of charges to be considered by the Council. Mr. Warburton suggested that a small fire brigade' . with a captain, should be formed in the village. About • half-a-dozen practices should, he thought, be hele dur- ing the year, and a grant of 2s. to the captain and is. to. each man should be made at each practice. It was intimated that-the matter would be consideredl, by the Parochial Committee.

div.head: THE" SOCIAL BROTHERHOOD:' First Meeting of the Committee.
div.p: THE" SOCIAL BROTHERHOOD:' First Meeting of the Committee.

The first meeting of the rP,—,-,tly-appointed com- mittee was held in Golbor., ~-.treet school last evening, the Rev. H. Dunnico presiding over a representative attendance. Mr. Edmund Osborne was appointed secretary pro tern. It was decide. to form a society, as proposed by Mr. Minato", to be named" The Social Service League." The prior ary object of the league will for a time be educational, and it was decided to issue a monthly magazine. Props" ganda work will ke undertaken in order to bring the' objects of the league directly before the public. A further committee meeting will be held shortly t° arrange a definite programme. It is the desire of those who are wtively connected with the leatue to bring all those with social sympathies into close correlation - irrespective of politics and creed. It is intended to take an active part in municipal affairs, and to support those candidates, irrespective of party, whose vievai! are most in -L harmony with the aims of the league. " cases where neither candidate is in sympathy with the programme the league vill bring forward an independ- ent candidate.

div.head: SONG OF THE FORGOTTEN
div.p: THE SONG OF THE FORGOTTEN
DEAD.

[Only £7OO has been subscribed towards the loaf War Me&orial,and of this more than £4OO has bee° subscribed by the officers of the South Lancashire Regiment themselves. Apart from the officers neither St. Helens nor Widnes have contributed anythinglt will be remembered that the fund was started about six months ago, and that it is desired to raise the sum of £lsoo,with a view to the erection of a suit- able monument in Warrington, the home of the Regiment.] It is five years since you sent us, while your thousands thronged to cheer And the heart of all the town was in a flame, To the trackless veldt of Africa—the call rang lona
and clear:

" Join the colours, for W 3 need yin!"—and we came. With your blood-red torches flaring in our eyes and on our brains, And your bands, and tNgs, and chorus loud and shrill, We departed, gallant-hearted—it was music in oar

veins, And the sound of it is somehow with us still. ct You have money, for your football, your tobacco* an your beer, And you know the lives of hardship that we led, But we saved an empire for you, and are lying voice' less here—

-- ----- Have you nothing to commemorate your dead? 0, the tortures that we suffered when we left the' crowded streets For the far Tugela river, Spion Kop, and Pieter's. Hill, Where the fierce enteric fever in the erenzied pulses
beats, And the hot mouths of the Mousers haste to kill; 0, the hell of the long waiting; 0, the wounds 3 °LI _ the disease;

0, the silent watches out amid the rain; But we faced the brave old burghers, and brouo them to their knees, And gave Ladysmith to England once again. You have money for your billiards, your cricket, all your. bowls We had biscuit—you are not content with breau ' For the sake of England's honour, and your On immortal souls, Have you nothing to commemorate your dead? Hour by hour, and day by day, and week by week, tlie months went by; 0 We were frozen, we were drenched, and we Wer worn; But we held the flag of England in the darkness fllizig high, And the honour of the town where we were borl.ll, And we faced_ the rolling river, and we climbed tau
fatal hill, , And we followed bold O'Leary to his doom, And were proud to fall beside him, for your cheers were with us still—
Ah, they reach us even here within the tomb! You have money for your horses, your champagne, Oa
your cigars; You have jewels for the ladies whom you wed; e Have you nothing for the "Tomtnies"' who orer
broken rn your wars?
Have you nothing; &;"-co-ni-in—e-morate your dead? And you, whose sons were with us, in the VT°
adjacent towns; You, who swelled the cheers with which we wellt away; You, whose manhood faced the blackest of old fickle'
Fortune's frowns,

And stood by us in the thickest of the Tray: .he Have you no desire to honour us, and keep t memory green Of the grand old " Fighting Fortieth," our 144 ment so true ? • Have you nothing else but cheers to give to those 141°. served the Queen ? Must our dead lips, unregarded, turn to you? You have money for your matches, your NOLttell' and your wine, But our heart's blood in your battles we have s „j We are lying here forgotten, in our graves her" the line : Have you nothing Co commemorate your dead. ARTHUR BENlgErt
Warrington, 11th June, 1904.

STOCKTON HEATH. RUMMAGE SALE.—A rummage sale was held in the church room on Saturday in aid of the parochial funds. There was a large number of stalls, well laden with articles of various kinds, kindly given by the ladies of the parish. The following were in charge :—Mrs.Pigot, Mrs. Picton, Miss Wilson, MiseTurnock, Mrs. Richard- son, Miss Edgeley and Mrs. H. J. Westbrook. The sale was well attended and numerous articles were sold. STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN locie'rv.—By the kind permission of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, about 33 members of the. above society had the pleasure of visiting the grounds, gardens:and greenhouses at Grappenhall Hayes on Tuesday evening last. Under the guidance of the head and assistant gardeners a very minute and critical inspection was made of all to be seen and the members Came away very pleased ,with their visit. Items of special interest were found in some roses (grown out- side at Hereford) which Mrs. Parr was good enough to shew the members, and in a Japanese dwarf tree,brought from Japan by Mr. Roger C. Parr. The members also were particularly struck with the fern grotto which looked beautiful, containing some splendid specimens of various ferns. Mrs. Parr and Miss Parr were present and did everything they could to make the visit enjoy- able. DECAPITATED BY A MOTOR WAGON. Early on Tuesday morning a, motor-wagon, driving a trolley loaded with produce, . was proceeding along King-street, Covent Garden, London, when a respect- ably-dressed unknown man fell between the engine and trolley. He wag decapitated. MEN WITH EYE-GLASSES NOT WANT.ED. The body found in the river at Mahon was identified on Tuesday at the inquest as that of Arthur Anguish (55), of 8, Argyle-avenue, Burmantofts,Leeds. Deceased last had worked at his trade of an iron-turner at Sheffield, but when he went to it he put on his glasses, and then the foreman said : "We don't want men with eye- glasses.here." He was very low spirited because he could get no work. At St. Helens County Police Court on Tuesday the Clerk read resolutions which have been adopted by the magistrates. They required that the system known as the " long pull " must be forthwith discontinued, and also set forth the prices to be paid for beer, porter, Sc., to be consumed on or off the premises.
